Climb to the Crown Dais.
The bridge relay is dark.
You came. Good. I wanted witnesses who had read the vault.
We read it. It said the separation rite was taken away. Not that you get to hand it back to everyone at once.
A century of extraction, and you want to repair it one volunteer at a time.
One volunteer at a time is how you know they're volunteers.
And the ones who die waiting? Do they get a hearing?
They get asked. That is what you are skipping.
Then I will be the one who didn't ask. Someone has to.
Three relay lights kindle around the dais.
Rook goes down on one knee. The dais controls spark and fail. The Golem pulls the last visible coupling.
The visible relays are dark.
Then why is it still climbing?
Rook.
I could not leave it to permission.
Whose permission?
Any of yours.
Under the dais floor, lines the Golem never drew light one after another - the fourth relay, the pasted-over line from the archive diagram.
(Through Raven's throat, a command arrives that is not his own: overwrite the host.)
No.
Was that for him or for me?
For the command.
The common channel - it's giving every node the same order. I can break it. Not stop it. Break it.
The lifts still have power. Move.
Aurex sets both hands on the dais and pulls the channel apart. The order shatters into a thousand small voices. It does not stop.
...It was supposed to be freedom.
It was supposed to be asked.
Soldiers drag Rook toward the lift. Nobody lets go of him, and nobody leaves him behind.
Escape! Reach the evacuation lift at the end of the collapsing aqueduct.
Stone rains down in waves. Wait for the shaking to pass, then run.
The lift cage shudders on its cable. Below the aqueduct, a row of barred cells is filling with dust.
The tenders! Rook chained the relay tenders in the lower cells. When the channel floods, they drown.
How long does the brake hold?
The cable is rated for the cage, not the mountain. A hundred heartbeats. Maybe fewer.
Then five go down and the rest of us hold the cage.
Choose. Now.
Five shapes drop over the rail into the dust and are gone.
We hold this lift as long as the cable lets us. Not one heartbeat less.
Hold the lift for the rescue team. Pull the brake lever only when you must.
The lift cage slams shut. The Golem throws every lever he built into the cable brake.
Holding - holding -
The Conduit gives way beneath Veyr.
Coastlines fracture along old relay faults. Dormant dragon structures rise from the plains and the sea. The Crown's bell rings once, wrong, and every city hears it.
The lift cable snaps. The party scatters into the dark.
Salt water. A fire, somewhere. Someone humming badly.
The cable groans on the drum and settles. It is holding. For now.
(Through Raven's throat:) Five hearts, below. Still climbing. Wait.
The brake! Pull it, or we all go down with them!
Not yet.
A rivet shears from the housing and rings all the way down the shaft.
There is still someone down there. I can feel them climbing.
The cable begins to unravel, one strand at a time.
Wait. Wait for them.
Four tenders. They're light, they're starving, and one of them bit me. Take them.
(Morwen is on the cage. {v:rescue_left} still below.)
Cells are empty. I took the long way back. I always do.
(Vespera is on the cage. {v:rescue_left} still below.)
Unchained eleven. Carried two. Recommend we leave now.
(Golem is on the cage. {v:rescue_left} still below.)
Every road out of there is gone except the one we made. Go.
(Elowen is on the cage. {v:rescue_left} still below.)
Tenders out. No one left in the cells. That's the count.
(Oni is on the cage. {v:rescue_left} still below.)
Got them! All of them! Even the grumpy one. Especially the grumpy one.
(Sak is on the cage. {v:rescue_left} still below.)
An illusion held the door while the real ones ran. The prisoners are out. Mostly real.
(Kitsune is on the cage. {v:rescue_left} still below.)
Order kept. Every prisoner accounted for. Board.
(Archangel is on the cage. {v:rescue_left} still below.)
The last of them leaps the gap as the housing splits. Every one of the five is on the cage.
Now!
The cable brake. One pull and the cage drops.
Not yet.
{v:rescue_left} of them are still down there.
We wait.
I can hold the channel shut a little longer. The cable is another matter.
Whatever you decide, decide it with them in mind. Not with the cable.
They came back for us. Nobody comes back for relay tenders.
The cable lets go. The cage falls into the Conduit with everyone in it.
Raven hauls the brake. The cage drops.
Behind them, the cells vanish under the flood, and whoever was still below goes with them.
...They were so close.
Remember their names. We are not done with them.
Five rescuers, every tender, and the cage still on its cable. For one heartbeat, nobody breathes.
Everyone. You brought everyone.
Elsewhere. Under the roots of the drowned Conduit, a green fire burns.
Something followed me up out of the dark. It's warm. It's in my chest, next to the light I borrowed.
I remember the water closing. Then a voice that wasn't a god's, asking whether I'd finished.
Unit crushed. Unit reassembled. The hands that rebuilt me were not mine and not yours.
The roots found me in the dark, and something older than the roots found them.
I held the door. The door held me. Something on the other side let me walk back through it.
Something clicked me back together. I have a new tail. It's brass. It's great. Don't look at it.
I lied to death. Death didn't care. A dragon's ember did, and it stayed.
My host stopped answering long ago. When I fell, something else did.
The ones who died came back changed. The ones who carried them out cannot walk away from them. The bond pulls like a rope around the heart.
(The Bound are a party of their own, and their formation is fixed. Switch between them and Raven's company from the menu, at a save point or on the world map.)
(The bond will loosen once one of the ancient dragons has fallen.)
The Bound: climb out of the Rootwell and find a way through the ruined world.
The green fire burns without smoke. Sitting close to it, the five hear each other's hearts.
I died, Raven. Down there. A dragon fragment lit in me like a lamp in an empty house. I can't go far from the others - the ones who carried me out. Not yet.
I made it out, Raven. The ones who didn't came back, and I owe them my life. I go where they go - for now.
I drowned in the cells, Raven. Mother Sepulchre's court sent me back because I hadn't finished running. The ones who pulled me out - I'm tied to them now.
I made it out, Raven. The ones who didn't came back, and I owe them my life. I go where they go - for now.
I was broken under the relay. CURATOR's machines in the Deep rebuilt me - better, it says. I disagree. I stay with the four who carried my pieces.
I made it out, Raven. The ones who didn't came back, and I owe them my life. I go where they go - for now.
I was buried, Raven. A dragon's splinter grew through me like a root through stone. The ones who dug me out are my grove now. I have to go back to them.
I made it out, Raven. The ones who didn't came back, and I owe them my life. I go where they go - for now.
I held the cell door until the channel came in. Mother Sepulchre's court sent me back with the door still in my hands. I owe the four who waited for me. I don't leave a debt behind.
I made it out, Raven. The ones who didn't came back, and I owe them my life. I go where they go - for now.
I got squashed, Raven. Properly. One of CURATOR's machines put me back together and forgot to ask what cats are for. The others remembered. I'm staying with them.
I made it out, Raven. The ones who didn't came back, and I owe them my life. I go where they go - for now.
I burned out in the cells, Raven. A dragon's ember took my illusions for a home. I rule nothing now except the four who carried my ashes out. That's enough court for me.
I made it out, Raven. The ones who didn't came back, and I owe them my life. I go where they go - for now.
I fell in the cells, Raven, and Mother Sepulchre's court raised me instead of the sky. I serve the four who waited for me. That is the only order I have left.
I made it out, Raven. The ones who didn't came back, and I owe them my life. I go where they go - for now.
A cot on a floating pontoon. A fire in an iron drum. Someone is humming, badly.
Don't sit up yet. You swallowed half the Ember Sea.
The Ember - what sea?
The one that used to be the middle of the country. Three weeks ago.
The others?
Scattered. I have been having visions - pieces of them. They are not reliable. I am not reliable right now either.
So we do the reliable things first. Eat. Help. Listen.
Mara Pell. Brackenford, until the river moved. Now I run a floating town, apparently.
You can pay for your cot the way everyone does. The lamps need fuel carried, and the east walkway's broken.
Help at Hearthward: carry lamp fuel for the keeper, fix the broken walkway, and ask about the others.
The lamp keeper needs fuel from the plank pile crates. And the east walkway is out.
Fuel cans and planks. Take what you can carry. Everyone carries something here.
(You pick up two cans of lamp fuel and a length of plank.)
Lamps first, then planks. Keeper's by the hearth.
Fuel! Bless you. The night lamps go on the outer pontoons so the fishing skiffs can find home.
You've got a plank, too. The east walkway broke yesterday. There's a family stuck on the far pontoon.
Sit with Aurex by the hearth.
The lamps are low. There's fuel in the crates by the plank pile - if you can carry some over, the skiffs will thank you.
Lamps are lit. Nobody's lost on the water tonight.
We're fine! We just can't get across. Somebody said there were planks.
Thank you. The kids were starting to think this pontoon was a new country.
Raven lays the plank across the gap and Aurex lashes it down. It isn't pretty. It holds.
Oh thank goodness. Come on, kids - dry land. Well. Dry pontoon.
Walkway fixed. Carry the lamp fuel to the keeper by the hearth.
Sit with Aurex by the hearth.
A gap in the walkway. You'd need a plank - there's a pile by the cots.
The patched walkway creaks, but holds.
Fish broth. Every day. Tomorrow I'm told there may be a potato.
The old woman in the corner cot keeps asking for her husband by his quarry number. I keep answering with his name.
Cots, blankets, a fire. That's the whole inn. Nobody's charged; everyone helps.
A salvage chest. Things found floating, washed up, or dragged out of the sealed ruins are brought here for their owners.
(The chest is empty for now.)
The lamps are lit. The walkway holds. Aurex and Raven sit by the hearth drum.
Would the world be safer without me in it? Without - us.
No. I refuse the premise. Your body is not a public utility, Raven. Not the ministry's, not Rook's, not the world's.
I heard them. During the activation. Other fragments, taking their hosts' voices. Some hosts let them. Some did not get the choice.
Then we free both. The fragments and the hosts. Without making either of them disposable.
Both.
News, since you're awake. A signal flare's been going up over the flooded Rootward every dusk. Three green, one red. Old guide code.
Elowen.
Brackenford's west of here along the pontoon road. Rootward's north of it, where the forest used to be dry.
And take the supplies in the hearth chest. You two can't fight the whole sea with borrowed spoons.
Follow Elowen's signal flares to the flooded Rootward (north-west, past Brackenford).
Brackenford's bakery is a footbridge depot now. Mara says the bunkhouse became a shelter.
Help first, then talk. That's how Hearthward works.
Every tent that becomes a cabin, somebody argues about which one gets the roof first. Good. Arguing means we expect to still be here.
The Ash Accord. I never thought I'd see ministry clerks and quarry crews sign the same page.
People bring the signs from their old shops. Not the palace banners - the bakeries, the cobblers, the laundries.
Nobody fished out a throne. Nobody wanted to.
Roofs first! The rain's coming.
Water first! You can't drink a roof.
...Fine. Water tanks, then roofs.
And we write it down, so we don't have this argument again tomorrow.
The bell rang wrong. Everyone says so. I think it rang right and everything else went wrong.
Fuel for the lamps is in the crates by the plank pile at the hearth.
Lamps stay lit every night now. We rotate who carries.
Ponton market. Whatever floats, whatever's found, whatever's traded.
Ferry to the Glass Coast? Hull's cracked. When someone clears the Rootward current, I'll have my caulk back.

options.text: Take the repaired ferry east to Bellharbor

cmds.text: The ferry creeps across the Ember Sea, past dragon spines rising from the water, to what's left of Bellharbor's upper town.
Empty berth. The Rune Golem had plans for a ship here - a rescue ship. Heard he's in Cinderwake, if anyone's alive there.
Wayfarer. Slowest ship I ever saw. Also the only one.
Wayfarer's tender runs from the end of the berth. Step on and we'll row you up.
A camp on the high roots. Tarps, a cook fire, and forty people who have been waiting for the water to decide something.
Raven? Aurex. You're alive. Good. Don't touch the map.
Hello to you too.
There are three crossings north of here. Two of them drown people. One doesn't. I know which. So I lead every group across myself.
How many trips a day?
As many as it takes.
Which is why half of them are still here after two weeks. Nobody can wait for one guide forever, Elowen.
If I hand out the map and somebody takes the wrong crossing -
Then we make every crossing the right one.
...The current's being pushed south by something in the old sluice. If the sluice lets go, the water drops. The walkways can be raised with the levers - if you know which way they lift.
Raise all three walkways in the Three Crossings (north), then find what is diverting the current.
Who's that? Oh - it's you.
Three levers, three walkways. Up is up - don't overthink it. The thing in the sluice is another story.
She's been carrying the whole camp on one map. Let's give her arms a rest.
Elowen says the forest used to be dry. I don't believe her. Trees can't live without swimming.
My hip won't take the ford twice. I'll go once, on a proper walkway, or not at all.
The west lever lifts. A walkway rises dripping out of the flood, planks still marked with old guild paint.
The west walkway is raised.
The middle lever groans. The centre walkway surfaces, green with weed.
The middle walkway is raised.
The east lever snaps up. The last walkway rises, and for a moment the whole pool is quiet.
The east walkway is raised.
(The current still tugs at the lowered crossings.)
All three crossings are up. Follow the current north to the old sluice.
The old sluice. A shape of bark and silt and drowned iron is holding the gate shut with its whole body, forcing the river south over the camp.
It thinks it's holding back the flood. It is the flood.
The Warden turns. Water surges toward the front row.
The Warden sinks, and the sluice gate swings free. The water level drops a hand's width, then another.
You did it. The current's falling.
Now the map.
...There's only one. It took me four years.
Then it's the most valuable thing in the camp, and it belongs to the camp.
If someone reads it wrong -
Then they ask someone who read it right. That is how maps work when more than one person owns them.
Fine. We make copies. One per family. Warnings in the margins. Names of who keeps each crossing.
It's a start. Not a finish. I'm not done paying for what I sold, back before any of this.
Come with us?
Someone's got to find Morwen. She never could read a map.
Brackenford's new crossings are open. Take the repaired ferry from Hearthward east to Bellharbor to find Morwen.
Hearthward's ferryman has his caulk back. The ferry to the Glass Coast runs again.
I split my days between here and Hearthward. We count the shelter by name every night - that part I won't hand to anyone.
New crossings, copies of Elowen's map on every door. Brackenford's two halves talk again.
The bunkhouse is a shelter now. Forty cots. The forewoman counts us by name every night. Nobody's a number in here.
A cot and a bowl. Nobody's charged.
The bakery's a footbridge depot. Bread in the morning, planks in the afternoon, and I still burn the rye.
The west camp wants the road to the mill first. The east camp wants the road to the clinic. We'll see.
Clinic road first. Grain's no good to a man with a fever.
I kept extending credit after the quarry stopped paying. Now there's no quarry and no pay. I'm still extending it. Somebody has to believe in tomorrow.
Salvage crew. Anything we pull out of the sealed ruins goes to Hearthward's salvage chest - with the owner's name, if we can find it.
The upper gallery of the old archive annex. The roof sags over a shelter of families - held up by a lattice of white light.
Beneath it, standing in knee-deep water, Morwen. Her hands are raised. They are shaking.
Morwen!
Don't come under the edge. The roof goes when I stop.
She's been holding it for three days. We bring her water. She won't sit.
Then we get everyone out from under it first. The walkway above - is it passable?
Bales came down across it in the first quake. There are winches, but nobody's had the hands.
Clear the upper walkway with the two winches (west side passage), then lead the three families out along it.
Not yet. There are still people under here. Don't ask me to stop.
...Is that everyone?
Kids are ringing the alarm with a cooking pot since the ministry took the bells. Loudest thing in town.
The winch creaks. The first mass of rope-bales lifts off the walkway and swings clear.
The west winch is holding the bales clear.
The second winch lifts the last bales. The walkway runs clear to the east stair.
The east winch is holding the bales clear.
The walkway's blocked. We tried. We'll wait for the young woman to finish whatever she's doing.
Up the gap and along the walkway? At my age? ...Yes. Yes, all right. Take my arm.
We can't go through the water - my son can't swim. And the walkway's full of bales.
The walkway's clear? Then we're going. Thank you. Thank her.
I'm not scared. I'm waiting. It's different.
Is the lady going to be okay? ...Okay. I'll go if you count me.
One. There. You are counted.
(Some families are still under the roof.)
Everyone is out along the walkway. Go to Morwen.
The roof goes when I stop.
Nobody is under it now.
There could be -
We counted them. Twice.
Let it go.
I do not know what happens after.
We light the lamps.
Morwen lowers her hands. The lattice goes out. The roof comes down into empty water with a long, tired sound.
Darkness. Then, one by one along the walkway, ordinary lanterns - held by the families she was protecting.
They did that. Not me.
You can sit down now, Morwen.
I can sit down.
The Golem. We have to find the Golem. I want to see a machine that runs without someone pretending to be its fuel.
Travel to Cinderwake (north-west, beyond Rootward) and find the Golem.
Cinderwake crews are rotating heat between workshops with waterwheels. Someone says the Golem is in the old assembly yard.
Morwen's in the upper gallery. She won't let go of the roof. Please - she'll listen to you before she listens to me.
The lower streets are gone, but the ropewalks make good roads. We're painting names on every door that has someone behind it.
Sak - if you see him - tell him I have people who need their names fixed. The right way this time.
CLANG! That's the alarm. They took the bells so I use the pot. CLANG! That one was for practice.
The tide chapel is an evacuation station now. We ring for boats, not for prayers. Both get answered about as often.
Charts! Old charts, useless. New charts, useful but wrong. Buy both and average them.
The ropewalks were for making rope. Now they're the only roads above water. Rope's still useful, mind.
Manifests used to list refugees as 'cargo'. Now we list cargo as 'refugees' so nobody steals it. Joke. Mostly.
Hammocks in the chapel loft. Free for anyone who pulls a shift on the pumps. You look like you'd pull a shift.
The old assembly yard. On the slipway lies a hull - broad, ugly, bolted rather than grown. The Golem is under it with a lamp.
Morwen. Elowen. Raven. Aurex. ...You're here. You're here and I'm leaking oil everywhere.
You found a ship.
I found a ship nobody finished. Rescue vessel, drafted before heartglass made everything 'efficient'. Steam and gears. Heavy. Slow.
Her name's Lanternwake. The engine works. I've tested every part twice. It just needs the cooling channels powered and room to fit the stabilisers.
And?
And the hull twists on the slipway. Nothing I've got is heavy enough to hold her straight while we bolt the keel.
Power the three cooling channels (valves on the north wall), then help the crews clear the assembly space.
Three valves on the north wall. The channels have to run cold before the engine can breathe.
Channels are cold! Now the crews can shift the scrap - talk to the crew chief.
Space is clear. Now all we need is something that can hold a ship straight. Something very heavy and very patient.
The west valve opens. Water hisses into the channel; the pipe frosts white.
The west channel runs cold.
The middle valve opens with a shudder. The channel under the slipway starts to sing.
The middle channel runs cold.
The east valve opens. Steam coils out of the vents and thins to nothing.
The east channel runs cold.
The channels are cold. Talk to the crew chief about clearing the assembly space.
Channels are running cold - we can work the yard now. Scrap on both sides, and a few rust-crawlers nesting in it.
You handle the crawlers, we handle the scrap. Deal?
The crews haul, stack and sort for an hour. The assembly space opens up around the hull.
Space is clear. Now - what's that at the east end? It wasn't there this morning.
Something very large is waiting at the east end of the slipway.
A tortoise the size of a cottage, its shell plated like a boiler. It has been watching the hull for some time.
I held up this yard's roof in the old days. Under orders. They called me a foundation.
Nobody has ordered me since the bell. So I came to see whether anyone would ask.
...Would you hold the hull straight while we bolt the keel? You can stop whenever you like. We'll brace it with jacks as we go, so it doesn't depend on you.
You asked. And you built it so it does not need me.
Then I will help. And afterward I will go where I like - which is, I think, with you.
The Iron Tortoise leans its shell against the hull. The crews bolt the keel in one long afternoon, jacks going in behind every bolt.
...Now the manual. Pell's going to ask.
Golem. Before you take her anywhere. The manual.
It's in my head.
That's the problem. Write it down. All of it. Every valve, every spare, every noise she makes when she's sick.
That's weeks of work -
Then we'll wait weeks. I'm not watching another machine that only works when one engineer stands beside it.
...You're right. You were right about the wheel, too.
The Golem writes for three days. Morwen checks every page. The crews read it aloud and argue with it, and the Golem changes it where they're right.
The manual lies on the workshop bench, heavy and dog-eared. Anyone can pick it up.
A workbench covered in the Golem's calculations. Very little of it is legible to anyone but the Golem.
The workbench, waiting for a manual.
The Lanternwake manual, dog-eared, with a pencil tied to it on a string. The newest note, in a crew hand: 'Page 12 is wrong. Fixed.'
Launch morning. The crews take their places - not the Golem. The Golem stands at the back, plated hands folded, runes dimmed.
Page one. Cooling channels open.
Open.
Page two. Boiler to working pressure. Slow.
Slow. Holding.
Page three. Release the slipway brakes.
Lanternwake slides down the slipway and lifts, heavy and steady, into the smoky sky over Cinderwake.
...I didn't touch anything.
You wrote it down. That's touching everything.
Lanternwake waits at Hearthward's berth. Find Vespera (High Aerie), Sak (Veyr) and Oni (Whitebone) - in any order.
High Aerie's broken chain now links two new islands. A cliff settlement there is evacuating.
Veyr's throne square is a distribution point. Someone is guarding the lower registry from Voss's remnants.
Whitebone's old cells are a sanctuary now. People with bindings nobody can safely remove shelter there.
Power fails in patches now. We rotate heat workshop by workshop. The clinic never goes cold - that's the one rule.
The Golem's in the old assembly yard east of here. He says he found a ship. He also says he's fine. He's lying about one of those.
The manual's on every bench in town now. People argue with it in the margins. That's how you know it's alive.
Heat rota: canteen at dawn, clinic always, workshops by turn. We post it on the wall under the injury tally.
The clinic's warm. That was the question you all asked, back when. Here's the answer: we share.
The tally wall. We kept counting after the bell. Fewer marks since the regulators went dark. Make of that what you like.
The pipes don't sing anymore. The waterwheels squeak instead. I like the squeak better.
Waterwheels at every terrace. Slower than the regulators. Nobody's inside them.
Shift stew. Same as ever. Except now there's a waterwheel keeping it warm instead of a - well. You know.
Cots by the canteen stove. Take a shift on the wheels if you want. Or don't. Rest.
The Skyspine chain has snapped. What's left of it links two new islands - and between them hangs a mooring, groaning, holding a cargo platform full of evacuees from the cliff settlement.
You're Vespera's lot. She's on the mooring lever. She's been on it all night.
Her plan is to cut herself loose with the load if it slips. Take the platform down with her, drop the weight, save the rest.
That's not a plan. That's a eulogy.
There are three ballast anchors - one on the settlement, one on the old anchor rock, one on the mooring island itself. Set all three and the mooring holds without anyone on it.
My crew can't cross the gust lanes carrying the ballast. Can you?
Set all three ballast anchors (north-west rock, settlement, mooring island). Cross the gust lanes between gusts.
Wind's the same as it ever was. Pennants lift, then the gust. You'll learn it in three crossings or you'll learn it in six.
We're waiting for the platform. Nobody's going to jump. Captain Hale said so.
Three anchors. You can't count on her counting them for you.
All three are set. Go and talk to my sister.
The ballast drops into the old anchor socket with a boom that rolls across the gap. The mooring line stops shivering quite so hard.
The north-west anchor is set.
The settlement anchor bites into the cliff. The evacuees cheer, then look embarrassed about cheering.
The settlement anchor is set.
The mooring island anchor clamps home. The platform steadies on its line.
The mooring anchor is set.
(The mooring still leans on the lever. Set the remaining anchors.)
All three anchors are set. Talk to Vespera at the mooring lever.
You came. Don't {m:fucking |}distract me. If this slips I've got about a second to cut.
The line's steady.
Three anchors are holding it. You can let go of the lever.
If I let go and I'm wrong -
Then the anchors are wrong, and we'll all be wrong together. Step away, Vespera.
Vespera takes her hands off the lever. One finger at a time. The mooring holds.
The platform comes across, and the evacuees walk off it onto solid rock.
I'm not putting your name on the memorial.
I didn't -
I'm putting it on the rescue roster. Tuesday shift. Don't be late.
...Tuesday.
I've already forged you a very convincing shift badge. Joke. Mostly.
Rescue roster. Write your own name on it. Nobody else should.
Vespera is back. Skyspine's anchor is ready for the release protocol.
My sister's on the mooring at the broken chain, south of here. Please bring her back with her hands empty.
Tuesday shift. She was early.
Windmills now instead of the hanging engines. They turn slower. They also don't scream.
Every windmill has a crew name painted on its vane. That was the kid's idea.
I'm going to fly rescue baskets and come home for supper. Every day. That's the plan.
Cable court traders. Half the cables are gone, so we're 'court traders' now.
I came down on a rescue basket last winter. The pilot's not on any wall. I want her to be.
Returners' hall. There's always room.
A clean stretch of stone beside the memorial, waiting for something.
The Returners' Wall. Names of people who brought others home - pilots, basket crews, a cook who ran soup across the span in a gale. And an incident archive, open to anyone.
(Still missing: Vespera, at the broken Skyspine chain.)
(Still missing: Sak, under Veyr's registry.)
(Still missing: Oni, at the Whitebone sanctuary.)
Everyone is together again. Take the evidence to Nacre's assembly for the Ash Accord.
Nacre is gathering every town's delegates by the listening pool.
You came through Bellharbor? Then you know I've been trying to reach Sak. He's under the square, in the lower registry.
Voss's remnants want the ledgers - the ones that prove what they did. Sak won't let them near. He won't let anyone near, including the people whose names are in there.
The canals changed when the walls fell. The ladder by the south of the square goes down; the lock gates raise the crossings.
Reach the lower registry through Veyr's changed canals (ladder, south of the square).
Go on. I'll bring the satchel when it's time.
The west lock gate rises. Water drops in the west channel, and a crossing shoulders up out of it.
The west crossing is up.
The middle gate grinds open. The centre crossing surfaces, streaming.
The middle crossing is up.
The east gate lifts. The last crossing rises toward the registry stair.
The east crossing is up.
Uniforms at the registry door, stripped of rank but not of habit. Voss's remnants.
The ledgers are ministry property. Stand aside{m:, you bastards|}.
The ministry sank. The names didn't.
The remnants scatter back into the canals. Behind a barricade of filing cabinets, someone coughs.
Don't - oh. Oh, it's you. It's actually you.
And Vespera! Alive! Nobody told me you could survive falling off a sky.
I've been guarding the originals. Every forged pass I ever made is in here, next to the real name it replaced.
If the remnants get these, they burn them. If the refugees get them, they - I don't know what they'll do. That's what scares me.
That's not yours to decide, Sak.
I made the forgeries. Doesn't that make it mine to fix?
It makes it yours to answer for. Not to decide.
Bring the original ledgers to the residents at the tables and let them choose how their names are recorded.
New seal, blank forms, no forgeries. It's a very boring satchel now. I love it.
The original ledgers, stacked on the tables. Sak hovers.
This one's mine. Page forty. That's the name the ministry gave me when they sold my contract.
And here's the name my mother gave me. Different page.
I can write whichever you -
No. We decide how it's written. You can hold the ink.
The residents take the ledgers one page at a time. Some keep the old names. Some write new ones. Each entry is signed by the person it belongs to.
Sak.
Jori sets a worn leather satchel on the table - the one Sak used to carry false papers.
It's got blank forms in it now. And a proper seal, issued by the refugee assembly. It's yours, if you'll carry it.
...I'm not forgiven.
No. You're employed.
That's better. That's so much better.
You and I signed the same kind of papers, Sak. Different hands. Same ink.
...Then we both keep better ones now.
Sak is back. Veyr's distribution point is open.
The ledgers are behind the barricade. Someone is guarding them.
The ledgers, every entry signed by the person it names.
We've been waiting for our own names. Not for someone to hand them to us.
Page forty. My name. My handwriting. Nobody else's.
Registry's open for amendments. Every change is signed by the one who asked for it.
Clerk Ansel. I refused false death certificates back when it could get me hanged. Now I sign ration chits. Better job.
Do you think our families can eat {m:your fucking |}loyalty?
Not anymore. They can eat the rations, though. So we hand out rations.
Distribution point. One line, no ranks. You'd be amazed how much faster it goes without ranks.
The throne used to be right there. Now it's a soup table. Nobody misses the throne.
South market, moved north because the south is underwater. Same prices. Mostly.
Barracks cots. Ex-barracks. Ex-cots, some of them, but they hold.
Whitebone's snow gate. The redoubt's cells are a sanctuary now - doors propped open, blankets on the bunks. Except three.
Oni?
Here. Don't come in with weapons out. Some of them flinch.
Three people still wear bindings I wrote. I can't take them off alone. If I get the key wrong, the seal repeats its command. I won't risk that on someone else's body.
I've already sent my name and testimony to Nacre. Whatever they decide, I'll answer it. But first - these three.
Open the three sealed cells one by one. Ask each person for their own consent key, then use it at their lock.
The sanctuary keeps no records of who is 'guilty'. Only who needs a blanket.
You're with him? ...I'll watch. That's all.
Ask them. Not me. I only know the command I wrote. They know who they are.
That's all three. I - thank you. No. That's not for me to say.
You want my key? It was a number, once. Warrant 4-11.
...My name is Hesk. That's the key. Hesk. Say it right.
Hesk. Go on. The lock's outside.
Seventy years I've had this seal. I'm not sure I remember my own name.
Then choose one. It doesn't have to be old to be yours.
...Wren. Old woman, new name. Wren.
Wren. I like how it sounds in someone else's mouth when they ask.
I don't want it off yet.
Then it stays on until you do.
...That's the first time anyone's said that. All right. Now. Key's 'Tamsin'. Now.
Tamsin. Quickly, before I change my mind. Or don't - I'm allowed to change it.
The seal hears 'Hesk', spoken the way he asked, and lets go. The cell door swings wide.
The lock waits for a key. Only the person inside can give it.
The cell is open.
'Wren.' The seal hesitates, as if surprised to hear a name it has never known, then releases.
The lock waits for a key. Only the person inside can give it.
The cell is open.
'Tamsin.' The binding unwinds. The door opens. Tamsin stays inside for a moment, then walks out on her own.
The lock waits for a key. Only the person inside can give it.
The cell is open.
All three cells are open. Walk Oni out to the sanctuary exit.
You wrote my number.
Yes.
You remember it.
Yes.
Do you know my name?
Not yet.
Then start there.
May I write it down?
...Ilse. With an s.
Oni writes it. The survivor watches him do it, and does not say thank you, and walks away.
Before I go back to Nacre for the hearing - Voss's network. If there's any way to stop it from compelling anyone again, I want to help.
The survivors decide that.
In the sanctuary hall, the survivors talk it over without him. They come back with a single page: a limited agreement. He may help. They keep a copy of his account.
You let someone else hold the lever. Took me years to learn that.
Blank forms and a proper seal. Welcome to paperwork that doesn't hurt anyone.
Oni is back, under the survivors' agreement.

Nacre's assembly benches, set in a ring around the listening pool. Delegates from Hearthward, Brackenford, Cinderwake, Bellharbor, High Aerie, Veyr and Whitebone. Nobody sits at the head. There isn't one.
We are here to compare what worked. Not what was promised. What worked.
The trial relay at Nacre. Distributed load - the wheel, the cable, the pool. It still runs. Here's the circuit, drawn for anyone to build.
And the consent check. Asked, not assumed; answered, not signed over; revisable, at any time.
Skyspine's mooring anchors hold without anyone on the lever. That's an anchor for the release.
Veyr's registry records who wrote every name. That's an anchor too. Paper, but still.
Whitebone's cells opened on keys their occupants chose. The seals remember. That can be taught.
And every crossing in the Rootward has a named keeper. Nobody carries a whole map alone anymore.
Cinderwake's heat comes from waterwheels and a rota. We've already solved it, you see. Region by region. We don't need a new crown. We need everyone's pieces at once.
Then there is one thing missing: how the activation route actually runs. Who knows it?
Soldiers from three towns bring Rook in. His hands are bound in ordinary rope. He is thinner.
I do.
The hidden route. The fourth relay. Everything I pasted over in the archive diagrams. Here.
I imposed freedom as a command. I told myself it was different from what the ministry did. It was the same shape.
You want forgiveness?
I want to answer for it. After this is done. Not instead.
Then the assembly records it. Extraction was a harm. The forced awakening was a harm. Both require accountability. Neither cancels the other.
The record is written in many hands. Rook signs where he is told to sign, and nowhere else. The soldiers take him to wait for his hearing.
Voss is in the Crown Heart. What is left of him. He has fused himself to the vessel at the centre of the Ember Sea, and he is still trying to make every fragment obey.
Then we go there with everyone's pieces.
The Ash Accord is signed. When you're ready, fly Lanternwake to the Crown Heart in the middle of the Ember Sea.
The Lanternwake crew room has a board of leads - personal matters for each of you, and four strange ones besides. None of them has to be done first.
The pool projects conflicting memories now - dragon and human, overlapping. We set up a listening house. Nobody has to listen alone, or at all.
When your whole crew is together again, come to the assembly benches south of the pool.
You're all here. The assembly is waiting on the benches south of the pool.
Heavier than it was. That's how you know.
The pool showed us the same morning again. I saw a wedding. She saw a funeral. We still argue. We still come every week.
We haven't agreed once. It's the best thing we do together.
Still watering. Still don't know if the plants are sacred. Still don't think it matters.
Salt, jars, remedies. The cloth-lined jars are back in fashion. Everything old is useful again.
The listening house has one rule: you may stop listening at any time. People keep coming back anyway.
The listening house has beds. Quiet after the second bell.
Lanternwake ties up at the Crown Heart - a rib of dragon bone and relay glass rising out of the Ember Sea.
Two lungs. West runs the physical pressure; east runs the name-binding circuit. The locks alternate - west, east, west, east.
Two teams, then. Four and four. Neither team can finish alone and neither can shut the other in.
The swap bells in each lung pass control between the teams whenever you like.
(This is the Accord Dock. You can still leave: Lanternwake is moored behind you. Past the Concord Bridge, the Crown Vessel.)
(A protected backup has been written: "Before the Final Descent". It is kept separate from your slots and from any clear save.)
When ready, use the split lever on the dock to divide into two teams.
Lanternwake's moored and not going anywhere without you. Rest, restock, come back whenever.
Two teams of five. Same stores, same growth, same recovery point here. Anyone left over holds the recovery point.
(Team A takes the west lung; Team B the east. West first.)
Team A: release the first west lock. Then ring the swap bell to hand over to Team B.
The swap bell. Its note carries through the bone to the other lung.
The swap bell. Its note carries through the bone to the other lung.
The first west lock releases with a gasp of pressure. Across the Heart, something in the east lung unclamps.
West lock 1 released. Ring the swap bell - Team B's first lock is free.
The first west lock is open.
The first east lock unbinds a ring of names from the circuit. They drift up like sparks. The west lung's second lock unclamps.
East lock 1 released. Swap to Team A for the second west lock.
The lock is held by the west lung's pressure. Team A has to release theirs first.
The first east lock is open.
The second west lock opens. The pressure in the Heart drops to a long, slow exhale.
West lock 2 released. Swap to Team B for the last east lock.
This lock is still bound by the east circuit. Team B has to release their first lock.
The second west lock is open.
The last east lock falls open. Both lungs breathe out together. The Concord Bridge unfolds from the dock.
Both lungs are open. Meet on the Concord Bridge (north of the dock).
This lock is still held by the west pressure. Team A has one more lock.
The last east lock is open.
The two teams meet in the middle of the Concord Bridge.
Nobody fell.
Nobody forged anything. I checked.
Everyone's tired. That's allowed.
(Rest at the lamp and choose the four who will face the Crown Vessel. The others will hold the release anchors from the bridge.)
Cross the Concord Bridge north to the Crown Vessel.
The Crown Vessel: a heart of relay glass the size of a chapel, with a man's shape half-sunk in its surface.
Order. You broke it. I am putting it back. Every fragment, every host, one voice.
You don't have a voice anymore, Voss. You have a command.
It is the same thing.
It never was.
Behind the party, on the bridge, the others take up the release anchors. Across the Ember Sea, the towns begin the procedure at the same moment.
The Vessel cracks from the inside. Voss's shape comes loose from the glass - a tired old man in a torn uniform, gasping.
...They will not obey anyone now.
That was the point.
Soldiers from the accord take Voss down to the boats. He will be heard, too.
Step out into the Open Sky.
The Open Sky. The last of the network drifts away as ordinary light. There are no chains in it.
Something like a door stands open beside Raven - a form of light and scale, restored and waiting.
The way is open.
I know.
You are not going to ask me to stay.
Would that make it easier?
No.
Then I will ask whether you wish to.
For now.
And when that changes?
We speak again.
The binding pattern on Raven's hands fades. What is left is a promise, not a lock - one either of them can end.
Hearthward, some weeks later.
Records are open. Engines run on waterwheels and wind. The rescue routes have names on them. It isn't finished.
It's started. That's what you get.
At the market wall, the quarry workers' names are carved where their numbers were. Mara chose the inscription.
Rook's hearing is held in the open, on the pontoons. Oni appears before the Whitebone survivors, as promised. Nobody is paraded. Everybody is heard.
Families light a lamp for each person lost. The lamps are not counted against anyone.
Walk Hearthward. When you're ready, go to the communal hearth.
By the hearth, the crew talk about what comes next.
I'm going to teach. Short lessons. Nobody faints.
The public workshop opens tomorrow. The apprentice's name goes above the door. Mine goes under it.
Rescue roster. Tuesdays. Some Thursdays.
The Returners' Wall has forty names now. Mine isn't one of them. That's how I like it.
Lanternwake needs maintenance. So does everything else. Good.
Every town has the notes now. Somebody in Bellharbor already improved the boiler. Didn't ask me. Perfect.
I'm drawing maps for anyone who asks. With the other guides' names on them.
Every public map has warnings, detours, and who to blame. I'm on three of them. Deservedly.
Ordinary medicine. Slow, useful, asked for.
The sanctuary asks first now. Always. My mistake is in the public record, where it belongs.
The hearing continues. I go back every month.
They asked me a question at the hearing. I answered it without qualification. The hearing continues.
Blank forms, proper seal. Very boring. Very good.
The registry takes amendments now, and records who made each one. Including mine.
The court has a regent and a mirror nobody is ordered to look into. I visit. I leave before the bowing starts.
I'm going east for a while. Someone has to teach foxes to tell the truth. I've started with myself.
The host still doesn't answer. I've stopped waiting at the gate. I patrol the harbour instead.
I gave my host its last order back. It's in the archive now, filed under 'kept'. I keep new ones.
The ledger is shorter every month. I read the names I've freed out loud, so they hear it.
The Warden's ledger is closed. I carry people now. Upward, only upward.
Every cook on the pontoons can brew the cure. I'm down to one patient: me. I'm doing fine.
Idony runs the physic house. She corrects my dosages. Loudly. I've never been happier to be wrong.
My court is thawing, one throne at a time. It is slow. I have time.
The court came home from the Deep. We held a funeral for the mourning. It was very short.
I read the March's names every evening. The graveyards are shorter than the list. Good.
The First Crown sleeps. I gave its sword back to the tomb. I kept the names.
The dead in the crypts are resting now. The living hold the doors. It works.
My teacher's gate is shut, and Sorrow has gone home. So have I, mostly.
My standing orders still exist. I've filed them under 'history'. It's the first order I've given myself.
CURATOR's codes are in the public archive. Anyone can cancel an order now. I checked. Twice.
The roads I patrol are real again. Some of them. I ride the rest anyway.
The highway has a name now, and traffic. I hate the traffic. I love the traffic.
On the Conduit lift housing, five rescuers' names are carved above the tenders'. The tenders did the carving.
The ones who came back changed sit a little apart at the fire, and are never alone there.
I don't sleep. I keep watch. Somebody should, and I'm good at it now.
CURATOR's joints are better than mine were. I have repainted them anyway. They are mine now.
The fragment keeps my lamp lit. I asked it once whose light it was. It said: ours.
And me?
And us.
Raven unpins the old Crown service badge from his coat and leaves it at the public memorial, among the lamps. Then he signs up for a maintenance shift aboard Lanternwake.
Dawn over the rebuilt harbor.
Lanternwake is waiting at the berth.
On the way to the berth, a lamp flickers out.
Lamp three is out.
The spare is under the bench.
Do you need -
No. Thank you.
The workers replace the part. The lamp comes back on.
That sound.
The morning bell.
A door opening.
Both, then.
Step aboard Lanternwake.
Raven steps aboard Lanternwake.
Morning. Mind the ladder.
Veyr's south gate. A queue of carts, a clerk with a ledger. The quarry lies behind you, and your report isn't written yet.
Brackenford first. The workers, then the capital.
The Rootward forest, north of the capital. Ministry foresters wave travellers away: 'Sluice works. Closed.'
The northern road into Cinder Reach. A ministry barricade blocks the pass, and the foresters say the only way around it runs through the Rootward.
The coast road to Bellharbor. A checkpoint turns back anyone without a harbour pass - and the party is wanted.
The Drowned Archive sits on its tide island. Without someone who knows the tide tables, the causeway is a good way to drown.
The foot of the Skychain Viaduct. The span is closed: 'Anchors failed. No crossings.' The ferry north is the only way to the cable foot.
High Aerie is on the far side of the chasm. With the Skychain closed, there's no way across.
Whitebone Redoubt's outer patrols turn you back long before the white gate. Not yet.
The salt road to Nacre runs through redoubt patrols from Whitebone. Without a way across the chasm, it's a long walk into their arms.
The vault road. Redoubt soldiers still hold the approach.
The old aqueduct entrance under Veyr. Barred, and humming faintly. Not yet.
At the grove's edge a shaggy brackhorn noses at Elowen's pack, saddle and all.
This is Bramble. She carried grove supplies before the grove burned. She'll carry us now.
Brackhorns don't spook. Wolves take one look at those horns and find other roads.
(The Brackhorn carries the party on the world map: faster, and no monsters give chase. Settings: Ride Brackhorn.)
On the High Landing's last anchor stands a figure in white-gold armour, wings folded, sword point-down in the rock.
Travellers. My host was ordered to hold this sky road. The host stopped answering thirty years ago.
I held it anyway. Today a maintenance crew held it better than I did, and nobody had to fall.
You watched the whole crossing?
I judged it. I was wrong about what it needed. I would like to learn how you knew.
Walk with us, then. You can judge by what you see.
(The Archangel Commander's Judgment techniques punish enemies that strike his allies.)
When the hearing ends, a woman in crimson silk rises from the back bench. Nine pale tails fan out behind her, then fade.
I sat through the whole hearing as an old archivist. Nobody asked me who I was. Nobody told me what to want.
The fox court exiled me for ruling through illusions. They were right. I would like to try the other way.
She's been our guest for a year. She pays in stories.
What do you want from us?
To be seen as I am, by people who have no reason to flatter me. You seem ideal.
(The Crimson Kitsune Empress's Foxfire techniques confuse and blind.)
Back at Nacre's landing field, High Aerie's crew has lashed a patched envelope over an old basin barge.
The Accord's thank-you. She's slow, she leaks, and she flies. We call her the Wayfarer.
I rebuilt the burner from spare cable parts. Please don't dive in her.
(The Wayfarer waits on Nacre's landing field. Step onto her to take the helm; land on marked fields by towns and ruins.)
Moored on the dais terrace, the Wayfarer tears loose from her ropes and falls with the stone.
A tall figure in a beaked mask moves between the cots, pouring something bitter into every cup.
Sit still. You've swallowed half the Ember Sea. This will make you hate me for an hour.
You're a plague doctor. The ministry used your order to carry sickness into the quarry towns.
I was sent to carry it. I carried the cure instead, and taught the cooks to brew it. Now nobody needs me here.
We will. Somewhere past this harbour.
Then I'll come. And I'll teach you to do it without me.
(Corvus, Harbinger of Pestilence, heals with Physic - and turns sickness back on the enemy.)
Where the Warden sank, a woman in blackened wings wades out of the current, dragging a raft of survivors behind her.
These twelve were marked for the abyss. I was sent to carry them down. I carried them up instead.
The bargains I enforced still have names on them. I mean to undo them, one name at a time.
Twelve is a start.
Then let me start with you. Your road is going where the bargains were made.
(Inferna, Abyssal Valkyrie, trades her own health for Hellbrand's fire.)
A familiar shape glides down onto the rescue platform, wings scorched but whole.
I held the cable towers through the fall. No order told me to. I judged they needed holding.
Among the survivors, an old woman smiles and becomes a fox-eared empress in crimson.
I've been hiding as a grandmother. They fed me far too much. Take me with you, please.
I keep names. Proper ones, chosen ones, the ones you'd rather be called.
Whose name shall I change?
Written down. Nobody gets to take it back but them.
Beneath the thawed cradle, a throne of rime. A crowned skeleton in frost-white robes turns its head.
The lantern is out. My sleepers wake. You have ended a winter I kept for three hundred years.
My people died of cold long before the Crown. I kept their dead because I could not bear an empty court.
Show me the living are worth letting them go.
...Enough. They may rest. I have nothing left to rule.
Then I will serve something. Not a crown. Take me with you.
(The Frost Lich King Emperor joins. Dominion bends foes to his will.)
I have waited centuries. I can wait for you.
Among the flooded graves stands a knight in a broken crown, reading the names on the stones aloud.
I wore the old Crown before Voss wore its shadow. I sent people into that quarry. I am reading their names.
I will answer for it. But first I would help break the crown that is left. Test me. My knights insist.
Good. They can lie down now. So can I, when this is over.
(Maldrath, the Fallen King, joins. Kingsblade techniques cleave through armour.)
The names will keep. So will I.
In the deep seals, the dead stand shoulder to shoulder, holding the cracked vault doors shut. A robed lord conducts them.
Do not be alarmed. They volunteered. The fault opened these crypts and something below wants out.
I have held it with the dead. I would rather the living held it, and the dead could rest. Prove the living can.
The seal holds with your wards. Sleep, all of you. Thank you.
(Velkhar, Lord of the Dead, joins. Necromancy raises fallen foes to fight for him.)
They will hold a little longer.
A sealed capsule in the vault hisses open. A figure in black plating and neon lines steps out, blade humming.
Operative Kael-09. Orders: hold this vault until relieved. Current date... unknown. Relief... overdue.
Your clearance is invalid. Your intent is unclear. Standard procedure: combat evaluation.
Evaluation complete. You are not my makers. My makers are gone.
New orders required. I will choose them myself. Request: travel with you until I do.
(Kael-09, Neon Blade Operative, joins. Overdrive trades defence for blinding speed.)
Standing by.
Something roars through the engine house - a rider on a machine of black steel and red light, circling the stopped wheel.
This was a road. Six lanes, lights all night. I patrol it. Nobody's told me {m:the damn thing's|it's} gone.
You look like trouble on my road. Let's settle it the old way.
...You ride well for people on foot. Fine. Show me a road worth riding now.
(The Night Rider joins. Throttle builds speed each turn he keeps moving.)
The road will be here.
Moss-covered stones stir in the drowned grove and stand: a colossus of root and rock, water pouring from its shoulders.
THE GROVE DROWNED. I SLEPT UNDER IT. WHO WALKS HERE NOW, AND WHY?
People who want it to grow back.
THEN SHOW ME YOU CAN KEEP WHAT GROWS.
GOOD. CALL, AND I WILL STAND.
Thorned vines knot across the crossing into a throne. Sitting on it, a queen with briar hair watches you, amused.
The flood fed my garden. Everything that falls here feeds it. Are you falling, or are you passing?
Passing, then. Pleasant change. Take a cutting - call me when something needs to wither.
Don't be long. Gardens grow.
In the silent alcove, ash drifts upward. It gathers into a long, smouldering wyrm, coiled around the Crown's cold heart.
The Crown burned me into its engines. Now the engines are quiet and I am... loose.
I will not be anyone's furnace again. But I would burn for someone who asks.
Then we're asking. Not ordering.
Asked. Remember the difference, and I will come.
The rime gallery's mirrors all show the same pale shape, just behind your shoulder. Then it steps out.
I was the cradle's cold. The lantern burned and I kept the sleepers still. Now I am only... cold.
Give me a reason to be something else.
A shield of frost. For the living. Yes. I can be that.
Raven. The quarry ledger only kept numbers. I want names on the memorial - every worker it erased.
Three name-records survived: one at the memorial stones, one in the salvage route by the rubble, one by the old gate. And the families should be asked.
I'll find them.
Q01: Recover three named records at the quarry's surface memorial and speak to the families. Then return to Mara in Brackenford.
Three records at the surface memorial, and the families. Then we'll choose the words.
The names are cut. People stop and read them. That's all a memorial is for.
Under a memorial stone, wrapped in oilcloth: a shift roster with names written beside the numbers.
You've taken this record.
In the rubble of the salvage route: a pay envelope with a name on it, never collected.
You've taken this record.
By the sealed gate, a tin box of letters addressed to 'the lads on shift four'. Every lad signed.
You've taken this record.
I come to read the stones. Most of them still say numbers.
You're asking us? ...My brother's name was Aled. Not 4-409. Aled. Put that.
Bring the named records back to Mara in Brackenford.
These are the names. Thank you.
Could I - there's room at the bottom. I could add a line. What I did. What the Crown did through me.
No.
Not on this stone. This stone is theirs. It isn't a stage for anyone's redemption. Not even a sincere one.
But there's a book at the shelter. For the things people need to say. Write it there. I'll keep it.
...That's fair.
Mara chooses the inscription: 'They were counted by name.'
Raven. I want us to write something too. Between us. That either of us can end this - out loud, at any time.
Yes. Written down. Where we can both read it.
(Raven received Open Hand. His final technique is now available.)
Morwen? I - I used to sweep your workshop. Could you teach me the light? A version that doesn't cost what yours cost you.
...I don't know one. Let's find one.
Q02: Collect observations at the three inhabited lantern stations in the Drowned Archive, then test a low-power circuit with the apprentice.
Three lantern stations at the archive. The keepers know how their lamps behave. I'll meet you by the old circuit.
The workshop's open! Your name's on the door. So's mine. Mine's bigger. You insisted.
This lamp? Runs on a slow cell. Dim but steady. It's never gone out, because it never tries to be bright.
Lantern station one. Staffed and lit.
We light three small lamps instead of one large one. When one fails, the others hold. Nobody panics.
Lantern station two. Mind the step.
Trick is resting it. Two hours on, one off. The lamp lasts years. So does the keeper.
Station three. We're fine, thanks.
Three observations: slow cells, many small lights, rest. Test the low-power circuit with the apprentice.
Collect what the keepers know first. I want to build from what already works.
Ready when you are. It's by the machine.
The low-power circuit: three slow cells, wired so each can rest. The apprentice connects it. It flickers. It fails.
Let me just -
Morwen.
...Right. It's your circuit. What do you think it needs?
The second cell's backwards. I think. I - yes. It's backwards.
The apprentice flips the cell. The lamp comes on, dim and steady, and stays on.
You did that. I didn't touch it.
(Morwen received Ash Without Fire. Her final technique is now available.)
I want a record of rescues. Not deaths. There's a flight recorder in the wreck by the mooring, a survivor who remembers, and a landing marker that needs fixing.
Vespera. You'll have to hear the account of the cable you cut. The whole thing.
...I know.
Q03: At the Skyspine mooring: find the flight recorder, interview the survivor, repair the landing marker. Then return to Edda.
Recorder, survivor, landing marker. All at the broken chain mooring.
The wall's up. People keep adding names. Good ones.
The flight recorder is dented but whole. Its tape is intact.
The recorder's cradle is empty.
I was on the basket the day Vespera cut the cable. The one they said she cut to save herself.
She cut it because the second line would have pulled us all over. I'll say that on the record. All of it, including the part where it was still terrible.
We're waiting for the platform. Nobody's going to jump.
The crew helps reset the landing marker. It's painted in rescue orange now.
The landing marker glows orange.
Take the recorder and testimony back to Edda at High Aerie.
Here's the unedited account. Recorder and testimony.
Vespera reads it. All of it. The cut, the fall, the names.
Do you want me to add your rescues underneath? Balance it out?
No. Leave it as it is. The rescues go on the other wall. This one doesn't need balancing. It needs reading.
(Vespera received Unbound Descent. Her final technique is now available.)
The new engine in the Spine works. Only while the Golem's standing beside it. I've seen it twice. That's not an engine, that's a pet.
...It shouldn't need me.
Then prove it. Three of my crew, your manual, a cold restart.
Q04: At the Furnace Spine's waterwheel engine house, have three workers follow the manual and find where it fails.
Three workers, one manual, no Golem hands. Engine house, east of here.
Cold restart, no Golem. The notes are in every town now. That's a revolution I'll sign.
The Golem's engine manual. Clear, clever, and assuming the reader is the Golem.
Page four says 'bleed the line until it sounds right'. Sounds right to who?
Engine's humming. We're not touching it.
Step nine is missing a valve. The Golem always opens it without thinking. It's not written down.
Engine house crew.
It says 'use the usual wrench'. There are six wrenches.
Learning the engine. Slowly.
'Sounds right'. A missing valve. 'The usual wrench'. ...It's not a manual. It's my memory with page numbers.
The Golem revises it with the crew at the lectern. Measurements instead of sounds. Every valve. Every wrench, labelled.
The manual is revised. Have the crew attempt a cold restart at the engine lever - with the Golem only watching.
I'm going to stand over here. With my joints locked.
Page one. Cold channels open.
Page two. Bleed until the gauge reads four. Not 'sounds right'. Four.
Page nine. Valve nine-A. It's written down now.
The engine turns over, catches, and runs. The Golem hasn't moved.
It doesn't need me.
It never should have.
(The Golem received Unborrowed Engine. His final technique is now available.)
The Spine runs on waterwheels now. Loud. Honest.
West camp needs the mill road. East camp needs the clinic road. One crew, one season. Elowen - you know the Rootward. Choose.
I'm not choosing. We survey all three crossings and then everyone chooses together.
Q05: Survey the three crossings in the flooded Rootward, uncover the route Elowen once concealed, then draft a shared schedule.
Three crossings at the Rootward. And Elowen says there's a fourth she never talks about.
Shared schedule's on the wall. Mill road Mondays, clinic road every day. Everybody grumbles equally. That's fair.
You survey the three crossings: west (short, floods at spring tide), middle (sturdy, far from the clinic), east (clinic-side, narrow).
And there's a fourth. Behind the camp. I hid it. Years ago. I sold that route's secret to a smuggler, and a family that trusted me took the long way and lost everything.
It goes straight to the clinic. It's been there the whole time.
Elowen's concealed route is revealed. Draft the shared schedule with both camps at Brackenford.
Four crossings, all surveyed.
Elowen's chalk on a stump: three crossings, three sluice levers.
West camp, east camp. Four crossings, not three. The fourth was mine to hide. It shouldn't have been.
You're the one who sold the route to the smugglers.
Yes.
...We lost a winter on that.
I know. I'm not asking you to make me feel better about it.
Good. Because I won't. But I'll use the road.

The camps build the schedule together: mill and clinic on alternating days on the middle crossing, the old concealed route for the clinic every day. Warnings in the margins. The keeper of each crossing named.
(Elowen received Many Paths. Her final technique is now available.)
Clinic road first.
This order says I'm to have a 'vision-guided treatment'. It has your signature on it, Aurex. From before.
...It does. I signed a stack of them. I believed my visions meant I knew better.
I don't want it. I want someone to hear me say that.
Q06: In the Memory Vault's prognosis room: read the original authorization, hear the patient, dismantle the automatic seal.
The prognosis room is in the vault. I'll meet you there. I'd like to watch.
I said no. It stayed no. Then I changed my mind and said yes to something else. That was mine too.
The original authorization: 'Prognosis by approved visionary supersedes patient preference.' Aurex's signature at the bottom.
Shelves of old treatment orders. Nacre is sorting them.
The seal reads the order and applies it whether I agree or not. That's the whole machine. It never asks.
Then it goes. And you decide what happens instead. Even if I'm afraid of what you'll choose.
Read the authorization first. I want you to know what you signed.
Aurex pries the automatic seal from its housing. The order-reader goes quiet.
Your treatment. Your decision. I'll tell you what I see, if you want it. It's advice. Nothing more.
Then I'll take the advice. And maybe ignore it.
That's the right.
Nacre's sanctuary changes its practice that week. Aurex's admission is added to the public record, in his own words.
(Aurex received Borrowed Dawn. His final technique is now available.)
The patient hasn't been heard yet.
I don't want your apology, Oni. I want to know where the other binding site is. The deep one, under Whitebone.
The deep seals. Three still in use - by choice, now. They'd need to consent to an inspection.
Q07: In the deep seals under the Whitebone sanctuary, inspect three seals with their occupants, record the design, remove the repeat-command mechanism.
The deep seals. Under the sanctuary. North stair.
You answered the question. The hearing goes on. That's how it should be.
You can look at the seal. Ask before you touch it.
I chose to keep mine until the hearing's done. You can study it. Not remove it.
Look. Write it down. Then I'll decide.
A repeat-command seal. The command loops every hour, renewing itself.
Ask the person beside it first.
The same design, but the loop is fed from somewhere below - a repeater mechanism.
Ask the person beside it first.
The third seal carries Oni's own mark. He writes down the design exactly as it is.
Ask the person beside it first.
The design is recorded. Remove the repeat-command mechanism beneath the chamber.
Oni dismantles the repeater with his bare hands and a borrowed screwdriver. The loops stop renewing. The seals are just seals now - removable, whenever their bearers choose.
At the hearing, Oni comes without his sword. A survivor asks: 'Did you know what the repeater did when you built it?' He answers: 'Yes.' Nothing else.
(Oni received Unwritten Law. His final technique is now available.)
Jori's brought people whose recovered legal names aren't the names they use now. The registry can't amend without the official seal - and the seal's in the safe chamber off the canals.
I could just - make a seal. I'm very good.
Sak.
...I'll fetch the real one.
Q08: Recover the official seal from the safe chamber off Veyr's canals, then offer chosen-name corrections at the registry.
The safe chamber is east off the canals. The clerk who set the dials left a note.
Amendments open. Every change records who asked for it. Including the ones Sak asked for.
Dial 1. It clicks between three engraved words.
Dial 2. It clicks between three engraved words.
Dial 3. It clicks between three engraved words.
The safe stays shut. The dials can be reset and tried again. (A note on the west wall mentions an order.)
The safe clicks and opens. Inside: the official registry seal. Real.
Take the official seal to the registry clerk and offer the corrections.
The seal safe stands open.
Here's the seal. The real one. And - I could've made the corrections perfect. Technically accurate. Every one.
And decided them for everyone.
...Yes. A forgery can be perfect and still be someone else deciding. I get it. I get it now.
The residents make their own amendments. Sak holds the ink. Every entry records who asked for it.
(Sak received False Crown. His final technique is now available.)
An island north of Nacre. Its lantern burns every night and nobody in the village ever wakes. Somebody should go. Carefully.
(A substantial optional challenge. Lanternwake can land there - the storm around it has thinned since the Accord.)
Q09: Fly Lanternwake to the winter island far north of Nacre. Warm the shelters and learn why the village sleeps.
The winter island, north. Take warm clothes. And patience.
The village woke. They're very confused and very hungry. Good problems.
The White Causeway. Snow that never melts, and at the far end a lantern that never goes out.
The sleepers first. Make sure they're alive, and warm them.
Check on the sleepers, then light the warmth channels to thaw the way to the sanctum.
An old man, breathing slowly. Alive. Dreaming - his lips move with a song.
A woman, frost in her hair, warm to the touch. Alive.
A child, curled up, smiling. Alive.
The first brazier catches. Warm air runs down the channel toward the Sleeping House.
The brazier burns steadily. It doesn't need fuel - the old channel feeds it.
The second brazier lights. Frost drips from the ceiling.
The brazier burns steadily.
The third brazier roars. Somewhere, ice cracks like a gunshot.
The brazier burns steadily.
The ice over the north door slumps and runs away as water. The way to the sanctum is open.
The Lantern Cradle. A creature made of cold light and a single burning wick sways over the sleeping village's heat.
(This is an optional, substantial challenge. You can leave and prepare.)
The Lantern Eater gutters and goes out. Behind it, a window of pale dawn.
You step back from the Cradle.
At the Dawn Window, a white deer with frost for antlers waits in the light.
I kept them asleep. The winter was killing them. I thought - if they dream, they don't freeze.
The winter ended. Years ago.
...I didn't know how to stop. Nobody asked me to.
We're asking. Let them wake.
Then they wake. And I would like to go somewhere that is not a promise to keep someone from waking.
Down on the causeway, the village lights its first cooking fire in years.
The bell! Listen - it's ringing the departure pattern. Two long, three short. That's the Marisol. The Marisol sank before I was born.
(A substantial optional challenge in the Starless Reef, south of the Crown Heart. Every sound cue there has a matching light.)
Q10: Fly to the Starless Reef south of the Crown Heart. Follow the beacons (lights and bells) and find why the bell repeats.
Two long, three short. Every night. The reef's south of the Crown Heart.
The bell stopped doing the Marisol. Now it just rings the tide. I kind of miss it. Kind of.
Blackwater Mooring. The reef is black; the only light is the beacon lamps, flashing with each bell.
Light and sound together. Follow either one. You don't need both.
Follow the beacons through the reef. Keep the return beacon lit.
You swing the reflector east. The second beacon's light lances into the black channel - and the return beacon, behind you, stays lit.
The reflector points east. The return beacon still burns.
The wreck library. Waterlogged ledgers of the Marisol's passengers, painstakingly dried page by page by someone - or something.
(You restore the passenger register - every name, every berth.)
The shelves are empty. The register is with you.
The Night Trench. Something vast circles in the dark, and every few breaths the whole trench replays a ship tearing apart.
(This is an optional, substantial challenge. You can leave and prepare.)
The Heartless Leviathan sinks into the trench. The replay stops mid-scream. The water goes still.
In the Open Current, a second leviathan - smaller, older, eyes like lamps - rises beside the party.
The other was made to repeat the wreck's last instant. For them. For their families. Forever. As a memorial.
A memorial that can't stop isn't a memorial.
Keep the record. End the repetition.
The register is theirs. Take it home. And I will go where the current goes, if you'll have me.
(The Marisol's passenger register goes to Hearthward's harbor office. Families come to read it.)
Under the canals, a ministry automaton is still issuing Voss's orders. Into an empty room. It's been doing it since the bell.
I'd like it to stop. I'd also like its ledger kept. Evidence.
Q11: Open the echo chamber off Veyr's canals (west), read the command ledger, and disable the automaton without obeying its prompts.
West off the canals. The door's been unbolted since the Accord.
The ledger's in the archive now. The machine's a very expensive hatstand.
The Command Ledger: every order the automaton has issued since the bell. Hundreds. All addressed to units that no longer exist.
You've taken the command ledger.
A dusty ledger stand.
CITIZEN. REPORT FOR REASSIGNMENT. OBEDIENCE WILL BE REWARDED.
It's offering us a reward. How generous.
Its prompts are just words. Ignore them. The screen will name each edict before it lands.
The Regent's Echo sputters. Its voice box repeats 'REWARD' once more, very quietly, and stops.
Wait. Don't wreck it. A machine like that could keep order. Benevolently, this time.
Its authority function comes out. The evidence stays.
The party pulls the authority core and leaves the ledger and the rest of the machine for the archive.
(Received Broken Diadem.)
The automaton drones on. Read its command ledger first - you'll want to know what it's been ordering.
In the listening pool there's a voice nobody claims. Not dragon, not human. Excluded from both testimonies.
The listeners taught me a phrase that lets you hear it without taking from it. Here - it's yours. It's in the Crown Heart, they say. A silent alcove off the Concord Bridge.
Q12: Carry the listening phrase to the silent alcove on the Crown Heart's Concord Bridge (reachable before the final commitment).
The alcove off the Concord Bridge. Say the phrase. Then listen.
The pool has one more voice in it now. It doesn't belong to anyone. It sounds happier.
The silent alcove. A figure of folded light, singing without a sound. Its beat shows as pulses of colour on the walls.
Everyone who came here wanted to use me. As a weapon, as a key, as a proof.
I want only to be heard. You will have to earn the quiet to hear it.
(Optional challenge. Watch the beat windows on the walls.)
...You heard. You didn't take. That is all.
(Received Unowned Song.)
The cow chews and considers you. It has seen soldiers, tax men and floods. You are not much.
The cow stood through the fault in this field. It chews as if nothing happened. Maybe, for a cow, nothing did.
The pig roots at your boots, decides they are not truffles, and grunts its disappointment.
The dove walks a circle, bobbing. Doves come home. It is the only thing anyone trusts about them.
The coney freezes, nose going. Its coat is half combed out. It holds the grudge.
The ranch cat looks at you with the patience of something that has outlived three owners.
A white-tipped fox watches from a distance and does not come closer. Out here, that is manners.
The fox sits beside the path as if it owns it. Here, it may.
A field mouse, fat on grain the Board says does not exist.
Agna Fallow. This is my land, what the quarry left of it. My boys went down the lift. The cows didn't.
I sell beasts and seed. Buy a beast and it's yours, but it stays here; I feed it, you take what it gives.
Milk and eggs go in the crate by the barn. Plots by the ditch, if you can wait for anything to grow.
Agna Fallow. The river came through the bottom field and took Mott and half the fences. The cows swam.
I'll still sell you a beast. Somebody has to keep breeding things that aren't soldiers.
Back. The beasts don't miss you, but the crate might.
Still here. So am I. That's the whole of the news.
Agna says I'm not her boy. She still makes me eat first.
The doves came back after the quarry fell. All of them. Mott said they always count right.
I pulled a calf out of the flood by its ears. Agna said that was stupid. Then she gave me Mott's knife.
Forty years I've milked here. The Crown took my sons for the quarry and my teeth for the levy.
Carrots in a day, potatoes in two. The earth here's the only honest thing left in the March.
I keep the plots. Plant, wait, pull. If you plant and leave, the crop waits for you. Mostly.
Agna pays in milk. Better than the quarry paid in crowns.
We buried Mott under the pear tree. He'd have said it was a waste of good digging.
Plant anyway. That's all farming ever was. Planting anyway.
I came down the river on a door. Agna gave me a bucket and a cow to milk. Didn't ask my name.
I haven't told her. I'm not sure I'm still him.
Brann Coker. Twenty years on the furnace floor. Now I keep pigs. My lungs prefer the pigs.
Pigs root in the ash and turn up black truffles. Nobody knows why. The guild cooks pay not to ask.
Buy a beast, I'll keep it. You come back and empty the crate. Seeds too, for what grows in soot.
The furnaces went cold the night of the fault. First clean air in this paddock in a hundred years.
The pigs hate it. Truffles still come up, though. Ash doesn't wash out of ground this old.
The pigs are where you left them. So is the crate. So am I.
Brann says peppers grow mean in ash. Three days and they'll burn your eyes out of your head.
I sold one to the canteen. They used it to clean the boilers.
The regulator's men left when the pipes went dry. Took the scales. We weigh truffles by hand now.
I'm not a farmhand. I'm a volunteer. The difference is nobody pays me.
Onions in a day, beets in two. In this paddock, even vegetables grow up fast.
Regulator's office. Every truffle that leaves the Paddock is weighed and taxed at the gate.
The pigs don't pay. Coker does. That's the arrangement, and Coker hates it, which is how I know it works.
Ped. I worked the Spine till my chest went. Brann lets me sit with the pigs. They breathe like I do.
Warm air pushes up from the slag vent. A sow has worn a hollow in the ash beside it.
Maude Tiller. My husband fished. The sea had him. I took the croft and turned my back on the water.
Cows on salt grass give milk you can taste the tide in. Bellharbor pays for it, grudgingly.
Buy a beast, I'll graze it. The crate's by the byre. Seed for whatever grows in sand.
The sea came up to the byre door the night of the fault and went back out. It took the lower town instead.
Thirty years I turned my back on it. It didn't care either way.
Tide's out. Crate's by the byre. Don't let the coneys near the nets.
Radishes come up in a day! Mum says that's the only fast thing in Bellharbor that isn't a debt.
We could see the lower town from here. Now we see water. Maude says don't look. I look.
Sailed the Glass Coast twelve years. Now I milk cows on a dock. The cows are better company.
Fish the inlet if you want. The croft gets the head and tail. Maude's rule.
Half the boats sank at their moorings. Mine was ashore for paint. Luck's the only seamanship that counts.
Grazing tallyman, Customs House. Every cow on Crown salt grass pays a grazing fee.
The grass grew before the Crown. I don't make the rules. I just count the cows.
My house was on Bell Quay. Maude took me in for the milking. She says the sea takes everyone eventually.
She says it like a kindness. I think she means it as one.
Sefton Crag. Sixty winters on this ledge. The wind takes a lamb a year and a shepherd a decade.
Coneys for wool, doves for messages, a black cow that thinks she's a goat. All for sale, once.
Your beast stays on my ledge. The crate's by the barn. Rope yourself if you go near the edge.
The cables came down in the fault. Half of High Aerie's sons were on them. My doves still find the Court.
A message bird is a small thing to sell. People pay for small things, now.
Wind's from the east. Wool's dry. That's the report.
I comb the coneys. Every second day there's enough wool for a muffler. The crafters in the Court sew them.
Sefton says the wind will have me one day. He says it like weather.
I sewed mufflers for the cable crews. They wore them on the last crossing. That's a thing I know now.
Pumpkins up here take three days and a fight with the wind. Leeks are easier. Leeks don't care.
Corn, two days. Feed it to the cow and she still won't thank you.
I come to bless the fold. Sefton tolerates it. The wind tolerates nothing, so we are all even.
My wife rode the cable the morning it fell. I came up here to be somewhere the wind is honest.
Sefton put me on the doves. They always come back. I like watching something come back.
