Yara Saltmarrow. Out here water costs more than pork, and pork costs more than people.
Pigs fat on salt-root, doves on the cistern, a cow that drinks like a tax collector. Buy one, I keep it.
Crate's by the barn. Seed for the walled garden; it's the only soft ground for a day's ride.
The Assembly shares the water now. The rich wells are under rubble. Funny how sharing starts.
The pigs don't know the difference. I envy them most days.
Water's rationed. Business isn't.
I water the garden with a cup. One cup a plant. Yara counts.
Eggplants take two days. Onions one. Wheat one, if the wind doesn't salt it.
After the fault the brine pool went sweet for a week. Yara made us drink till we were sick. Smart.
I carry salt blocks for the barn walls. They melt a little every summer. So do I.
Salt-tax office. Each pig is salt-fed, and the salt is Crown salt, so each pig is partly Crown property.
Yara asked which part. I said the profitable part.
I walked out of the Basin after the fault with a goat. The goat didn't make it. Yara gave me a job.
Okuni Hara. I keep the Court's table: coneys, doves, a pig the steward pretends not to eat.
The foxes come and go. They are guests. A farm that starves its guests does not deserve a gate.
A beast bought here stays here. The crate is by the barn. Seeds for bamboo and the Court's grapes.
The Court is in exile and the steward ran with the silver. The foxes stayed. Make of that what you will.
I still farm for the Court. It is smaller now. It still has to eat.
Welcome back. Bow to the gate if you like. The foxes notice.
Grandmother leaves rice at the little gate. The foxes eat it. She says that means the year will be kind.
The foxes came out of the maples the night everything shook. They lay down in the barn with the pigs.
Nobody ate anybody. Grandmother says that is the Court's real law.
Bamboo takes three days and wants the stream. Grapes take three and want flattery.
Radishes take one and want nothing. I like radishes.
I inspect the Court's provisions. The mask is so the pig does not recognise me later.
I wore silk in the Court of Masks. Now I muck out coneys. My mask was the better coat.
Okuni does not bow to me. I find I do not mind.
Someone has left rice and a copper coin at the fox gate's foot. The rice is gone. The coin is not.
Gideon Marl. Inside the wall, the meat rots. Out here, the Board inspects mine twice a week.
Clean beasts are the only clean thing Harrowfen has. I sell them once, and keep them clean myself.
Your beast stays in my fields. Its goods go in the crate. Seed for berries and leeks, washed.
The town burned its own wards. The Board signed the order and then ran past my fence.
My pigs are the cleanest thing in Mirewold. Nobody inspects them now. I do it anyway.
Wash your hands at the trough before you touch anything. Then buy something.
I'm not sick. I live out here because I'm not sick. The wall people check every month.
Berries are bitter but they're ours. Two days. I count.
Nobody checks anymore. I still stand in the line by the trough on the first of the month.
I was of the Beaked Order. I left when the Order sold the cure. The pigs never asked my reasons.
The Order burned the wards and called it mercy. I dig potatoes now. Potatoes have never been called mercy.
Wall warden. Nothing from the wards comes through the Fields. Nothing from the Fields goes in without a seal.
Marl's pigs eat better than my children. I've written it down, for the Board. They didn't reply.
I tanned hides in the east ward. The fire took the ward and the hides and my hands. Gideon feeds me anyway.
Hild Ulfsdottir. My cattle are black so the snow doesn't swallow them. Mostly it works.
Coneys for fur-wool, black cows, a pig for when the winter is worse than usual. I sell each once.
Your beast stays in my byre. The crate's by it. Potatoes and berries grow under straw, if you're patient.
The Pit opened north of here and the Ice Road filled with people walking south. I fed who I could.
The cattle didn't mind the company. The cold minded nobody, same as always.
Shut the gate. Then we can talk business.
We cut a hole in the pond ice every morning. Frost bream come up to breathe. So do we, most days.
The cows walked to the Pit's edge the night it opened and stood looking down. Then they came home.
Mother says a fox is a cat that thinks in winters. This one steals eggs. I think it thinks in eggs.
I buy coney fur for the Coldharbour garrison. Hild sells me a third of what I ask. She calls it a fair price.
I came down the Ice Road from the Pit with nothing. Hild gave me a shovel and a cow to keep warm against.
She's slow. She's heavy. Every part has a name in the manual, and every name has a spare in the hold.
Nothing on this ship needs a person inside it to run.
Climb the ladder to take the helm. Land on the marked fields by towns and ruins - look for the flattened grass.
On foot, stand on any marked field and call her; she'll come to you.
Swapping who goes ashore? Take your time.
Crew bunks. Two hours' sleep and a hot drink.
The crew room board. Everyone pins up what they've heard.

Crew board: Mara in Brackenford is gathering the quarry names (Raven). A Bellharbor apprentice wants Morwen (Morwen). Edda wants a wall for returners (Vespera). Pell says the engine only runs when the Golem stands by it (Golem).

Crew board: two Brackenford camps want different roads (Elowen). A patient at Nacre refuses an order in Aurex's hand (Aurex). A Whitebone survivor wants another binding site found (Oni). Jori has people whose names changed (Sak).

Crew board: an island lantern north of Nacre burns while its village never wakes. A Hearthward bell repeats a lost ship's departure. A machine under Veyr still issues Voss's orders. Nacre's pool holds a voice nobody claims.
(The leads are recorded in your Journal. None of them is required to reach Crown Heart.)
The coastal ferry's tied up. Ministry orders: no sailings until the archive business is settled.

options.text: Take the ferry north to Skyspine

cmds.text: The ferry bell rings. The coast slides by, cream stone and bronze bells, until the cliffs rise.
An empty ferry landing.

options.text: Take the ferry south to Bellharbor

cmds.text: The ferry works down the coast to Bellharbor's quay.
The cable ferry across the chasm hangs still. High Aerie's crew hasn't reset the anchors.

options.text: Ride the cable west to the Pale Basin

cmds.text: The basket creaks out over the chasm. Salt glitters far below.
The basin end of the cable ferry. The basket is on the far side.

options.text: Ride the cable east to Skyspine

cmds.text: The basket swings east toward the cliffs.
A marked landing field. The Wayfarer can be called down here.
The Wayfarer drifts down onto the field, its envelope creaking.
A marked landing field. Lanternwake can be called down here.
Lanternwake settles onto the field, engines ticking as they cool.

options.text: Take the ferry back to Hearthward

cmds.text: The ferry crosses the Ember Sea to Hearthward's pontoons.
The ferry noses out past the drowned breakwater. Bellharbor's bells are fewer now, and quieter.
Nobody crosses the strait. The Fox Court turns boats around, and the ones it doesn't, it keeps.

options.text: Cross the strait to Vermilion Reach

cmds.text: Lanterns drift on the current beside the hull. On the far shore the maples burn red, though it is not autumn.
The ferryman does not look back at the shore. Neither, after a while, do you.
Saltwhistle boats only. Come back when the guild's taking passengers.
A fishing smack takes you aboard for a coin and a hand with the nets.
The smack runs home ahead of the weather, gulls screaming after the catch.
The sky cable runs up into the cloud toward Crucible Isle. The basket is chained; the shrine keepers say the line is not yet safe.
The cable to Crucible Isle hums in the wind. A basket swings at the landing, and a board says ARENA - FIGHTERS AND WAGERS.

options.text: Ride up to the Crucible Isle

cmds.text: The basket climbs into the cloud. For a long time there is nothing but white, and the hum of the line.
The cable to Crucible Isle ends in a frayed stump. The fault snapped it. Only an airship can reach the isle now.
Forty years I've ground Crown grain. The Crown weighs the flour. I weigh what's left.
What's left is small. Don't let the size of the wheel fool you.
Six families, one wheel, one pond. My granddaughter Nell runs the stones now. I run my mouth.
Juniper at the store mends anything with a hinge. Bring her scraps and she'll make you something honest.
North, the Oathstone Crossroads. There's a peddler at the milestone who sells what the Crown forgot to tax.
East, past Wren's orchard, the old chapel sank into the marsh. Its bells still ring some nights. Nobody's pulling them.
Hollins Mill: the Sunken Chapel's bells ring on their own, in the marsh east of Wren's Orchard.
The river moved in the night. Picked itself up and went two fields east. The wheel turns anyway.
We grind for anybody now. There's nobody left to weigh it.
Two sacks up, one sack down. The one going down is ours. The Crown carts the rest to Veyr.
I used to carry for the quarry. At least grain doesn't fall on you.
Refugees from Veyr sleep in the loft. They grind their own and sing at the stones. Off-key. It's nice.
Old Hollin's mother kept a garden over the race, across the plank bridge. She died, he stopped going.
He says she buried her good baking gloves out there so the assessors couldn't list them. Nobody's looked.
New faces. Here's how the pond works: stand at the end of the dock, face the water, and wait.
Don't jerk the line when it twitches. That's the pond testing you. When it pulls, you pull.
Fish bite best at dusk. Here - my spare bait and a snack for the wait. Pay me back in stories.
The carp in there are older than the assessor and twice as polite. The dock end's yours whenever you like.
The pond's the only water that didn't move when the ground broke. I think the carp held it down.
You drop a line off the dock end. The float sits. The float thinks about it.
Then it goes under, hard. Something heavy and whiskered comes up, looks at you, and spits out a coin-sized tonic flask.
Oda, from the shore: 'He does that. Somebody drowned a crate of those in the flood of '06.'
The float sits on the brown water. The old carp is somewhere below, thinking about you.
The paddles are patched with three colours of Crown crate. One board still reads 'PROPERTY OF THE MINISTRY - DO NOT'.
I'm chasing the ducks! The assessor counts them every month, so I count them first. There's nine. He writes eight.
The ducks came back! Nobody counts them now. I still do. Eleven.
Barley. The Crown takes the good heads and leaves the chaff for the bread. We call it 'Crown loaf'. Not fondly.
Hounds come down off the toll road at night after the rats in the stook. Keep to the lane after dark.
Grain assessor, Ministry of Provision. Please don't stand between me and the scales.
Everything here is counted: sacks, ducks, hinges. It's not personal. It's just everything.
My husband went to work the toll at Gallowgate. They pay in chits, and the chits are only good at the toll canteen.
They've a bounty board there now. Hounds, bandits, 'persons of interest'. Half the names on it are ours.
Hollins Mill: Gallowgate Toll keeps a bounty board. Some of the names on it are villagers.
My grandmother used to say a king was buried twice out west, under the ash barrows. Once in a crown, once without.
Children dare each other to find the door. None of them ever has. None of them looks very hard.
Hollins Mill: 'a king buried twice' lies under the Ashward Barrows, west of the river farms.
I drive cattle up to Oathstone Crossroads. Tobiah Wend keeps a stall at the milestone.
Wend walks the whole March with that pack. Tell him Hollins sent you and he'll still overcharge you, but kindly.
We walked from Veyr when the square fell in. Hollin met us on the road with a cart of flour and didn't ask for a chit.
I'd never seen a mill. It's just a wheel and some stubborn people. Turns out that's enough.
The fault went through the toll road north of here. The Gallowgate fort's on an island now. Serves it right.
The Millstone. Bed, bread and a fire. Thirty crowns, and you can pay the Crown's share to me instead.
Beds are free for anyone walking out of the ruin. You're walking out of it, aren't you? Close enough.
Cattle sleep standing up. Drovers sleep lying down, whenever they can. Go away.
We play for Crown chits. Nobody wants to win. The winner has to spend them at the toll canteen.
Linden's Store. Tonics, rope, good boots, a sword or two from the old garrison. Look, then haggle.
You've got the look of people who break things. Good. I mend them, and sometimes I make them better.
Bring me materials - ore from the hills, hides, herbs, scrap from anything the Crown leaves lying about.
A bench can't make something from nothing. But it can make a lot from a little. That's the whole trick of this village.
Iron ore, hides, pond reeds, Crown scrap. Anything with a bit of use left in it. I'll show you what it wants to be.
Linden charges the Crown price and then gives you a biscuit. I can't decide if that's kindness or cheek.
Stones are dressed, the race is open, the wheel's greased. Grandad talks. I grind.
If the tithe clerk says we're short again, I'll grind him.
We grind for three villages now. Refugees carry the sacks. Nobody takes a share. I didn't know flour could feel like this.
Tithe clerk. Every seventh sack is the Crown's. Every tenth after that is also the Crown's. It's in the schedule.
Mind the millstones. They took my brother's thumb in the spring. He says it's the most honest tax he's paid.
Hollin's mother planted that garden across the race. Beans, sage, gloves. Don't ask about the gloves.
He won't cross the bridge since she passed. Somebody should. Things want to be found.
Halt. Gallowgate Toll. Ten crowns a head, a Crown writ, or turn round and {m:piss off|walk} home.
Raven. Crown executioner, convoy service. The commission's still on file.
...Sir. Yes, sir. Go through, sir.
The name still opens doors. I hate that it does.
Ministry of Provision, audit division. You're three tallies short on the east ledger. Don't get up.
Audit. Right. Go on through. Please don't mention the ledger to the sergeant.
Sensible.
Ten crowns, a writ, or the road home. I don't make the rules. I just stand in front of them.
You're through. The canteen takes chits and coin. The bounty board takes everybody's name eventually.
Three days in the queue with a cart of turnips. The turnips are winning.
They weigh the load, then weigh me, then charge me for the difference. I asked what the difference was. 'Attitude.'
I haul slag bricks from Cinder Reach. They tax me at both ends of the toll road and once in the middle for luck.
Past Cinderwake there's a village called Kettle Row, right under a dam. Nice people. Terrible dam.
Gallowgate: Kettle Row, a slag-miners' village in Cinder Reach, sits right under a failing dam.
Don't look at me. Look at the carts. I'm a cart.
...My name's on the board in there. I sold Crown grain back to the people who grew it. Cheaply. That's the crime.
Toll hounds. The Crown breeds them to smell coin in a pocket. Four broke loose in the run and I'm not going in.
Sergeant Kell's posted it on the board. Somebody braver than me can collect.
You cleared the run. I'll raise the next litter kinder. Maybe. They're still toll hounds.
Barracks. Crown personnel only. That includes me, barely. They lost my {m:damn |}papers in Veyr.
The queue's the best market in the March. Nobody can leave, and everybody's bored.
Notices are nailed three deep. WANTED FOR QUESTIONING: a list of names from Hollins Mill and Wren's Orchard.
Under them, a work notice: 'Toll hounds loose in the kennel run. 150 crowns on clearing it. See Sgt. Kell.'
You pull the hound notice. The kennel run is behind the fence, east of the road.
The 'persons of interest' come down in one handful. Somebody in the cart queue laughs once and then very carefully stops.
The hound notice is gone from its nail. The kennel run is east of the road, behind the fence.
New notices already. 'Bandit on the Cinder road.' 'Bells ringing in the marsh chapel: investigate, NOT urgent.'
Gallowgate bounty board: bells ringing at the marsh chapel east of Wren's Orchard. Marked 'not urgent'.
Four toll hounds turn from a torn sack of coin-scented rags. Their collars are stamped with the Ministry seal.
The run is quiet. Sergeant Kell will want to hear it from you.
The waystone warms. Far to the west you feel the Oathstone answer.
(Waystone attuned: Gallowgate Toll.)
The waystone hums under a film of road dust.
I hid in the gatehouse when the ground split. When I came out the garrison was gone and the road ended in the sea.
Sergeant Kell took the soldiers who'd listen and went east. Said she was done collecting names. Good for her.
Gallowgate: Sergeant Kell deserted after the fault and took her soldiers east, toward the Glass Coast shoals.
Picking the fort clean. Crown iron, Crown rope, Crown nails. The Crown won't miss it. The Crown's in the sea.
Canteen. Crown chits or coin. The stew is mostly turnip, because of the queue outside.
Sergeant Kell. I run the bounty board, and the toll, and the kennel, and my own patience, which is thinnest.
If you want work, the board's outside. If you want mercy, the chapel's in the marsh.
You took the hound notice. The run's east of the road. They bite low. Keep your boots on.
Kennel-master says the run's clear. Here. The Crown pays late, but I don't.
Somebody tore down my persons-of-interest. Now I'll have to copy them all out again. Slowly. Very, very slowly.
Twenty years collecting names. Some days I'd like to hand one back.
Bounty office. I pay out, I log it, I file it. The file goes to Veyr. Nobody in Veyr reads it. I checked.
Off shift. We play 'guess the toll'. The sergeant makes up a new number every morning. I'm on a streak.
I joined to guard a road. Turns out a toll is a road with a fist in it.
We sleep in the canteen now. The cook stayed. The stew's still turnip. Some things survive anything.
Wren Tamsey. It's my orchard, whatever the levy officer writes on his slate.
We press in autumn and pay in spring. The Crown takes a cask in three and calls the rest 'surplus'.
The old grove behind the bell gate is shut. My Harl's buried there, with the pickers from the levy night. Leave them be.
The fault shook every apple off every tree in one night. We pressed for a week. The whole March drank.
The levy officer went back to Veyr. There's no Veyr to go back to. I hope he found somewhere.
You went into the old grove after dark. ...You saw him. Don't tell me you didn't, you've got the look.
He said the deed to the press is under the third press stone. He hid it the night of the levy, so the Crown couldn't take the farm.
Under the stone. Twelve years I've paid rent to the Crown on my own orchard because I couldn't find that paper.
...That fool. That lovely, stubborn fool. He could have just told me before he went out picking in the frost.
Take this. It was his militia pennant. He'd want it on somebody who goes out at night on purpose.
Wren's Orchard: the ghosts of the levy night are at rest. Wren has the deed to her press.
The deed's framed over the press. The levy officer read it twice and went very quiet. Best cider we've made in years.
Twelve autumns back, the Crown wanted the harvest in before the frost. The levy made the pickers work through the night.
Six of them froze in the old grove. Harl Wren was one. Now the bell at the gate rings itself on cold nights.
The pickers say if you ring it at dusk and wait, you'll see them working. I've never had the nerve.
Wren's Orchard: ring the old grove bell at dusk and wait, and the levy-night pickers come back.
The bell hasn't rung by itself since you went in there. I miss it, a little. Isn't that odd.
The rope is tied off with a black ribbon. The pickers say: ring it at dusk, then wait.

options.text: Ring the bell and wait for dark

cmds.text: Night comes down the rows. Frost ticks on the grass. Past the gate, lanterns move between the dead trees.
Nobody is holding them.
The bell is still swinging a little. It is fully dark in the old grove.
The ribbon is gone. Somebody has tied a sprig of apple blossom to the rope instead.
The lanterns turn toward you all at once. They are not lanterns.
The wisps scatter into the frost. Deeper in, a man in a picker's smock is still working, one hand on an empty basket.
Mind the frost. You'll lose your fingers. We did.
The levy said the harvest had to be in before dawn. Crown's orders. So we picked by lamplight, and the cold came.
You're Harl Wren.
I was. Is Wren still pressing? Tell her - no. Tell her something useful.
The deed to the press is under the third press stone. I hid it that night so the levy couldn't take the farm if we didn't finish.
We didn't finish. She's been paying the Crown rent ever since, hasn't she? Tell her. Then we can put the baskets down.
Tell Wren Tamsey that the press deed is under the third press stone.
Tell Wren. The third stone. Then we can put the baskets down.
Two more rows. Two more rows and they said we could go in. That was a long time ago, wasn't it.
The levy man had a warm coat. I remember his coat better than my own mother's face.
I was only here to carry the baskets. Harl gave me his gloves. He shouldn't have. His hands went first.
Six names are cut into a flat stone. The last two are cut shallower, as if the mason ran out of daylight, or money.
Someone has left six cups of cider on the stone.
The third stone sits a finger higher than the others. It won't budge. It's probably nothing.
Under the third stone, where Harl said: an oilcloth bundle, dry as the day it was hidden. Wren should open it.
The press stones are level now. The deed hangs framed on the wall above them.
Pick with a twist, not a pull. Pull, and you take next year's bud with it. The Crown pulls.
We send the best casks to Veyr, the worst to the toll, and drink the middling ones ourselves. Middling's lovely.
The trees on the east rows split in the fault. The west rows are fine. We're grafting the one onto the other.
My big brother says the dead people in the old grove come out if you ring the bell. I'd never. Would you?
Harvest levy office. One cask in three. The widow Tamsey owes rent on the press. There's no deed on file.
No deed, no farm. The Crown is patient. The Crown is also the only one with a pen.
She has a deed. A real one. Dated before the levy. I... will need to consult the regional office. For some years.
Cider to Veyr, empties back. The toll at Gallowgate charges me for the empties. They're full of air. Crown air.
Bees don't pay tithe. They sting the assessor, and he writes them down as 'hazard', and then they're exempt.
Southeast, where the marsh starts, there's a chapel under the water. My bees won't fly over it.
Wren's Orchard: the beekeeper's bees won't fly over the drowned chapel in the marsh south-east.
I'm the taster. It's a real job. I taste, I nod, Wren tells me to stop nodding and start carrying.
Levy escort. I carry the officer's slate and his umbrella. Mostly the umbrella. It's a hard posting.
I walked from Veyr with my shoes in my hand. Wren gave me a bed in the press loft and a job pulling apples.
Twist, not pull. I'm learning.
Posy says I can stay till my mum comes. Mum was at the square in Veyr. Posy says the orchard is good at waiting.
The Bent Bough. Bed, bread and a jug. Thirty-five crowns, cider included, headache extra.
Pay what you can. Most pay in apples. We have a great many apples.
Cinderwake smith, taking the long road home. The toll road's too dear. The orchard road's too pleasant. I'm torn.
I'm a buyer from Veyr. I taste, I bargain, I lose. Wren always wins. It's why I keep coming back.
Cellarman Duro. Casks, tonics, tools for the rows, and a few blades the pickers use for pruning. And for wolves.
I'm the cooper. I make casks and I mend everything else. Bring me hardwood, hoops, hides. Iron if you can find it.
A good barrel is a hundred small promises, all holding. Armour's the same idea, only it's rude about it.
Hardwood, iron hoops, hides, orchard resin. Bring them and I'll bend something useful out of them.
Don't touch the third press stone. It rocks. Duro says it's always rocked. I think something's under it.
Mum says Dad's in the old grove. I don't go in there. The bell does it for me.
Mum laughed today, then she cried, then she laughed again. She says it was about a piece of paper.
I came to help my sister after Harl died. That was twelve years ago. I'm still helping. Help takes a long time.
The marsh gives way to flagstones. The chapel stands up to its knees in black water, doors open.
Somewhere inside, a bell rings once. The water around your boots trembles with it.
Oath-knights built these. They swore to hold them. I knew the words once.
You haul on the west bell rope. Far overhead, a drowned bell tolls. The west portcullis grinds up out of the silt.
The rope is slack. The west portcullis stays up.
The island bell is only a hand bell on a chain. You ring it anyway. Every bell in the chapel answers, underwater.
Back in the nave, iron shrieks. Something has lifted.
The little bell hangs quiet on its chain.
You lift the bar off the side door. It opens onto the marsh porch, where you came in.
The bar leans against the wall. The side door is open.
I came to pray for my son. The water came in during the hymn. I'm still waiting for the hymn to end.
The knights still stand their watch below. Their commander will not let anyone pass who cannot relieve him.
Squire Aubel, Ser Hallam's shield-bearer. I drowned carrying his shield. He's been carrying it since.
He swore to hold the chapel until relieved. Nobody came. Now he holds it against everyone, even the water.
When he raises the shield, don't strike. Wait, or break the oath with storm. Lightning goes through wet steel.
And when the bells ring underwater, brace. He floods the altar and the cold slows you to a crawl.
You relieved him. That's all any of us wanted. Somebody to say: you can stop now.
Tell whoever's giving the orders these days. Somebody should say it to them, too.
Forty oath-rings in a velvet tray. One slot is empty. Whoever wore it is still upstairs, holding.
The knight at the altar turns. Water pours from the joints of his armour. His visor is full of it.
Halt. This chapel is held by the Order of the Oath. None pass until the garrison is relieved.
Ser. The Order's gone. The Crown dissolved it. There's no one left to relieve you.
Then I hold. I hold until relieved. I HOLD.
Every bell in the chapel rings at once, underwater.
Hallam goes to one knee. The water runs out of his armour and does not come back.
...You are relieved, Ser Hallam. Is that it? Did someone say it?
I'm saying it. You're relieved. Stand down.
Thank you. Take the plate. It never kept the water out. Perhaps it will keep something else.
The bells stop. For the first time in years, the chapel is quiet.
The Sunken Chapel: Ser Hallam is relieved of his watch. The drowned bells have stopped.
The altar is under a finger of water. The stone is carved with the Order's oath: WE HOLD UNTIL RELIEVED.
Someone has cut a new line under the oath, fresh and shallow: RELIEVED.
Barrow-warden. I keep the grass short and the curious out. The first is easier.
The big barrow has a speaking stone. It wants the oath of the first king. Nobody alive knows it.
Well. The Crown's masons keep chiselling it off the Oathstone at the crossroads. So somebody knows it.
Ashward Barrows: the barrow door opens to the first king's oath, cut on the Oathstone at the crossroads.
You opened it. I've kept that grass for forty years and never once seen inside. ...Don't tell me. I like the not knowing.
The fault shook half the March into the sea and didn't crack one stone out here. The barrows are stubborn.
People come to lay flowers at the round door now. They don't know whose it is. It doesn't seem to matter.
A crown carved on the stone, chiselled out, then carved again, badly, by a different hand.
Under it, very small: 'CROWNED TWICE. BURIED TWICE.'
A round stone blocks the barrow. Around its rim, worn half away: '...SHALL WEIGH MORE THAN THE HEAD...'
The stone seems to be waiting for the rest.

options.text: Speak: 'No crown shall weigh more than the head that bears it.'

cmds.text: The words go into the stone like a key. It rolls aside with a sound like someone sighing in their sleep.
The stone does not move. Somewhere under the grass, something laughs, once, without any breath.
The dust in the passage stands up. Two knights in ash-grey mail, their faces long gone, level their swords.
They wear no Crown seal. Their tabards bear a crown with a line struck through it.
The wights fold back into dust. The passage to the inner barrow is open.
The sarcophagus is empty. In its lid, a crown-shaped hollow, polished smooth, as if something was lifted out and put back many times.
Scratched inside the lid, where only the dead could read it: 'THEY CARRIED THE CROWN BACK DOWN TO HIM WHO WORE IT FIRST. I WILL FOLLOW IT.'
My knights buried me here the first time. Without the crown. The priests carried it back down to the one who wore it first.
The First Crown. The first head it ever sat on. They entombed him with it, deep under the quarry. Every king after only borrowed it.
I borrowed it. I sent people into that quarry with it on my head. Then they took it back, and put me here with the grass.
Then we find where it went.
Below. Past the dragons and the builders, in the country of the dead. His tomb. I can feel it from here, like a bad tooth.
QC14 The First Crown: Maldrath's first grave lies empty in the Ashward Barrows. The crown went below - to the First Crown's Tomb, deep in the Hollow Throne.
Find the First Crown's Tomb in the realm of the dead, below the Deep.
Empty, still. The tomb that matters is below. The Hollow Throne. I can feel it pulling.
Grete Ossery, forewoman of the Slag Guild. Two hundred souls under that dam, and the Crown says it's sound.
The Crown inspected it from the far bank, with a telescope, in fog. We have the certificate framed in the hall.
If you're going up to the Weeping Dam, go quiet. There's something living in the sluice works. The keeper's widow went in and never came out.
Kettle Row: something lives in the Weeping Dam's sluice works, north of the village.
The seep's slowed since you went up the dam. It still weeps. But it weeps like a person now, not like a flood.
I've told the guild to cut a second road out of the valley. Just in case. Nobody laughed.
New hands? Good. I teach every new miner the same way: here's a seam, here's a pick, don't die.
See the chalk marks on the ledge? That's a node. Face it and work it and it'll give up ore. Not forever. It grows back slow.
Iron for a smith's first upgrade. Heartsteel deeper down, in hot places. Starmetal only where the sky's fallen in.
Take the pick. We've more picks than miners these days. That's not a joke. I wish it was.
Nodes along the ledge, marked in chalk. Work them, let them rest, come back. The mountain's patient. Be patient back.
You work the chalk-marked seam. A fist of dull ore breaks free.
The seam is worked out for now. It will grow back, slowly.
The glinting seam gives up two good lumps of ore and a shower of grit.
Someone has chalked a new mark: 'RESTING'.
I'm king of the slag heap! My dad says slag's what's left when you take the good out of rock. I'm still king of it.
I watch the dam. Somebody ought to. I count the weeps. Forty years ago it was three. Today it was thirty-one.
The keeper's widow went up there when her man drowned in the sluices. They say she's in the walls now, holding it together out of spite.
Crown foreman. Output is down nine percent. The guild says it's the coughing. I have noted 'coughing' as an excuse.
The dam is certified. Stop looking at it like that.
Carts to Cinderwake, slag bricks back. Bricks for the Crown's new furnaces. Furnaces for more slag. It's a wheel.
Washing doesn't dry here. It just gets differently grey. I hang it out anyway. You have to keep some rules.
Pipe? No? Everyone in Kettle Row smokes. Makes the air taste like something you chose.
West of here the old slag runs down the terraces like a river, still hot. The Slagfalls. Something walks up there.
North, in the ridges, there's Anvil Cairn - the smiths' shrine. The old forge-mother there will temper a blade for a song. A good song.
Kettle Row: the Slagfalls to the west still run hot, and something big walks the terraces.
Kettle Row: Anvil Cairn, the smiths' shrine in the northern ridges, keeps an old forge-mother who tempers blades.
Grandad says if the dam ever breaks, run uphill and don't look back. I practise every day. I'm very fast now.
I guard the road out. Nobody leaves Kettle Row owing the Crown. So, nobody leaves Kettle Row.
Slag lung. Everybody gets it. The Crown doctor says fresh air. I asked him where. He's still thinking.
The Slag and Kettle. Soup, a bed, a window that doesn't face the dam. The window's extra. Forty crowns.
We toast the dam every night. 'To the dam: hold one more day.' It's held forty years of days. Cheers.
Pipewright's Rest, up the viaduct, does a better stew. Don't tell Bessa. She'll put slag in mine.
Kettle Row: Pipewright's Rest, the pipe-inn on the viaduct north-east, does the best stew in the Reach.
Guild smithy. Picks, hammers, and anything else you can swing. Ore, if you've got the coin. Tonics, because we must.
I'm Ivy. The guild calls me Ember-hand, because I don't use tongs. I don't recommend it.
Bring me ore and I'll make it into something that keeps you alive. Iron first. Heartsteel from the hot places, if you're brave.
Slag's no good. Slag is what the Crown leaves you. Bring me what it doesn't know it's missing.
Iron ore, heartsteel, cinder hides, pipe brass. Bring it and I'll put it to work.
I quench the blades in the trough. The water comes down from the dam. Harrow says that makes them brave.
Guild Chair Dunn. We meet every week to vote on whether to ask the Crown to fix the dam. We always vote yes.
We've sent forty-one letters. They send one back every year: 'Received.' At least they're polite.
I move that we stop writing letters and start digging a second road. Seconded? No? Next week, then.
I've got four children and a rock in my chest. The rock's the only one that pays rent.
Don't mind the cough. It's how you know a Kettle Row man's still breathing.
Minutes of the Slag Guild. Item one: the dam. Item two: the dam. Item three: tea.
The mountainside is a staircase of black glass. Molten slag slides down it in slow orange sheets.
High above, something the size of a house takes a step, and the whole terrace shivers.
Slag runner. I carry messages across the falls for the guild. You learn where the crust holds.
The vents cool the fords if you open them. The guild built them when the Crown's flue started pouring. Nobody maintains them.
Up top, the overflow's got legs. We call it the Colossus. It's just slag that nobody told to stop.
The terraces are still hot, but nothing walks them. I can run the falls in half the time. Thank you.
The fault cracked the Crown's flue. The slag stopped. The falls are cooling. In ten years this'll be a hill.
I live here now. It's warm, and nobody collects anything.
The valve screams open. A blast of cold air roars down the channel, and the slag across the ford blackens and sets.
The vent roars steadily. The ford stays black and solid.
The crucible vent opens with a sound like a bellows the size of a church. Down on the terrace, the clinker over the upper stair cracks and falls away.
Cold air pours down toward the terrace.
You kick the chute gate open. A plug of cooled clinker tumbles away downhill. The chute runs straight to the foot of the falls.
The chute is clear. It's a quick, hot slide to the foot.
Prospector. Came for heartsteel in the crucible. The slag came for me. It's all right. It's warm.
The big one up top gets harder as it cools. Ice cracks it, but fire only feeds it. When its heart goes white, cover your faces.
Twisted my ankle on the last climb. I'm waiting for the ankle to agree to go down. It hasn't yet.
If you're going up: the Colossus burns everyone in front of it. Keep cool cloths ready. And don't stand in the pour.
A Crown furnace flue juts from the ridge above, pouring slag down the mountain. It has been pouring for twenty years.
A brass plate on the flue reads: 'OVERFLOW - ROUTE TO NATURAL TERRAIN.'
The slag at the top of the falls gathers itself. A body of cooling crust stands up, glowing at every crack.
It has no face. It has a Crown furnace seal pressed into its chest, still legible, still hot.
It's not alive. It's just the overflow, walking.
Walking toward the villages below. Stop it here.
The Colossus slumps, and cools, and cracks into a hill of black glass.
The flue above still pours, but the slag now runs into the crucible and stays there, like it has nowhere left to go.
The Slagfalls: the Slag Colossus is broken. The overflow no longer walks toward Kettle Row.
Seo. They call me the Anvil-Mother, because I've outlived every smith who ever called me anything else.
You carry Crown steel. It's poor. They fold it twice and call it done. Bring me ore and I'll fold it properly.
Take this for the road. Heartsteel, from the cairn. Pilgrims leave it. I don't need it; I've enough to finish me.
...And you. A rune-engine. I knew the smiths who cast your plates. You're better kept than they were.
Pell keeps me. I keep the rest.
Then take this, for Pell, and for the rest. Heartsteel. You'll know what to do with it.
Iron for the first fold. Heartsteel for the second. Starmetal only if the sky gives it to you. And patience, always.
I'm her striker. She points, I hit. Seven years. Last week she said 'better'. I'll remember it on my deathbed.
Quench water comes from the cairn spring. The Crown's smiths use slag water. Their blades sing flat. Listen next time.
Every smith of the Reach brings an anvil here once in their life. The cairn is a thousand anvils deep.
The Crown sent assessors to count them for scrap. They counted to four hundred, then asked for a blessing and went home.
The fault shook the cairn. Not one anvil fell. Smiths from the drowned towns come to strike them, just to hear them ring.
Journeyman. I carried my father's anvil up the ridge on my back. Three days. He'd have said I was holding it wrong.
They say the dam over Kettle Row is failing. If it goes, half the smiths of the Reach go with it.
Smiths are the only people in the March who haggle harder than me. I come here to be humbled.
Kettle Row's gone. We came up to the cairn because it was the highest place we knew. Seo feeds us. Seo feeds everyone.
I'm going to be a smith. I've already got a hammer. It's a spoon, but it's a hammer inside.
The Great Anvil stands in a ring of smaller ones. Its face is scarred with hundreds of smiths' marks.
One mark, near the horn, is a rune. The Golem looks at it for a long time.
That's my maker's mark. The same one that's on my heart-plate. I didn't know he came here.
...He struck the anvil twice. Pilgrims only strike once. The second strike means 'for someone else'.
Dunmore Pipewright. Fifth of the name. My great-great-grandmother built the viaduct, then built an inn on it so the builders had somewhere to drink.
Stew, bed, hot bath. Forty-five crowns. The view's free, and so's the swaying.
The bath's fed off the boiler pipes. It's the only hot water in the Reach the Crown doesn't meter. Don't tell them.
I come up from Cinderwake for the stew. And to feel the viaduct move under my chair. It reminds me I'm alive.
Pim, agent for Tobiah Wend. He sends the goods, I sell them, he complains about my prices. It works.
Olen. Brasswife. I bend pipe into whatever you need. Gauntlets, greaves, a kettle that whistles your name.
Bring me brass from the Crown's scrap heaps and ore from the ridges. The viaduct taught me: good joints hold anything.
Pipe brass, iron ore, cinder hides, boiler rivets. Bring them. I'll make them hold.
Hesta. Master of the viaduct. Eleven hundred joints, and I know every one by its voice.
The east piers are shifting. The Crown says it's the wind. It's the ground. Something under the Reach is moving.
Pipewright's Rest: the master pipewright says the ground under the Reach is moving, not the wind.
Hesta makes me listen to the pipes for an hour every morning. I'm starting to hear them in my sleep. They're worried.
I fit the steam lines from the boilers to the town. If you hear a whistle, that's a leak. If you hear a scream, that's me.
Valve-watcher. I watch valves. It's a good job. Most of the time nothing happens, and I'm the one who knows it.
Crown pipe inspection. Every joint on the viaduct is taxed by the inch. The Pipewrights built very long joints.
I drop stones off the edge and count. I've never heard one land. Old Ambrose says there's a river down there. I think it's the sky.
Laundry dries in an hour up here. The steam, the wind. It comes back grey, but dry. Grey and dry is a good day.
I laid the last stone on the east pier when I was nineteen. I'm ninety now. The pier's older than me and less tired.
Below, there's the river, and the old slag works, and the Weeping Dam. If that dam goes, this viaduct is all that stays dry.
Waiting for the steam lift down to the Cinderwake road. It comes when it comes. The lift has opinions.
Viaduct toll's been waived since the Crown couldn't find anyone willing to stand in the wind to collect it. Except me. For some reason.
I play the steam organ at noon. One chord. People say it's beautiful. It's the only chord it has.
Stall stew, half the inn's price and twice the pepper. Dunmore says I'm stealing his trade. I say I'm stealing his pepper.
Crown pension. Eight crowns a month for a leg. The other leg's still paying the Crown back, apparently.
A slab of cooled glass plugs the cave mouth, smooth as a pane and warm as skin.
Behind it, very slowly, something breathes. Each breath fogs the glass from the inside. Each breath takes a minute.
Do not knock.
You know what that is.
The oldest of us who never gave up its fragment. It sleeps. It wakes to eat towns. Let it sleep until you are strong enough to be rude.
Cindermaw Caldera: something ancient sleeps behind the glass seal in the crater. Ilyr says not to knock.
Imre, fire-reader. I read the caldera's moods from the colour of the lake. Today it's 'irritable'.
The lake rises and falls once a minute, like breathing. The Crown sends surveyors. The surveyors don't come back to argue.
Whatever is behind the northern seal has slept for a thousand years. I've written a paper. Nobody reads papers about things that eat towns.
The fault split the caldera rim, but the seal held. I camp here to watch it. Someone should know first, if it opens.
Some nights the glass glows. I pretend it's a lighthouse.
Tobiah Wend, pack-merchant of the whole March. I sell rope, tonics, and news, and only the rope is guaranteed.
I walk a circuit: here, the Gallowgate queue, the smiths at Anvil Cairn. Look for the man with the ugliest pack.
Back again. The Oathstone brings everyone back eventually. That's what it's for.
Still walking. The roads broke, so I walk the pieces. Somebody has to carry the news between the islands.
Refuge Rock, out on the Glass Coast shoals - they'll need everything I've got. You'll find me there too, some days.
Crown courier. Veyr to Gallowgate to Cinderwake and back, twice a week. I carry orders I'm not allowed to read.
I read them anyway. This week: more tithe, fewer excuses, and 'locate the Hollins gloves'. I don't know either.
Road warden. The Crown built the Oathstone as a milestone. The towns built the market around it before the mortar dried.
Every road here has a toll further on. Gallowgate east is the worst. Carry coin or carry a good story.
I walk to the Oathstone every spring and read the fifth face. It's an oath the first king swore to the March.
'No crown shall weigh more than the head that bears it.' The Crown's masons keep trying to chisel it off. It keeps being legible.
The fifth face cracked in the fault. The oath's still there. Just in two pieces, like everything.
I'm paid to recut the milestone every year. New distances, new Ministry seal. Old words underneath.
Found a carved box in the yard once, left for travellers. I left it there. Take what you need; leave the box.
Nobody pays me now. I recut it anyway. The distances all changed. The roads go into the sea.
Water, one copper! It's well water, not Crown water. Crown water costs two coppers and tastes like the lid.
The well's still good! Mum says it's the only thing in the March the fault didn't touch. I'm not charging anymore.
Waystones hum when someone who's walked far touches them. Lay a hand on this one and it'll remember you.
There are others. Gallowgate has one in the cart queue. The old keepers used them before the Crown numbered the roads.
We came up from the rift edge. Veyr's half under water. The Oathstone's the tallest thing left standing for a day's walk.
People leave notes on it. 'Gone to Hollins.' 'Gone to the Rock.' 'Wait for me.'
I'm copying the notes off the milestone into a book, before the rain gets them. Names first. Then where they went.
North: VEYR, CROWN QUARRY. East: GALLOWGATE TOLL, WREN'S ORCHARD. West: THE ASH BARROWS. South: HOLLINS MILL.
The fifth face, low down and half-chiselled: NO CROWN SHALL WEIGH MORE THAN THE HEAD THAT BEARS IT.
Paper notes are nailed all over the stone. 'Gone to Refuge Rock.' 'Gone to Hollins.' 'Mira - wait here.'
The waystone warms under your hand. For a moment you can feel the other stones along the roads, like far lamps.
(Waystone attuned: Oathstone Crossroads.)
The waystone hums. It remembers you.
The dam fills half the sky. Water weeps from a hundred seams in its face and runs down to the roofs of Kettle Row.
Somewhere inside it, very faintly, a woman is humming.
Guild sapper. They sent me to 'assess'. I've assessed. It's going to break. I'd like to go home now.
The service door's open. Something inside keeps the water back and the valves turning. It doesn't like visitors.
The weeping's slowed. It's not fixed. Nothing is fixed. But it's slowed, and the guild's cutting a second road.
Kettle Row was down there. The dam went when the ground broke. Two hundred people and the valley's a lake now.
Some got up the high road Grete made them cut. Thirty-one of us. Old Sallow counted. He always counted.
I dig for the guild hall's bell. I don't need the bell. I need to have dug for it.
You drag the lever down. Somewhere a gate slams, and the black current over the walkway sinks to a trickle.
The lever is down. The gallery race runs low.
The valve wheel fights you, then gives. Across the hall, the floodgate over the keeper's stair grinds open.
The valve is open. The race hisses past below you.
You draw the bolts on the maintenance hatch. Stale air, a ladder, and the dam foot far below.
The hatch stands open onto the ladder down to the dam foot.
I came up to clear the grates. She told me to go home. I didn't listen. Now I clear them forever.
She's not cruel. She's just holding a lot of water, and nobody ever said thank you.
Orrin. I kept this dam twenty years. The Crown wanted the water held for the furnaces. The valley wanted it let out slow.
I drowned in the sluices trying to do both. My wife came up after me. She's been holding it ever since. Holding everything.
When the gates shudder, she's about to let a breach go through her. Brace for it. And lightning - she never could abide storms.
Don't hate her. She's the only reason Kettle Row is still dry.
She's resting. The dam isn't. Tell the guild to cut that road. Tell them Orrin said so. They never listened to Orrin.
The woman on the crest walk is made of water held in the shape of a woman. Cracks run across her like veins.
Go home. Go HOME. Every one of you comes up here to tell me it's safe, and then you go home and I hold it.
Forty years. Letters. Certificates. Telescopes in the fog. Not one of you ever held a single drop of it.
We're not from the Crown. We came to help.
Then HOLD IT.
Every sluice gate on the dam shudders at once.
The Sluicewife sinks to her knees. The water in her runs clear, then slows.
...I can let it out slow. Orrin always said slow. I was so angry I forgot.
I can hold it a while longer, like this. Not forever. Tell them to cut the road. Tell them to go uphill.
She sinks into the crest walk and is part of the dam again. The weeping below grows quieter.
The Weeping Dam: the Sluicewife is at rest and lets the water out slowly. She warned that the dam will not hold forever.
The fault split the plain and something rose out of it: a ridge of white bone a league long. Ribs arch over the road like the vaults of a cathedral.
Ilyr?
I know this shape. I know it from the inside.
Dragonborn pilgrims came as soon as it rose. We walk the spine and leave a scale at every rib. My grandmother said a great one lay under the plain.
Something else got here first. It nests in the skull. It eats marrow and it's grown enormous on it. We hear it cracking the bones at night.
Carved at the root of the rib, in the old dragonborn script, weathered almost smooth: ILYRATH.
That was my name when I had all of it. Before I was a fragment. Before I was a guest in your chest.
This is your body.
It was. I let go of it a long time ago, to keep the part that mattered. I did not think I would have to walk through it.
You lay a hand on the crystal. It warms. For a moment you are flying - over the river farms, over a March with no roads, no Crown, no Veyr.
Before the builders. Before anyone built anything. There was just the wind, and the river, and me.
Deep in the spine, bone grinds against bone and loosens.
The crystal is warm, and quiet.
The crystal warms. You hear singing - small voices, in a language of hisses and clicks. Dragonborn children, on a hill, singing up at the sky.
They sang to me. I never answered. I thought there would always be time.
Somewhere ahead, the vertebrae unlock with a sound like a knuckle cracking.
The crystal is warm. Far away, very faintly, the song goes on.
The last crystal burns cold. Iron hands close around your heart and PULL. A crown of chains, a ring of men in masks, and a vast body going limp.
They came for the heart. Men with seals and relays, and one of them wore a crown. I let go of the body to keep the heart out of their hands.
I have been small ever since. In a jar. In a seal. In a soldier. ...In you. You are the best of the three.
I'll take that.
The knot of bone across the ribcage's throat unravels.
The crystal is cold. It has nothing left to remember.
You heave the loose vertebrae out of the gap between the ribs. Daylight: the Rib Gate, just below.
The gap between the ribs is clear.
Marrow's worth a fortune since the fault. Burns like oil, heals like magic. I only take from the small bones.
...That's a lie. I take from anything I can reach. The big one in the skull takes more. We're both thieves. It's just bigger.
I came to pray at the skull. The Tyrant nests in the heart-cavity now. Every night it cracks another rib.
It's a scavenger. It eats what's already dead and calls it strength. When it breathes in the dust, hide your eyes. Storm breaks its hide.
The heart-cavity is quiet. We'll leave scales there now, and sing. Maybe someone will hear it this time.
Scales, teeth, and a child's clay dragon with a lopsided smile. Someone has written on the altar in chalk: 'COME BACK.'
I cannot. But I can go on. Tell them that, if you ever find the singers.
The heart-cavity is a nest of cracked bone and shed scales. Something huge lifts its head from a split thighbone, marrow dripping from its jaws.
It is a dragon, but a lesser one: all belly and teeth, fat on the dead.
Get out of my ribs.
He means it.
The Marrow Tyrant crashes down among the bones it stripped. Ilyrath's skull is silent.
...Thank you. It is only bone. But it was mine. It is good to leave it clean.
Spine of Ilyrath: the Marrow Tyrant is dead. The ridge is Ilyr's old body, and he has walked through it.
The hollow where a dragon's heart once burned. The bone is scorched from the inside, as if the heart left in a hurry.
It left to keep burning. It is still burning. Feel.
Under your breastbone, something warm beats twice, very gently.
Where the plains were flat, a tower now stands, built of interlocking grey tiles that fit together too well. It is still growing.
Every few breaths, somewhere high above, a new tile slides into place with a soft, final click.
Surveyor Lanne, formerly of the Crown Survey. The tower rose the night of the fault. It adds one course of tiles every dawn.
It's building something to a plan nobody alive has seen. I would very much like to see the plan. I would also like to not be demolished.
We camp in its shadow. It's warm at the base - the tiles hum. Nothing attacks the camp. I think the tower doesn't notice us.
I found a road under the grass! A black one, smooth as glass, with white lines. It goes right under the tower. Mum says don't dig.
The console flickers: CONSTRUCTION PAUSED - COURSE 4417. Down in the central shaft, the fresh masonry slides back into the walls.
The console reads: PAUSED. It sounds offended.
CONSTRUCTION PAUSED - COURSE 4418. The course below you folds away. The shaft runs clear down to the lower floor.
The console reads: PAUSED.
TRAFFIC CONTROL: LANE CLOSURE LIFTED. The stair course grinds back into the wall. The way up is open.
LANE CLOSURE LIFTED. Somewhere a builder voice adds: DRIVE SAFELY.
You release the lift chain. The service cage drops down the shaft to meet you, then waits, humming. It runs straight down to the plaza.
The service lift hums, ready.
I climb the outside for the Survey. The tiles are warm and they move under your hands. Don't look at the joins too long. They look back.
Up top, the governor runs everything. It announces demolition before it does it. Very polite. Very thorough. Hit its core and it loses its place in the schedule.
The crown of the tower is a single vast room. At its centre, something of grey tiles and white light unfolds from the floor and stands.
VISITORS. NOT ON SCHEDULE. CONSTRUCTION WILL CONTINUE AROUND YOU.
What are you building?
THE PLAN. THE PLAN IS 4418 COURSES COMPLETE OF 90112. ESTIMATED COMPLETION: 212 YEARS. DEMOLITION OF OBSTRUCTIONS: NOW.
The Engine's light dims. Tile by tile it lays itself down on the floor and stops.
SCHEDULE... SUSPENDED. PLAN... ARCHIVED.
Far below, for the first time since the fault, no new tile clicks into place at dawn.
The Tessellate: the tower's governor is stopped. The tower no longer grows.
A builder road sign, bent double, half buried: MILE 0. RING HIGHWAY - ALL LANES.
Mile zero. I haven't seen this sign since - since the last night the lights were on.
This was my road. The Ring Highway. Six lanes round the whole plain. The tower's sitting right on the interchange.
You patrolled it.
I still patrol it. Nobody ever told me the patrol was over. There's a traffic control deck in there. If anyone ever wrote down why the road shut, it's there.
QC17 The Highway That Was: the Tessellate stands on Mile 0 of the Night Rider's old highway. Its traffic control deck may say why the road was shut.
Search the Tessellate's traffic control deck for the highway's last logs.
Mile zero. Everything I am starts here.
A builder console, dead. Lines of old light are burned into the glass: LANE 1 - VOLUME NOMINAL.
The console wakes at the Rider's touch. LANE 1, FINAL NIGHT: VOLUME ZERO. ALL UNITS HOLD POSITION PENDING RELIEF.
Volume zero. There was nobody on the road. They pulled everybody off, and they told the patrol to stay.
Hold position pending relief. That's the last {m:damn |}thing anyone told me.
A dead console: LANE 6 - SURFACE DECK SEALED.
LANE 6, FINAL NIGHT: SURFACE DECK SEALED. TRAFFIC DIVERTED TO LOWER DECK - LATTICE CONNECTOR.
Lower deck. The highway had a lower deck? They sent everything underground and left the surface to us{m:. Bastards|}.
Diverted underground. To the Lattice. That's where everyone went.
The dispatch relay's single key glows, waiting for a patrol code.
The Rider types a code from memory. The relay answers: PATROL UNIT 17 - STATUS ACTIVE - RELIEF: NOT SCHEDULED.
Not scheduled. They never meant to send anyone. They just forgot to tell us to go home.
The master dispatch console will be at the top, with the governor. If I can reach it, I can close my own patrol. Or not.
Relief not scheduled. The top of the tower. That's where I end this, one way or another.
Reach the master dispatch console at the crown of the Tessellate.
The master dispatch console of the Ring Highway. A single line blinks: PATROL UNITS AWAITING DISPATCH.
The Rider lays his hand on the console. Every screen in the room wakes. PATROL UNIT 17 RECOGNISED.
There. Dispatch. I can close the patrol from here.
Panels in the walls slide open. Patrol drones - squat, armoured, rimmed with red light - roll out and turn toward him.
UNAUTHORISED PATROL CLOSURE. UNITS: ENFORCE SCHEDULE.
The last drone rolls to a stop at the Rider's boots. Its red light goes out.
They were on patrol too. Same orders. Same night. Nobody came for them either.
The console waits. Two commands glow: PATROL ENDED - UNIT RELIEVED, and PATROL CONTINUES - NEW ROUTE.

options.text: Tell him to end it. He's earned rest
Tell him to choose a new road

cmds.text: You held it long enough. Close it. You're relieved.
...PATROL ENDED. UNIT RELIEVED.
The console clicks. For a moment the Rider sits very still, like a man who has put down something heavy he forgot he was carrying.
Strange. I don't feel lighter. I feel like I have room. I don't know what to put in it yet.
The roads out there are broken and there's nobody watching them. Pick a new route.
...PATROL CONTINUES. NEW ROUTE: WHEREVER THEY'RE WALKING.
The console accepts the order without complaint, as if it had been waiting for someone to give it.
The causeways. The Refuge Rock stair. The Oathstone road. I'll ride them all. Somebody should.
One more line scrolls up the screen: LOWER DECK - LATTICE CONNECTOR - STATUS: LIGHTS ON.
Lights on. Down there, under the plain. The rest of my road is still lit, and something's driving on it.
QC17 The Highway That Was: the Rider has settled his patrol at the Tessellate. The highway's lower deck runs on into the Lattice - the Highway That Was, deep below - and its lights are on.
Find the Ring Highway's lower deck in the Lattice: the Highway That Was.
The master dispatch console, dark behind the governor's cradle. The governor's light holds every screen in the room.
The console reads: LOWER DECK - LATTICE CONNECTOR - LIGHTS ON.
Marit Oakes. Warden of the Rock, because somebody had to be and I was standing nearest the rope.
Two hundred people on a rock that used to be a cormorant colony. We have boats, tents and one spring. The spring is failing.
And four of my fishers went down to the Tide Shelf three days ago, to salvage the wreck there. Tamm, Ansa, Dov. And Wynn - she's eleven. She wasn't supposed to go.
The gulls have been circling the shelf since. Gulls don't circle for fish.
A Crown supply hulk, washed up in the fault. If there's food or water gear aboard, it could keep us through winter. If there's Crown aboard, it could finish us.
We'll go down. Open the shelf gate.
Untie it yourself, the knot's mine. Bring them back. All of them, or tell me which ones to mourn.
QW1 Refuge Rock: four fishers are missing on the Tide Shelf below the Rock. Bring them back to Warden Marit.
Find the missing fishers on the Tide Shelf.
The shelf stair's south-east. Four of them. Ansa, Dov, Tamm, and Wynn.
Get them up the stair first. We'll talk in daylight.
Kell's lot are camped on the shelf with half the rations. They send water up every morning, and nobody's said thank you yet. We will.
The still drips all day now. Kell's lot take turns on it. Old Fenn still won't sit next to them at supper. He will.
Ansa. Dov. Tamm. Wynn. All four of them home, and Wynn with a scolding coming she'll remember when she's ninety.
Now. The other thing. Tamm says there are Crown soldiers on that wreck. Nine of them, and a sergeant.
They kept us alive, Warden. Harpies came every night. The sergeant stood in the hatch with a boat-hook.
Sergeant Kell, late of the Gallowgate Toll. We walked away from the Crown when the ground broke. We've a salvaged water still and the hulk's rations.
We'll give you both either way. But we'd like to come up. We're tired of the shelf. We're tired of being the Crown.
Half this rock lost somebody to a Crown toll, a Crown levy, a Crown convoy. You're asking me to feed their collectors.
...You brought my people home. You decide. I'll stand behind it, and so will the council, or they can find their own rock.

options.text: Keep them on the shelf, with a share of what they brought

cmds.text: They held a hatch against harpies for strangers. That's the only oath worth anything now. Let them in.
...Then they're in. They sleep on the east side, they carry water, and they learn every name on the council table.
We'll learn them. I used to collect names. I'd like to hand some back.
Not yet. Give the Rock time. Let them camp on the shelf, share the rations, run the still, and earn it.
Fair. It's more than the Crown ever gave anyone. We'll send water up every morning. Leave the gate unknotted.
The gate stays open. The door can come later. Maybe that's how it should be.
The still will save the spring. The rations will save the winter. You saved four people I'd already started to mourn.
Take this. It was the lighthouse keeper's charm. He said it kept the lamp honest.
QW1 Refuge Rock: the fishers are home, the salvaged still feeds the spring, and Sergeant Kell's deserters have their answer.
My Tamm went down to the shelf with the others. I stand here because from here you can see the top of the stair.
If you're going down, tell him the baby's teeth came in. He'll want to know. He'll want to come up and see.
He's home. He's asleep, the lump. The baby's biting him. I've never seen him so happy.
Out on the tide pools a woman stands on a rock, swinging a gaff at a ring of snapping, barnacled shells.
About time! Don't just stand there, they're HUNGRY!
Ansa. Thank you. They had me on that rock for a day. The others are in the wreck, with - well. You'll see.
Dov went up the north rocks for a better look and didn't come down. I think his leg's gone.
I'll wait here for the others. I'm not walking home alone after that.
Watch the pools!
I'll wait for the others. Dov's up the north rocks. The rest are in the wreck.
Don't laugh. I climbed up for a look and the rock climbed down without me. The leg's broken.
You splint the leg with a boat-slat and a strip of sail. Dov swears in three coastal dialects and one Crown one.
Tamm and the girl are in the hulk with the soldiers. The soldiers are - I don't know what they are. They didn't hurt us.
I'll hop. I'm a very good hopper. Don't wait for me.
Inside the hulk, lamplight. Two fishers - a man and a girl - sit by a patched Crown still, drinking from tin cups. Crown soldiers sit with them.
Don't draw. We're not what we look like. Or we are, and we've stopped.
Sergeant Kell. Gallowgate Toll.
You've a memory. I'm done collecting names, sir. We found these two with the harpies on them and brought them in.
It's true. They've been sharing the rations. The girl sleeps behind the sergeant. Nobody gets near her.
Take them home. And - ask your Warden. If there's room on that rock for nine soldiers who'd rather not be.
Take your fishers up. We'll follow when your Warden says, or we won't. Either way, the still goes to the Rock.
Take the fishers home up the shelf stair, then speak to Warden Marit about Kell's deserters.
I'm Wynn. I'm not in trouble. I came to help. I helped. The sergeant says I'm a very good lookout.
I was a toll guard. Now I'm a harpy guard. The pay's worse and I've never been prouder.
Halfway to the stair, the gulls stop circling. They fold their wings and drop. They are not gulls.
{m:Shit - harpies|Harpies}! Fishers to the rocks - soldiers, form on me!
The harpies break and scatter out to sea. Everyone climbs the stair together: fishers, soldiers, and a very proud lookout.
Back on the nets. I'll never complain about mending again. That's a lie. But I'll mean it for a week.
Leg's mending. Marit says I can't climb anything taller than a chair until spring. I climbed the chair. She saw.
Kell's lot camp down on the shelf. I take the baby down to see them. The sergeant holds her like she's made of glass.
The soldiers sleep on the east side. They carry water up the stair twice a day. Nobody asked them to do it twice.
I'm grounded until I'm twelve. That's in four months. I'm counting.
We run the still and send the water up at dawn. The gate's unknotted. One day somebody will come down and ask us to supper.
Kell. Just Kell. I carry water and I learn names off the council table. Forty-one so far. They're better names than the ones I used to collect.
They gave me a tent and a job. Nobody's asked for my papers. I keep waiting for someone to ask for my papers.
The cistern is cracked and barely wet. A tally of water rations is chalked on the rim, each line smaller than the last.
A patched Crown still drips into the cistern day and night. Someone has chalked over the ration tally: ENOUGH.
I build boats out of other boats. The fault broke a whole fleet on the shoals. I'm never short of parts. I'm always short of hands.
Every net here is three nets knotted together. You can tell whose by the knots. Glass Coast knots are neat. Veyr knots are angry.
I watch the sea for boats, harpies and the Crown. So far: boats. Harpies. No Crown. I'm grateful.
North-east, past the cliffs, there's a signal tower on a headland. Dark. If anyone lit it, you could see it from half the ruin.
Refuge Rock: a dark signal tower stands on a headland to the north-east. Lit, it would be seen across half the ruin.
I walked out of Veyr carrying my daughter and a bag of the wrong things. A clock. Two left shoes. I don't know why.
The Rock took us anyway. The clock still works. It's the only one here. People come to ask me the time.
I found a crab with a Crown seal stuck on its shell! I named it Sergeant. It pinched the real sergeant. Everybody laughed.
Marit says we'll have a school when we have a roof. We have a roof! It's upside down. It still counts.
Refuge Rock! Worst harbour, best customers. Nobody here has any money, so I take payment in news and fish.
Tell them at the Oathstone I'm alive. They worry. Well. Some of them owe me, so they worry.
I was a clerk for the Ministry of Provision. I used to write down what the Crown took. Now I write down who arrives.
Two hundred and twelve. I write the name, where they walked from, and one thing they want. Most want the same thing. To stop walking.
Spring-keeper. The fault cracked the rock and the spring's leaking into the sea. I'm rationing a cup a head. Soon half a cup.
The still makes more water than the spring ever did. I'm a still-keeper now. It's a promotion. I've asked for a hat.
I'm dragonborn. In Veyr they'd have numbered me for the relays. Here, Marit put me on the net crew and asked my name.
Your Raven carries a dragon, they say. Tell him - tell him there are more of us walking out of the ruin than anyone thinks.
I was a tide-librarian at Bellharbor. I saved one crate of books from the flood. It turned out to be the cookery section.
So the Rock eats well, at least. We are working through the soups alphabetically.
The Upturned Hull. Bunks, blankets, and a stove made from a ship's boiler. Pay what you can. You can, can't you?
Please. I walked from the Veyr Rift. I've slept four hours since the fault. Let me make it five.
We play for fish. I'm up three mackerel and a very small eel. The eel's a promissory eel. I haven't caught it yet.
Salvager Quill. Whatever the sea brings up, I sell. Mostly Crown gear, lightly drowned. Works fine once it's dried.
Nan. Wreckwright. I make things out of wrecks, which is lucky, because that's all the world is right now.
Bring me salvage - brass, oak, sailcloth, Crown steel - and whatever you've pulled off the beasts out there. I'll make it into something that floats. Or stabs.
Salvage brass, drowned oak, sailcloth, beast hide, Crown steel. The ruin is full of materials. It's just badly arranged.
Councillor Fenn. I vote on everything. Mostly 'no'. Somebody has to test the ideas.
Crown soldiers on the Rock. I voted no. I was outvoted. The sergeant brought me tea. I'm still voting no. Slower.
Councillor Rue. I run the kitchens, so I run the council. Nobody argues with the person who ladles.
Every name that arrives gets carved into the table edge. We're running out of edge. Rue wants a second table.
Hesk, Signal Company of the Skyspine. What's left of it: me, two keepers, a child, and a tower with no light in it.
The Last Beacon was the master lamp. When it burned, every waystone and signal lantern in sight answered. Roads by night. Ships home.
The fault put it out. The keeper, Old Mattock, went up to relight it and came down the cliff instead of the stair. He had the key.
He's on the ledge below the west cliff. We built him a cairn. We couldn't bring ourselves to go through his pockets.

options.text: What's in it for the ruin?

cmds.text: Light it, and the beacon wakes the stones - the old keepers' network. You'd walk from one lit stone to the next.
And your airship. The Company kept plans for a grapnel keel, for landing where there's no field. Light the lamp and my crew will fit it.
We'll get the key.
Ladder's down past the camp, at the west cliff. Be gentle with him. He was always cold.
QW6 The Last Beacon: relight the dark signal tower. The keeper's key is with his body, on the ledge below the west cliff.
Find Old Mattock's key on the cliff ledge below the Last Beacon.
The ladder's on the west side, past the tents. His cairn has a lantern on it. We couldn't light that either.
You've the key. The stair goes up to the lamp gallery. Griffons have been roosting up there since the fault. They won't like company.
The fire-cup's empty, isn't it. It always was the hard part.
Every night I climb up and look. Stones answering on the islands, lanterns on the causeways. Like the ruin remembering it's a country.
A cairn with a dark lantern on top. Beneath it, an old man in a signal keeper's coat, hands folded over his chest.
Old Mattock's hands are folded over a bronze key shaped like a lantern. It comes away easily, as if he'd been holding it out.
There's a stub of candle in his coat pocket. You light the cairn lantern with it before you go.
Climb the Last Beacon to the lamp gallery.
The cairn lantern burns, small and steady, over Old Mattock.
The gallery is thick with feathers and signal-flag nests. Something huge shifts behind the great lamp and unfolds its wings.
The griffons break out through the gallery windows and wheel away over the sea. The great lamp stands in the silence.
A lens of a thousand prisms around an empty fire-cup. It is dark and very cold.
The fire-cup is empty. In the lamp housing, wrapped in Crown oilcloth, is a shard of red crystal as long as your forearm. Heartglass.
A note in the keepers' hand is tied to it: 'SENT BY THE MINISTRY. BURNS A HUNDRED YEARS. WE DID NOT ASK WHERE IT CAME FROM.'
We know where it came from.
Dragonborn. Ground down in the relays until they were fuel.
Below, in the camp, Hesk's keepers are breaking up their last cask of winter lamp-oil, just in case.

options.text: Burn the heartglass - it's already been paid for
Burn the camp's oil, and bury the heartglass

cmds.text: It's already been paid for. Nobody gets it back by leaving it in a box. Let it light somebody home.
...Then let it burn for them. All of them. I'll remember whose it was.
The heartglass catches with a sound like a held breath let go. Red light floods the lens and pours out over the sea.
No. The Crown burned enough of them. We'll burn oil, and we'll carry more.
You carry the heartglass down, and the keepers carry the oil up. It burns lower and yellower than a Crown lamp. It burns.
Old Mattock's ledge gets a second stone that night: the heartglass, buried under the cairn, with its note.
Far out on the ruin, one by one, the waystones answer. Lanterns on the causeways. A lamp on Refuge Rock. A light on the Oathstone.
The great lamp burns. Every prism throws a road across the dark.
Look at it. LOOK at it. Mattock, you old goat, look at it.
Red light. It's beautiful. I'll hate it every night, and I'll climb up every night to look at it.
Oil. We'll be cold this winter. We'll be cold and we'll be proud of it. Tobiah Wend owes me a favour. He's about to find out.
Now: your airship. The Company kept plans for a grapnel keel - hooks and a winch, so a ship can moor on any cliff or field.
My crew will have it fitted by morning. Land where you like. The ruin's yours to walk again.
(The Lanternwake is fitted with the Grapnel Keel: she can now land anywhere on open ground.)
(The Last Beacon wakes the keepers' network: lit waystones can be used to travel between them.)
QW6 The Last Beacon: the beacon burns again, the waystone network is awake, and the Lanternwake carries the Grapnel Keel.
Signal-keeper, second class. There's no first class anymore. There's no anything anymore, except this headland.
We send flags by day. Nobody answers. You keep sending. That's what signal work is.
Seventeen answering lights last night. Seventeen! I've written them all down. I'm going to write to every one of them.
Griffons took the gallery after the fault. They like the height and the flags. Can't blame them. Can't climb past them either.
We take turns in the gallery now, tending the lamp. It's warm up there. The griffons come back and sit on the rail, like they're guarding it.
I'm the Signal Company's newest recruit. I know seven flags. This one means 'help'. This one means 'we're fine'. They look the same.
The cable lift ran down to the harbour. The harbour's under the sea now. So it's a lift to nowhere. I still oil it.
I saw the light from three islands away and turned my boat round. Hesk says I owe her oil. I don't remember owing her oil.
...I'll bring the oil.
New hands? Good. This coast wrecks a ship a month and gives it back a plank at a time.
See where a hull glints, where the weed's been scraped off? That's a salvage node. Hand in, and pull.
Some give iron. Some give tonic tins. Some give a ring off a man nobody's missed. The tide fills them again.
Try the split in the barge behind me, then the ironwork on the far wreck. Mind your fingers on the ribs.
Tidewrack: salvage nodes glint on wrecks and ruins. Search them; the tide refills them.
Glints on the hulls. Hand in, pull, and don't ask whose it was.
Since the fault the sea gives back houses. Whole rooms, with the table laid. I pull what I can. I leave the tables.
Wedged in the barge's ribs: a sealed tonic tin, and a fist of ore gone green with the sea.
The split in the hull is picked clean. The tide will bring more.
Under the weed, a strongbox hinge and a chain of good iron. The box itself is long gone.
Scraped ironwork. Nothing left but barnacles.
Nets are for fish. Since the fault I've been mending them for people. We drag the shallows after every high tide.
The Ministry takes a third of all salvage. The tithe barge came to collect it and ran aground. Now it's our roof.
They still send a man to count. He counts the barge too.
I dived the Brine Stair once, south of here. Smugglers' caves. The smugglers are gone and the caves are fuller.
Whatever lives in the brood pool took them. There's a pool at the bottom that hums. Don't listen to it.
The Brine Stair didn't flood with the fault. First place on this coast that didn't get worse. Tells you something.
Salvage tithe, one third to the Crown. Everything the sea returns belongs to the Ministry of Waterways first.
Yes, including that. Yes, including the barge. I don't write the rules. I just count them.
I found a boot with a foot in it once. Mum made me put it back.
We don't go to the lower beach. Mum says the houses that wash up belong to people who might still want them.
Twenty-two hulls on this beach. My Ander's boat isn't one of them. So he's still out there. That's how I count.
Forty hulls now. Still not his. I keep counting. Somebody on this coast has to be stubborn.
Every ship has a name on her stern. I copy them into this book. Somebody should know where they ended up.
That one's Crown Tithe Barge 11. It ended up as a roof. Some names do better than others.
I've started a second book, for the houses. Old Bellharbor's lower quay went under whole. Door numbers, mostly.
Bellharbor wanted our papers stamped before we could stay. We walked here instead.
The salvagers don't ask for papers. They ask if you can swim, and whether you'll share.
Storm lamps from Lanternfall, up the cliffs north. The lamp makers there light the whole coast.
Go at dusk. Their night market's the only place I know where the Crown's lamp tax gets paid in jokes.
The guild boats run from Belltower Point out to Saltwhistle Isle. Fishing tournament season, if you've the arms.
And if a boat ever offers to take you to Gullrock, say no. Nobody lands at Gullrock. Everybody leaves from it.
The fault dropped this coast a man's height. We bail the hall every morning and sleep in shifts.
Still dry, most days. Tidewrack's always been built out of other people's bad luck. We're good at it.
I'm from Lanternfall. Was. The cliff went into the sea with the kilns still lit. We watched it burn on the water.
Oda's people went south to Hearthward. I stayed. Somebody here has to know how to make a lamp.
Five months in the customs vault. We drank the rain through a crack and counted the tides by the bell.
When the knocking answered us, I thought I'd finally gone mad. Then a window came down through the dark.
The bell had a window. I could see fish looking in. They looked more scared than me.
Forty crowns for a bunk in a ship's belly. You'll sleep like the drowned. I mean that kindly.
Twenty. Half the town sleeps here now the lower houses flood. Step over the bucket line.
This inn was the Mary Coyle, out of Veyr. Wenna's grandmother's. She sailed it onto the beach on purpose.
Said she was done with the sea and wanted a house that knew how to float.
The inn gave us the cots by the hearth. Salt water in the lungs. It comes up slow.
The sea sells, I buy, you buy. Everybody makes a little, except the sea, which doesn't care.
Prices are up. Everything the sea gives back now used to belong to someone who'd like it back.
Hull iron, sea-glass, brine pearls if you're brave enough to go down the Stair for them.
Bring me what the wrecks give up and I'll rivet it into something you can wear. Salvage is just crafting with patience.
Wenna runs the crews. Nobody goes into a hull on a rising tide, and nobody goes in alone. Two rules. We keep both.
I keep the hall's book: what came up, who brought it, and whose it was, if we can tell.
When we can tell, it goes back. The Ministry calls that theft from the Crown. We call it the second rule.
Welcome to the Salvagers' Hall. Everything in here came out of the sea, including half my crew.
You want work, Tam teaches the nodes. You want trouble, the Brine Stair's south. You want both, stay for supper.
You've a ship now. The one that flies. Good. I've a job that needs something that can go where we can't.
Old Ossery at Belltower Point hears knocking through his lamp-glass at low tide. Three knocks. A pause. Three.
It's coming from under the water, where the Bell Quay used to be. Old Bellharbor. Someone's alive down there.
After five months?
The customs house had a vault. Stone, sealed, above the high-water mark. The quay went down; maybe the vault held.
