Go to Ossery. He's got the only thing on this coast that's ever been down there and come back up.
QW7 Old Bellharbor: someone is knocking under the sea at Old Bellharbor. Speak to Keeper Ossery at Belltower Point.
Speak to Keeper Ossery at Belltower Point.
We drag the shallows after every tide. Most of what we pull up is Old Bellharbor. Most of it is furniture.
Some of it isn't. If you ever find a way to go deeper than a rope, come and see me.
Ossery at Belltower Point, and whatever he needs. Every low tide the knocking's a little slower.
Eleven for eleven. I've been doing this thirty years and I've never had a count come out whole before.
Wenna sent you. Good. Listen. Put your ear to the glass. There.
Through the lamp room's cold pane, very faint: three knocks. A pause. Three knocks.
Every low tide. Coming up the old sea-stair from the drowned quay. Somebody's knocking on stone.
This tower's named for a bell, and the bell's a diving bell. My grandfather built it for the pearl beds.
It still hangs in the lamp room. But its window cracked the night of the fault. Without a window it's a coffin.
The smugglers in the Brine Stair had a diving helmet of real sea-glass. They used it to reach the brood pool.
Bring me that glass and I'll set it in the bell. Then we'll need a strong back on the crane, and a braver one inside.
QW7: find the smugglers' sea-glass diving helmet in the Brine Stair (the contraband hold), and bring it to Keeper Ossery.
Find the smugglers' sea-glass helmet in the Brine Stair's contraband hold.
The sea-glass, from the Brine Stair's hold. Low tide's in four hours. It's in four hours every day. Hurry anyway.
That's the one. Thick as my thumb, not a bubble in it. Hand it here.
The keeper works the glass into the bell's brass collar with tallow and patience. He does not hurry, and does not stop.
There. She'll take six at a time, standing, if they're friends. The tide gives us two drops before it turns.
Go down the sea-stair on the point and wait at the bottom rung. I'll lower her to you from the tower.
Descend the sea-stair on Belltower Point; Ossery will lower the diving bell.
The sea-stair, on the point. I'll be on the crane. Knock three times when you're in. I'll know.
Eleven came up in my grandfather's bell. He'd have been insufferable about it. I intend to be.
Under the oilcloth, packed in straw: a diving helmet of thick green sea-glass, bolted into a brass collar.
The smugglers used it to reach the brood pool and come back. Mostly. The collar has a name scratched in: 'ours'.
Bring the sea-glass helmet to Keeper Ossery at Belltower Point.
Old diving gear, a helmet of sea-glass in a brass collar. The smugglers left in a hurry, or not at all.
Iron rungs down the rock to the old fishing ledge. Gulls have made the bottom rung their business.
The sea-stair runs down into dark water. Somewhere below, the Bell Quay. Nothing is knocking now.
The sea-stair runs into the water. Ossery has painted the top rung white: 'Eleven. All of them.'
At the bottom rung the water is black and very still. Then the bell comes down out of the lamp-light, swinging.
Green glass, brass ribs, a hatch in the floor. The party climbs in. Someone knocks three times on the brass.
Down. The light goes green, then grey, then goes. Only the glass shows anything: a street, a door, a lamp post, fish.
Old Bellharbor. The Bell Quay, whole and drowned. Customs House, three doors down. A knocking, very near.
The bell settles on the customs steps. Behind a stone door a pocket of air, and eleven people, and a bell-rope.
You came. We heard you. We heard you every day and thought it was the tide lying to us.
Eleven. The bell takes six, and the tide gives us two drops. Everyone comes up.
Then who's first? There are children here. There's Harl, who can't stand. There's me, who wants to go first and hates it.

options.text: Send the children and Harl first
Ask them to decide among themselves

cmds.text: Children and Harl in the first drop. Everyone else holds the rope. We'll be back before the tide turns.
...That's fair. It's fair and I hate it. Go.
You've kept each other alive for five months. You know better than we do. Decide, and we'll carry it.
They talk for a long minute. The children go first, and Harl, and the woman who wanted to go first stays and holds the rope.
We chose. Thank you for letting us. Nobody's let us choose anything since the water came.
The first drop rises. Halfway up, the glass goes dark: something long has wrapped itself round the bell.
It lets go. The bell breaks the surface in the lamplight and Ossery is already hauling, shouting for blankets.
The second drop, before the tide turns. Five more, and a bell-rope, and the last of the air in Old Bellharbor.
Eleven. Eleven. I'll paint it on the rung.
Tell Wenna Coyle in Tidewrack that everyone came up.
Eleven? All of them? ...Sit down. No. Stand up. I need to shout at somebody and you're the nearest.
Ossery sent me the bell's plans by gull. A pressure skin, ribs, a glass keel. Built big, it'd fit under a ship.
Your ship. We fit the Lanternwake with a diving hull, and she goes under the sea like the bell did. Deeper.
There are more quays down there. More vaults. Maybe nobody in them. Maybe somebody. Now we can look.
(The Lanternwake has a Diving Hull: she can dive and sail under the sea.)
QW7 complete: everyone came up from Old Bellharbor. The Lanternwake can dive.
North to Skyspine, first bell, every day the sea lets me. The trigger's at the ferry bell on the Bellharbor road.
Two hours to the cliffs if the wind's kind. Four if it's Ministry weather. Pay me, not the Ministry.
Tied up by Ministry order until the archive business is settled. Whatever that means. It means I drink.
Skyspine's still there. The cliffs came down to meet the sea halfway. I run the Hearthward crossing now.
The timetable's the tide's, not mine. Nobody argues with it. That's the only thing the fault improved.
Saltwhistle boats go when the guild flag flies. Green flag, guild's taking passengers. Red flag, tournament.
Black flag, somebody's been lost off Gullrock and we're all out looking. We don't talk about the black flag.
Saltwhistle kept its flagpole through the fault. The guild flies green every day now, whatever the weather.
Doesn't mean passengers. Means 'we're still here'.
Ferry timetable, by tide: north boat at the first bell. Guild boats when the flag flies. Ministry boats never.
I also keep the drowning book. Two columns. The second one's always shorter. That's the lighthouse's doing.
The keeper feeds the gulls fish heads so they'll yell at boats that come in wrong. They're very good at yelling.
My husband rang the harbour bell in Bellharbor for thirty years. The Ministry took the bell for inspection.
He came up here and rang this one instead, in a storm, so the boats could find the point. The storm won.
They've added a line to the cairn for Old Bellharbor. One line for a whole quay. The bronze ran out.
We came off the lower quay on a door when it went. Floated here. The keeper pulled us out with a gaff.
He hears things through the lamp-glass. Knocking, he says. Everyone says he's mad. I don't.
Eleven came up in the keeper's bell. I knew one of them. I'd been lighting a candle for her. I still am. Different reason.
Lighthouse keeper. The Ministry stopped paying for the oil in spring. I light it anyway. Boats don't read budgets.
The bell up top's a diving bell. Grandfather built it for the pearl beds. Nobody's dived for pearls in forty years.
The lamp's still lit. The sea's higher, the rocks are new, and there's a whole town under the point now.
Some nights I put my ear to the glass and I'd swear I hear knocking. Wenna at Tidewrack says I'm not mad.
The lamp room: a great oil lamp in brass, and above it, slung from a crane arm, a bell tall enough to stand in.
The lamp room. The diving bell hangs from its crane, green glass eye facing the sea. The oil smells like weather.
Sea caves under the coast cliffs. Chalk arrows on the rock, crates rotting on the ledges. The smugglers' road.
The water here doesn't move with the tide. It moves toward the back of the cave, and stays.
The wheel groans round. Somewhere to the west the sea falls away from a gap in the rock with a long sigh.
The west sluice is open. The wheel won't turn back without a crew of six.
The second wheel turns. The channel north drains to the ankle, then to wet rock. The way up the Stair is open.
The north channel stays drained.
You take the key from the drowned man's neck. The cord has been tied and retied many times. It was his job.
The drowned smuggler. His hands are folded now. Someone had to.
You loose the rope ladder. It unrolls into the dark and slaps rock far below: the sea mouth. A short way back.
The rope ladder hangs down to the sea mouth.
DATE. CARGO. PAID TO HER. Salt, silk, forged passage papers. Paid: one man. One man. One man. Two men (storm).
The last entry is in a different hand: 'She wants all of us now. We are not paying. God help whoever finds this.'
Forty-one trips. Forty-one men. We told ourselves they were volunteers. We told ourselves a lot of things.
She's past the hold, in the brood pool. She sings. Don't sleep. Whatever you do, don't sleep.
She's quiet. The ledger's closed. Burn it, or read it out loud somewhere. Either's fair.
The brood pool is still. Then the water draws back from the edges all at once, toward the centre.
Something rises with it: a woman's shape to the waist, and below the waist, coils. She is humming a lullaby.
More of them. The men who came before paid in men. What will you pay?
Nothing. We're closing the account.
Then sleep, little debtors, and I'll write you down.
The coils go slack into the pool. The humming stops in the middle of a bar.
The Brine Stair is quiet. Tidewrack's divers will want to know.
Receipts, hundreds of them, in her hand: a crude drawing of a man on each. Some have names. You take the ones with names.
One tarred box is marked differently: 'HER SHARE. GULLROCK - UNDER THE STONES.'
Tidewrack's hall keeps a book for names like these. They will know what to do with them.
Blown glass, lamp chimneys, lenses for the lighthouse. Hold one to your eye: the whole market's on fire, safely.
Lamp oil, whale-free, fish-free, mostly-free of Ministry tax. Seal oil for the storm lamps. Don't drink either.
Moth-lamps! A jar, a wick, and a moth that's decided to stay. They only light for people they like.
...It went dark. Don't take it personally. It went dark for the tax man too.
Grief lamps. You write a name on the paper shade and hang it in your window. The light says: still counting you.
Most of mine go to Belltower Point and Tidewrack. The sea's very busy on this coast.
Lantern buns: baked in the kiln flue while the glass cools. Everything in Lanternfall tastes a bit of smoke. You get used to it.
Maps of the coast by lamplight, drawn by people who actually walk it. South of Tidewrack: the Brine Stair.
I've marked it 'no'. It's the only honest mark on the map.
Lamplighter. I light every lamp in the village at dusk and every one on the cliff stair. Two hundred and six.
The Ministry charges a tax per flame. So the lamp makers made one flame, and split it two hundred and six ways.
The Tallows up the lane lost their boy off the cliff stair in the wind. The whole village lit for him that night.
You could see it from the sea, they said. The boats came in by it. That's what a lamp's for.
I'm going to be a lamp maker. Oda says my hands are good but my patience is a moth.
Curfew's at the second bell, but nobody's enforced it here in years. You try telling a lamp maker to go to bed.
The cliff's creaking more this season. The old men say there's a line of builder stone under it. They say it hums.
I'm carrying grief lamps to Belltower Point for the cairn. Twelve names. I only knew two of them.
Hear ye: the night market opens when the lamps do! Glass, oil, charms, buns, and whatever Ysa's calling art.
By order of the Lampmakers' Moot, the lamp tax will be paid in full, in candle stubs, on the Ministry's steps.
I came to buy the Galloway works outright. Oda said she'd sell the moment the sea stopped needing light.
I'm told that was a no.
Galloway Lampworks. Four generations, one kiln, and a great deal of burned hair.
Bring me sea-glass, good tallow, a bit of ore for the brass, and I'll make you something that burns right.
The kiln sits on old builder stone. Keeps the heat like nothing else. Hums, some nights. We don't ask it why.
Don't touch the gather, it's hotter than it looks. Everything here is hotter than it looks. Especially Oda.
The Wick and Wind. Thirty-five crowns, a bed, and a lamp in the window that I'll put out when you ask. Nobody asks.
I came up the cliff stair for the night market and missed my boat three nights running. I think I live here now.
Tallow and Wick. Lamps, oils, charms. Every lamp we sell is lit once before it leaves, so it knows what it's for.
I've bought a lamp for every window in my house in Veyr. My neighbours will hate it. That's the point.
Tourney Master Oyle. The Saltwhistle Open: one day, one rod, the whole Ember Sea to fish in.
Biggest catch takes the Silver Hook. Second and third take smaller hooks and the right to complain loudly.
No entry fee. The guild pays for the tournament out of the fish. The fish have not been consulted.
Written in. Your name goes on the board under the ones who've won, and the ones who drowned trying.
Cast off from any guild pier. When you've a catch worth weighing, bring it to the scales. Good luck. You'll need it.
Saltwhistle Isle: signed up for the fishing tournament. Fish from the guild piers and bring the catch to the scales.
The sea'll be there tomorrow. So will I, unfortunately.
You're entered. Guild piers, one rod, and nobody's allowed to use a net. Yes, Gorse, that means you.
The champion of Saltwhistle! You're on the board in big letters. Vane's already practising for next year.
Winner of the Saltwhistle Open! Somebody fetch the chalk. Somebody fetch Vane, he'll want to sulk.
The Silver Hook. It's not silver. It's older than silver on this island. It's been lost overboard nine times.
Second place. A fine fish. Not the finest. You'll hear about the difference for years.
Third! On the board, in small letters. Everybody starts in small letters.
BIGGEST CATCHES. A grouper, 'the size of Oyle's mother'. A ray 'seen from Belltower Point'. A boot, 'with owner'.
At the bottom, newer chalk: 'NOT A RECORD: the Crown's fish tax, which is larger every year.'
Guildmaster Vane. Saltwhistle is the guild and the guild is Saltwhistle. Everything else on this rock is fish.
The Crown's tax on the catch doubled again. So we fish twice as much and eat half as well. That's arithmetic.
Stay for the tournament. We hold it every year the Crown forgets to ban it.
The Ember Sea boils in the east now. The fish came west, to us, all at once. Too many to land. Too many to sell.
So we feed Hearthward. Nobody pays. The guild has never been poorer or less ashamed of itself.
You're entering? Good. I like to know who I'm beating. I've come second four years running. Fifth year's mine.
I keep the guild rolls: every boat, every hand, every catch. The Crown asks for copies. I send them the old ones.
Nobody at the Ministry has noticed they've been reading the same year since I was an apprentice.
We lost six boats the night of the fault. The sea stood up. The guild flies green for them every morning now.
Smoked eel, pickled eel, eel pie. We have one fish on this island and we are going to make you like it.
Salt cod from the Pale Basin salt, cured on Saltwhistle racks. Keeps a year. Keeps a family through a bad one.
Bait! Lugworm, sand-flea, and the special, which I'm not allowed to tell you about until you've signed up.
Bait's free now. Nobody needs it. The fish jump into the boats. Grandmother says that's a bad sign.
Shell charms. You carry one at sea so the Tide Serpent knows you're a fisher and not a meal. It hasn't been proven wrong.
Weighmaster. I weigh the tournament catches and the Crown's tax catches, on the same scales.
The scales are honest. Mostly. The tax weights are a little heavier. We've never found out why. We've never looked.
Fish on the racks, salt on the fish, wind on the salt. Three days and it's cod you could build a house with.
I'm going to win the tournament this year. I've been practising on the harbour. The harbour's winning so far.
There's a cove on Gullrock, east, where the smugglers used to go. Mum says it's empty. Mum always says things are empty.
Brine Stair smugglers used to run their cargo out of Gullrock. Salt, silk, people. Captain Rask ran the boats.
She quit one night. Came in on the tide, sank her own cutter in the shallows, and never sailed again. Still lives out there.
Fish tax, salt tax, boat tax, pier tax. I'd tax the gulls if I could catch one. The guild says I can't. The guild is correct.
I'm from Hearthward, over the water. The guild sends a boat of fish every morning. I came over to say thank you.
They put me on the eel stall. I think this is my life now. It's not a bad life.
I watch the east. Since the fault, the sea over there is red at night. Something moves under it. Something big.
Guild boats back to the mainland from the south pier, whenever you like. Tell Brisa at Belltower Point we're still here.
The Gutted Herring. Thirty crowns, a hammock, and a bowl of whatever the guild didn't sell.
No charge. Everyone on Saltwhistle's family now, and family pays in washing-up.
~ Oh the Crown wants a third, and the sea wants the rest, and the fisher gets the bones and the salt in her chest ~
It's a cheerful song. You have to hear the second verse.
Tackle, stores, salt, oilskins. Everything a fisher needs except luck. Luck's on the shelf behind me; it's not for sale.
Net-wright. I knot nets, and I knot other things: charms, straps, harness. Bring me fish scale, shell and good line.
Brine pearls from the Stair make the best charms. The divers who bring them back make the best stories.
Sea-stones, fitted tight. The gulls scream when you touch them. Whatever is under here, somebody meant it to stay.
GULLROCK - UNDER THE STONES, the Matriarch's receipts said. You pull the stones down one by one. The gulls watch.
Beneath them, a strongbox, tarred and dry. The smugglers' share. They never came back for it.
Captain Nell Rask. Retired. Don't bother asking from what; the answer's on every Ministry wanted board from here to Veyr.
I ran boats out of the Brine Stair for eleven years. Then I saw what we were paying for the right to use it.
I sank my cutter in the shallows so nobody would sail her back. The others kept paying. Most of them paid in full.
You went down the Stair. And she's quiet. ...Sit down. I've been waiting eleven years to pour this for somebody.
The share's under the gull stones, north end. Take it. It was never ours. Maybe it's yours.
Nell says if a Ministry boat comes, I whistle twice. If a guild boat comes, I whistle once. I've never whistled.
I rowed for Rask. The fault took the cove's mouth and the sea came in grey and fast.
She got the lookout out on her back. I stayed with the boat. I'm still with the boat, it seems.
The flocks go up to the high pasture in spring and come down in autumn. The wind decides the days in between.
Rocs from Eyrie Hollow take a lamb a week. The queen takes more when she's nesting. We call it rent.
Half the flock went up the ridge the morning of the fault. The road came down behind them. We hear them some nights.
Carding wool. You comb it till it forgets it was ever on a sheep. Windrest wool goes to High Aerie for cable lining.
The Crown pays for it by the stone. They weigh it wet. We card it dry. Everybody's cheating a little.
I've spun on this step for sixty years. The wind turns the wheel if you let it. I mostly let it.
The wind's changed since the fault. It comes up from the new sea now, wet and salt. The wool won't dry.
We'll learn. We learned the last wind. It took a hundred years, but we learned it.
I'm going to ride a brackhorn over the mountains. Maddoc says brackhorns don't climb. Maddoc says a lot of things.
Wool assessor, Ministry of Provision. I weigh the clip and take the tithe. They hate me here. It's a small village. I hate me too.
Cable porter. Wool goes down the valley to the High Aerie cable, and the cable takes it over the chasm.
The Ninefold Shrine keepers run the other cable, up into the clouds. Nobody I know has ridden it and come back talkative.
I watch the sky for rocs. When I see one I ring this bell and everybody gets their lambs inside.
Eyrie Hollow's north-west, up in the crags. Poachers go up for the eggs. Poachers don't come down, mostly.
Brackhorn shoes. Iron for the road, horn for the rock. A shod brackhorn goes anywhere a goat can. Almost.
The old ridgehorns, the wild ones on the high pasture, go where goats can't. Nobody knows how. They don't tell.
My boy's up on the ridge with the Harl girl and the flock. The road's gone. I shout up every morning.
Sometimes somebody shouts back. I tell myself it's him and not the echo.
He came down on a ram's back, laughing. Laughing! I nearly killed him myself.
We lost the lower houses when the valley dropped. The cliff kept us. It always has. We're a stubborn cliff.
Old Crook's back in his pen, eating everything. He saved forty sheep and six people and he knows it.
Dad's teaching Bramble the high paths. She hates it. She's brilliant at it.
I was on the ridge four months. Snow, sheep, and Ysolde's cooking. I'd take the snow again. I'd take the sheep.
Maddoc Harl. I bred Bramble's mother, and Bramble's grandmother, and I'd know that saddle-sore walk anywhere.
Brackhorns don't climb, they plod. Plod long enough and you're at the top of anything. That's the whole secret.
You. You've been places. I need someone who's been places.
My daughter Ysolde took the flock up to the high pasture the morning of the fault. The ridge road came down behind her.
Four months. We see smoke up there some nights. Somebody's alive. The road's broken and I'm too old for rope.
I've untied the shepherds' gate at the top of the village. Go up. Bring her down. Bring whoever's with her.
QW2 The Ridge Road: climb the broken ridge road above Windrest and bring down Ysolde Harl and the stranded shepherds.
Climb the ridge road above Windrest to the high pasture.
The ridge road, through the gate at the top of the village. There was a winch at the second bend, for hauling hay.
Bramble's shoed with ridgehorn iron now. She'll take you over mountains. Plodding, mind. Always plodding.
I muck out, I feed, I get kicked. Brackhorns kick when they like you. I'm very well liked.
The Shorn Fleece. Forty crowns for a bed under two blankets and a sheepskin. Wind's free.
Twenty-five. The blankets are thinner. So is everybody.
I rode the Ninefold cable once, up to the Choir anchorage. There's a whole island up there. Crucible, they call it.
Arena. People pay to fight things. I paid to watch. I don't recommend either.
Wool and Iron: coats, spears, horseshoes and knitting needles. Everything a cliff needs.
Horn, hide and iron. Bring me roc feather, ram's horn, good ore and I'll make you something the wind can't get through.
Eyrie Hollow's full of feathers. Full of rocs, too. Those come with the feathers.
The old hay winch groans. A cable runs up the cliff; far above, a long timber beam swings out and drops across the gap.
It lands with a crack that echoes down the whole valley. It holds.
The hay beam spans the gap in the road. It creaks when the wind leans on it.
You came up the road? The road's GONE. ...You came up the road. Dad sent you. Of course he did.
Broke my leg the morning of the fault. Ysolde splinted it with a crook. It's been four months; I'm mostly crook now.
The high pasture: tents, a fire pit, a stone pen, and a great many sheep, all of them looking at you.
Ysolde Harl. I've six people, forty sheep, one broken leg and a ram who thinks he's in charge. Is the road open?
There's a beam across the gap. It holds a person at a time. Not a flock.
Then there's another way. Old Crook knows it. The ridgehorn ram, there. He goes down to the valley every week and comes back.
Goat paths. Ledges, the width of a hand. The rocs hunt there. It'd take all day, with the flock.
Or we carry Davin down the road now, and leave the sheep. They're Dad's whole living. But it's quicker, and Davin's leg is bad.

options.text: Carry Davin down the road now

cmds.text: Davin first. The flock can wait a day.
...Right. Right. We'll come back for them. The rocs will have some. Not all.
You carry Davin down in turns across the beam. At dusk the shepherds go back up with rope, and bring down what the rocs left.
Everyone and everything. Show us the way, Crook.
The ram stamps once and steps off the edge onto a ledge you hadn't seen. The flock follows him, one by one.
Halfway down, with the sheep strung out along the cliff, a shadow crosses the ledge.
The rocs wheel away. Old Crook does not look back. By dusk, every sheep and every shepherd is in the Windrest pens.
Tell Maddoc Harl at the Windrest stables that the shepherds are home.
Ysolde. ...Ysolde. Don't. Don't say anything. I'll cry on the brackhorns and they'll never respect me again.
And the flock? ...We'll rebuild the flock. We can't rebuild her. You chose right.
And the whole flock, down the goat paths behind Old Crook? That ram. That impossible ram.
Crook's paths. He's been walking them all his life, and now I know where they are. So will Bramble.
Ridgehorn iron on her shoes, and a week on the high paths. She'll carry you over mountains. Plodding.
(Bramble is now a Ridgehorn: she can cross mountains on the world map.)
QW2 complete: the shepherds are home, and Bramble can cross mountains.
Nine grooves run out from the basin to nine poles. The wind fills them one after another, never two at once.
Eight poles have bells. The ninth has only a groove, worn deep, as if something heavy once hung there and rang for a long time.
Windkeeper Aun. We keep nine winds here. Eight blow. The ninth stopped before my grandmother's grandmother.
It came down from the sky, they wrote. Choir-wind. Voices on it, singing orders. Then one day, nothing.
The sky cable runs up to where it came from: the Choir Anchorage, and the Crucible beyond. We keep the cable too.
Since the fault the eight winds blow all at once. The bells never stop. We sleep in wax.
And the ninth groove... hums. Just a little. Like a choir that's forgotten the words, humming the tune.
Cable's locked until the Arena crews re-rig the far anchor. The winch key's with the keepers. Talk to Aun.
Sky cable, basket, two hours up through the clouds. You come out over the Choir Anchorage. Don't look down; there isn't one.
I walked up from Windrest to ask the West wind for my brother back. He went over the edge in a storm.
The keepers say the West wind comes back as weather. So I'll stand in the rain. It's something.
Novice keeper. I polish bells. Eight bells. There used to be nine. I polish the empty hook too. Aun says it's respect.
I put my ear to the ninth groove every night. Somewhere up there somebody is still conducting.
The cable's down since the fault. Anyone going up now goes by ship.
The ninth wind belonged to the host in the sky: Seraphel. The Choir. They sang the Skyspine's weather once.
Our book says the Choir stopped answering its own soldiers first. Then it stopped answering us. Then it stopped.
Barley, mutton, wind. That's the shrine menu. The wind's the seasoning. You'll taste it by the second bowl.
'Day of the South wind. Asked for: a safe birth.' 'Day of the North. Asked for: nothing. It has nothing.'
An old page, in faded ink: 'The Choir-wind has not blown for a year. The keepers still ring its bell. Nobody answers.'
The crags above the Skyspine. Rocs' nests crowd every ledge; feathers the length of a man drift in the updraft.
Somewhere above, very large and very close, something shifts its wings and settles again.
You knock the brace free. The wind-shutter above swings open with a bang and the updraft howls through the chimney.
The brace lies in the snow. The shutter stays open.
The second brace gives. Across the chasm the upper shutter slams open. The poachers built these to keep the rocs out.
The upper shutter hangs open.
You work the great gold feather free. It smells of the queen: warm, dusty, dangerous.
Carrying it, you smell like her kin. The nest-walls might let you through.
Branches, and the smell of roc.
Egg-poacher. Was. We came up twelve. Eggs fetch a fortune in Veyr; nobles hatch them for hunting birds.
The queen came home early. I hid under the eggs. She sat on me for three days. I'm still up here.
She's calmer. You didn't take her egg? ...Good. Don't tell anyone in Veyr I said that.
You let the feather-rope down. It falls away and slaps the rock of Nestfall Ledge far below. A quick way back.
The feather-rope hangs down to Nestfall Ledge.
Drifts of moulted feathers. Beyond the cave mouth, open sky, and a nest built round the whole top of the crag.
A rest before it would be wise. So would going home. Nobody has ever called poachers wise.
The nest is empty. Then the sun goes out: a shadow, vast, sliding across the rim of the nest toward you.
Aurelle, the Roc Queen, drops onto her nest with a sound like a sail filling, and screams.
We're not here for the egg!
She does not care. Her shadow crosses the back of the party, and she rises to stoop.
Aurelle breaks off, bleeding gold, and settles over her egg with her wings spread. She does not strike again.
She watches you go. That is as close to a truce as a queen will come.
One egg, warm as a hearth, and a roc chick the size of a dog, hissing at you with its whole body.
Aurelle's eye is on you from the rim. You leave the nest alone.
You set a stick in the seep, and the brine climbs it and leaves lilac crystal. A month, and it's a flower you can't pick.
Nacre's glassmakers buy the crystal. The Crown buys the brine for the relay works. We sell the flowers to anyone who's sad.
Salt pans. We rake them at dawn before the wind gets up. The wind here takes the skin off your face if you let it.
The basin rang like a bell the night of the fault. The pans cracked. The brine comes up hot now, and it smells.
Water-warden. The seeps are the co-op's, not mine and not the Crown's. I say which pool rests and which works.
A pool worked too hard goes bitter. Like a person. We let them rest before that. Mostly we do.
I named my crystal stick Sorrel, after the herbalist. It grew crooked. She says that makes it hers.
Mineral assessor. Relay works want twice the brine this year. The co-op says the seeps can't give it.
I've been told to write down that they can. I've been writing slowly.
I've come from Nacre to study the Glass Orchard, west of here. Crystal trees older than the kingdom. They're not trees.
What are they? That's the grant application. I'll know when they pay me.
I'm walking to Sorrowmere, east. You leave a thing at the lake and it takes the memory. Just the one.
My daughter. I don't want to forget her. I want to forget the morning she drowned. The lake doesn't take mornings.
They say the lake's gone quiet. That it gives things back now. I went. I remembered her laughing. I'd forgotten that.
Crystal to Nacre, salt to Cinderwake, brine to the relay works. The cart goes out full and comes back full of paperwork.
This fence keeps the goats off the resting pool. Goats lick the crystal. Then they lie down for a day and see things.
The quake split the east seep. We're digging it out by hand. The crystal came up black on that side. We don't sell it.
I went to Sorrowmere after the fault. I wanted to forget the sound. The lake took it. Now I don't know what I'm afraid of.
I'm still afraid. I just don't know of what. Don't go to the lake to forget. Go to remember.
My mother's stick is in that pool. Her mother's too. Every family here has a stick in the seep, growing.
When I die they'll set mine. It'll grow crooked. I'll insist.
The Resting Pool. Forty-five crowns, a clean bed, and a cup of seep-tea that will make you sleep like a salt pan.
Twenty-five. The tea's still good. The beds are fewer; we gave some to the east seep families.
Salt caravan to Nacre. I'd take the long road round the basin if I were you. Sorrowmere's on the short one.
Sorrel. Herbalist. Seep-mint for the lungs, salt-root for the stomach, lilac-moss for when you can't stop remembering.
I grow everything in pots on the brine. It's bitter. Medicine should be a little bitter; it's honest.
Lungs. From the relay works, where they boil the brine. Sorrel's mint helps. The works don't.
I cut crystal and I set it. Brine-glass, lilac crystal, glass-orchard shards if you can find a fallen branch.
Bring me those and a bit of ore and I'll set you a charm that hums when danger's close. Or when it's windy. Hard to tell.
Temperance, chair of the co-op. The Crown wants twice the brine. The seeps want rest. I'm in the middle, like chairs are.
We've voted to give the Crown exactly what the pools can spare. The Crown hasn't voted. It doesn't need to.
The relay works are gone. Nobody wants brine now but us. We voted to rest every pool for a season. First time in a hundred years.
The co-op ledger. Every stick, every family, every pool. When a pool gives, the whole village gives. When it rests, so do we.
Pellam. Last orchardist. There were forty of us once. The glass trees don't need tending. We tended them anyway.
They're not trees. They grew here before there was a here. The builders planted them, the old songs say, and waited for fruit.
The fruit's empty. Perfect, and empty. My grandmother said they're waiting for something to be poured in.
The fault shook half the orchard down. The fallen trees are regrowing already. Out of their own glass. I've never seen it happen that fast.
Something in the Heart Tree woke. It hasn't opened its eyes. It's thinking about it.
Glass-cutter. Nacre pays for orchard glass by the pound. I only take fallen branches. Pellam watches me like a hawk.
Fair enough. I watched a man cut a living tree once. It rang for a week. He didn't sleep for a month.
The builder marks on the wall: nine circles, one filled. The same ring is on the Ninefold Shrine in the Skyspine.
Nine of something. One of them used. I think the orchard grew the Vestiges. I think the Heart Tree is a tenth, not yet picked.
People come here now to sit by the Heart Tree. It hums at night. It's the only thing in the basin that isn't afraid.
You put a hand on the glass. It is warm. Deep inside, the curled shape turns over in its sleep, like a child.
For a moment the whole orchard rings, very softly, one note, and then is still.
...It's dreaming. My blood knows the shape. It dreams in dragon. It's saying: not yet. Ask me again when you've asked yourselves.
The Glass Orchard: something sleeps in the Heart Tree. The builders called it a seed Vestige. It will not wake without consent.
The glass is warm. The shape inside sleeps on, curled tight, dreaming of something that has not been decided yet.
A lake so still it holds the sky upside down. Mourners' cairns along the shore. Nobody speaks above a whisper.
Look into the water too long and you forget, for a heartbeat, why you came. Then you remember. Mostly.
I leave something every month. A ribbon, a button. The lake takes a little of the grief each time.
It takes a little of him each time too. That's the price. I pay it. I don't know what else to do.
The lake gave something back. A morning, with him in it. I sat here and cried for an hour and it was the best hour I've had in a year.
The lake remembers everything it drowned. Villages, whole ones. It's full of other people's memories and it's heavy with them.
Whatever lives in the deep mere eats what we leave. Eats, and grows. Don't go out there to forget. It's hungry for forgetting.
No boat. The last one went out to the island of the lamp and didn't come back. The raft's still out there, tied up.
If you get out there, cut it loose and push it back to me. I'll owe you the fare.
You brought the raft back. The island's a short row now, for anyone who needs to sit by the lamp a while.
You light the drowned lamp. Its light goes down into the water, and the water draws back from it like a held breath.
The causeway rises out of the lake, wet stones, cut with names.
The lamp burns. The causeway stays above the water.
The second lamp catches. The lake shrinks back from the far causeway, and the drowned village's roofs break the surface.
The second lamp burns steady.
You pull the rope. Underwater, the chapel bell rings, slow and huge. The whole village shivers.
The lake remembers the lane out of the village. It gives it back, stone by stone.
The bell rope hangs still. The lane out of the village is dry.
Are you here for the bread? Merrow's is closed today. The water came in. It's always today, now.
Tell my daughter I kept the shop. Tell her. I can't remember her name. Tell her anyway.
You cut the raft loose from the island and push it off. It drifts across the black water and grounds on the shore.
A short way back to the mourners' beach, whenever you need it.
The raft line runs from the island to the shore.
The last lamp burns without oil. In its light the lake is clear: villages on the bottom, streets, a well, a school.
Beyond the island, the deep mere. The light does not reach that far.
The deep mere is flat as glass. Then, at the edge of it, the lake begins to climb the shore.
Heads rise out of the water: one, then another, long-necked, pale, weeping. Each one is humming a different village's song.
Leave it. Leave it with me. You'll feel better. Everyone feels better. Give me the worst thing and walk home light.
And what happens to the rest of it?
I keep it. I keep all of it. I'm so full. Give me yours.
The heads sink one by one. Where each goes down, the water clears, and something rises: a sound, a smell, a morning.
The lake is giving back what it took. All along the shore, the mourners are standing up.
The deep mere is clear to the bottom. Village after village, small and still. Nobody left in them to forget.
But the mourners on the shore will remember them now. That will have to be enough.
The old cable yard, painted over with a landing ring. The Lanternwake rides the updraft at her moorings.
Anchormaster Cleave. The cable from the Ninefold Shrine lands here, and the Crucible cable goes on to the Arena isle.
The Crucible line's shut while the Arena crews re-rig the far anchor. Ask me tomorrow. I've been saying that for a month.
See the chains on the rock? Stamped SERAPHEL. The host moored here once. It drifted north before my grandfather's day.
Cable crew. We grease the drum, check the strands, and try not to look over the edge. The edge is everywhere.
Some nights you hear singing from the north. No words. Just the tune. The old crew called it the Choir and spat.
Crucible Isle! Fighters from five kingdoms, beasts from the deep sky, and odds I'll give you personally. When the cable runs.
Until then I'm practising my patter on the cable crew. They've started betting against me.
Airfield now. The cable snapped in the fault; half the drum went down with it. We painted a ring where the yard was.
Put your ship on the ring and the updraft holds her. North of here, Seraphel's broken up and drifting. Don't moor there.
I came up the cable the day before the fault, to see the Arena. The cable went, and here I am. Six months.
At night the wreck to the north plays one chord. Just one. Over and over. I'd give a lot for a second chord.
My anchorage is an airfield. My cable's in the clouds. I'm still the anchormaster. Somebody has to hold the chains.
Seraphel's come close since the fault, drifting on its old chains. If you go in, tell whoever's conducting to stop.
The host's landing stair drops away beneath you to the Lanternwake's moorings.
Seraphel: a sky host of white stone, broken into islands, strung together by chains and old bridges.
Somewhere inside, an organ holds a single chord. It does not stop for breath. It has not stopped in thirty years.
At the broken gate, the Archangel stops. He does not draw his sword. He takes off his helm.
This is Seraphel. My host. I commanded its sky road for thirty years, waiting for it to answer me.
I thought it stopped answering because it fell. ...No. Look at the statues. It stopped answering long before it fell.
Do you want to go in?
I want to know why. I'll judge it by what I find in there, not by what I was told. Walk with me.
QC10 The Host That Stopped Answering: the Archangel has come home to Seraphel. Learn why the host stopped answering.
Find the host's muster roll in Seraphel.
You draw the organ stop at the altar. Far off, the chord gains a second note. The north gate's first silver bar hums and lifts.
The stop is drawn.
The second stop. A third note joins the chord, and for a moment it is almost music. The second silver gate lifts.
The stop is drawn.
Nine hundred names in nine columns. At the head of the first, one name has been struck through with a single clean line.
Beside it: 'RELIEVED OF COMMAND BY ORDER OF THE CHOIR. NOT TO BE INFORMED.'
That's my name. Relieved. Thirty years ago. They relieved me and didn't tell me, so I would keep holding the road.
I held it because nobody told me it had ended. That was the order. That was all I was, to them.
They made you dead on paper so you'd stay useful. I know that trick. I'm sorry it was done to you.
The sentinels on the walk will have been told the same. Let's see what they were told.
Find the sentinels still holding their posts on the Sentinel Walk.
Halt. The host holds this walk until relieved. We have no order to let you pass. We have no order to stop you.
We hold.
The chord has changed. Something happened in the loft. We have no order for this. We are holding anyway.
I am thinking about what the Commander told us. Thirty years is a long time to think about nothing. Now I have something.
Stood down, by the Commander's order. I don't know where to stand now. I will stand here until I do.
Commander? ...Commander. We held. We were told you had been relieved. We were told to hold until the Choir called.
The Choir has not called in thirty years. The conductor still conducts. We hear it every night. Nobody sings.

options.text: Tell them what you have seen, and let them choose

cmds.text: Sentinels. By my authority as your commander: stand down. You are relieved. All of you.
...By your order, Commander. It is good to have an order again. It has been so long.
It was easy for them to take. I gave it for that reason. I hope it was the right one.
I won't order you. Orders are why you are still standing here. I'll tell you what I've seen.
Below us the world broke. People are rebuilding it with their hands. Nobody commands them. They choose to.
You can hold this walk, or come down, or go anywhere at all. It's yours to judge.
...Nobody has asked us anything in thirty years. May I think about it, Commander?
As long as you need. That's the answer I should have been given.
Climb to the choir loft, where the conductor still conducts.
You lift the latch-bar. The braced arch groans open onto the broken gate: a short way back to the landing stair.
The arch to the broken gate stands open.
Rows of empty choir stalls. At the front, a tall winged shape in rotted white, its back to you, conducting.
The baton moves in perfect time to nothing. Then, far off, the broken organ answers with its one chord.
Late. You are all late. Take your places. The Choir will answer. The Choir always answers.
There's no choir. There's nobody left to sing.
Choirmaster. It's me. You relieved me thirty years ago and let me keep holding the road. Why?
Commander. You were needed to hold. Holding needs no reasons. Take your place.
The baton falls. The Seraph's wings fold, and it kneels in the empty loft. Far off, the organ's chord falters.
The Seraph kneels by the stand, wings folded, very still. It is waiting for an order nobody here will give.
Commander. Give me an order. I have conducted thirty years because no one told me to stop. Tell me to stop.
I ordered the sentinels to stand down. It was kind, and it was easy, and it was one more order.

options.text: Light the fire and wait for dark

The last one. North-east, by the old toll post.

Open it. Whatever it holds now, it's been waiting longer than me.

The water in it is warm, and it moves against the current.

The east brazier burns.
The south brazier lights. The frozen well in the ward begins, very faintly, to steam.
The south brazier burns.
With all three braziers burning, the barbican gate weeps.
The ice sheathing it slumps and falls away in great wet slabs.
A sentry frozen solid at his post, spear still grounded. Frost has grown over his face like a visor.
As you pass, you would swear his eyes follow you.
The winch screams with frost, then turns. A portcullis rises into the middle hall.
The winch is wound.
The second winch turns. The inner portcullis lifts, dripping.
The winch is wound.
You drag the bar from the sally-port. It opens onto the frozen causeway: a quicker way back.
The sally-port is open.
A courtier half-thawed from the ice, still kneeling. Her lips move.
"...is it spring? Has the Emperor called for us? We were told to wait for his call..."
I called, Dama Irelle. Three hundred years ago I called you to stay.
I am sorry. I am calling again. Rest.
The woman smiles and is still.
Before the inner court's sealed doors stands a titan of frost: a horned warden, armour grown over with rime three hundred winters deep.
NONE ENTER THE COURT. THE COURT IS IN MOURNING. THE COURT WILL ALWAYS BE IN MOURNING.
Warden. It is I. The one who set you here. I was wrong. Stand aside.
THE ONE WHO SET ME HERE ORDERED THAT NONE ENTER. NOT EVEN HIM. ESPECIALLY NOT HIM.
...Yes. I did say that. I was very thorough, when I was grieving.
The Warden kneels. Its horns crack, and the frost falls from its armour in a long white sigh.
Inside, there is nobody at all.
Behind it, the seal on the inner court stays shut: a yard of blue ice, carved with a crown.
Whatever it keeps, it keeps.
The Frosthorn Warden is broken. The inner court of Coldharbour remains sealed in ice.
Behind it, the seal on the inner court glows faintly, and a line of old writing surfaces in the ice: FOR HIS HAND ONLY.
The seal answers to my hand. Come. Let us see what I kept.
QC13: The Warden is broken. Enter Coldharbour's inner court with the Lich King.
Enter the inner court of Coldharbour
The seal on the inner court: a crown carved in the ice, and under it a line that will not stay legible, however you look.
The seal has thinned to a skin of blue ice.
The Lich King's handprint is pressed into it, fingers spread.
At the causeway's midpoint the Lich King stops, and does not move for a long time.
Coldharbour. My seat. I made it a tomb and called it a court.
The Frosthorn Warden still stands at the inner gate, I think.
I told it to let no one in. My court is inside, waiting for me to tell them they may rest.
I told them to wait. I was their emperor. They did as they were told.
They have been doing it for three hundred years.
QC13: The Frosthorn Warden guards the inner court of Coldharbour. Break it, and let the Lich King into his own court.
Break the Frosthorn Warden
The Warden is already broken? ...Then someone came before me. And the seal waits for my hand.
QC13: Enter Coldharbour's inner court with the Lich King. The seal on the Warden's gate answers to his hand.
Enter the inner court of Coldharbour
Majesty. You are late.
You are three hundred years late, and I have had nothing to do but keep the minutes.
Vesk. Where is the court? The hall held four hundred.
Gone below, Majesty.
When the singing came up the stair - a woman's voice, from the Hollow Throne - they went down to her.
She promised them a court that never ends.
I stayed. Somebody had to keep the minutes. Somebody had to tell you.
Minute the last: The Emperor returned. The Chancellor was, for once, glad to be interrupted.
My Emperor. The guard held the gate. The guard held it against everyone.
Even the court, when they wanted to come back up.
They came back once, Majesty. Up the stair. Changed.
Pale-eyed. I didn't let them in. You'd said none enter.
You kept my order past its meaning, Ormund. So did I. We will have to learn to stop together.
The gate is yours, Majesty. It was always yours. I'm only very tired of standing at it.
You came back. I told them you would.
They said an emperor who freezes his court doesn't come back, he just gets colder.
The ones who went below - she calls them her guests. The Mother.
She keeps them the way you kept us. Only she doesn't grieve. She collects.
Mother Sepulchre. Velkhar's teacher. So my mourning court is someone's treasury now.
The Rime Throne's cold. It always was. Sit on it or don't, Majesty. But tell us what you've decided.
(The three who stayed are waiting by the Rime Throne.)
The Rime Throne. Empty.
The frost on the seat has the shape of someone who sat there for a very long time.
Not yet. Let me hear all three of them first. I owe them that much listening.
The Rime Throne. Empty, and not waiting for anyone now.
The Rime Throne. Empty.
The frost on the seat has the shape of someone who sat there for a very long time.
Vesk. Ormund. Ysolde. You stayed when the court went down. You kept my orders past all meaning.
I gave up a crown that outlived its people once, in the cradle.
I am learning that I have to keep giving it up.

options.text: Ask them to keep the seat until the court comes home

cmds.text: You may rest. That is not an order. It is the thing I should have said three hundred years ago.
Minute the last. The Emperor, for once, said the right thing.
The three of them bow, all together, and the frost takes them gently, like sleep.
They do not get up again. They do not need to.
Keep the seat. Not for me. For them - the four hundred below.
When I bring them up, someone must be here to open the door.
That's an order I can keep, Majesty. It has an end in it.
Bring them home. Bring her guests home. We'll have the fires lit.
The stair behind the throne goes down.
Down past the roots of Coldharbour, into the Hollow Throne. My court is there.
I will not leave them in another's keeping. We go down.
QC13: The Lich King's mourning court went down into the Deep, to Mother Sepulchre's Hollow Throne. Follow them to the Lich Stair (U35), below the Hollow Throne.
Find the Lich King's court at the Lich Stair, in the Deep
A stair cut down into the ice, going further than the citadel's foundations.
Cold air rises from it, and faint singing.
The stair goes down into the dark and the singing.
It is sealed by a slab of black ice from below - the Lich Stair must be reached from the Deep.
She has closed it from her side. Of course she has.
We'll come at her from the Hollow Throne, then, by the long way.
The rim. Far down, where no light should be, something is lit.
The Crown's iron cap covers the rest, bolted and chained.
Across the cap, stencilled in letters a yard high: CROWN PROPERTY. GREAT PIT No. 3. SEALED BY ORDER.
The aurora burns green above it, and the green goes down into the cracks around the cap as if it were being drunk.
The cap is gone. The Pit is open: a round black well a mile across, and at the bottom, very far down, pinpricks of light.
Lanterns, or eyes, or cities.
The rim is flat and wide enough to set an airship down.
Someone has already painted a landing mark in red on the snow.
Crown pit-warden. I guard the cap. From what? Thieves, I'm told. What would a thief steal? The hole?
Some nights the cap is warm. Some nights it hums. I've asked for a transfer eleven times.
I paint the aurora.
It's brightest here, right over the Pit - it pours down into it like a river going home.
My grandmother said the lights are the dead of the north, looking for a way down.
I think they found one.
Delver pilot. We came up the Pit when the cap fell.
The rim makes a fine landing field. You bring an airship here, you can go down.
Down needs a drill, mind. The Deep's not a hole, it's a country.
You'll want Horrach's auger if you mean to fly into it.
You came down the slope? On purpose? Then you're either Crown or mad.
The floor just went. Forty feet of quarry, straight into this. The lift came with us.
Hess broke his leg on the fall. We've been splinting it with rail.
Don't touch the red stone. It's warm. It's always warm.
The foreman's lot went south with lamps and picks. Said the Crown had a camp down here already.
Already. Before the floor fell. You think about that.
Stay back from the crack. It moved twice since your people fell in.
I'm from Emberwell, south and east. Dragonborn. We felt the quarry come down in our teeth.
...You smell of fire, scale-kin. Old fire. Come to Emberwell. The Matron will want to see you.
A lift cage lies on its side, cable coiled beside it. The brake shoes are worn to the rivets.
Scratched into the frame: 'Shift four. Nobody sent the cage back up.'
A crust of cooled rock bridges the lava crack. It rings like a pot when you step on it.
Karag Dun. Mind the bridge, it's older than your family.
We don't search strangers. We used to. The Crown's men made it a habit and we stopped out of spite.
Since the fault the moat's risen a hand. The bridge sweats now.
Ore goes out that gate on the Crown's carts. Food comes in on ours. You can guess who counts which.
Cap bread! Grown on the Fungal Terraces, baked on a forge-back. Tastes of smoke and dirt, like home.
The terrace folk are west and south, past the geode trees. They trade spores for iron.
The Geode Wood, south-west. Crystal trees taller than the hall. You can hear them grow if you lie still.
Something big lives in the heart of it. Many mouths, all glass. We stopped sending lads.
(A long cough.) Deepforge lung. Firedamp and iron dust. Half the second shift has it.
The king says the mines will open again. The king says a lot of things to the Crown, too.
Scale-cloth from Emberwell. Won't burn, won't tear, won't sell - not since the Crown dig took their menfolk.
Emberwell's a day south-east, by the warm rivers. Ask for the Matron.
My da says a dragon sleeps under the whole city and if you're loud it'll roll over.
I'm very loud. Nothing's rolled over yet.
Crown escort, ore detail. Move along. The carts have right of way here - king's own word.
The Crown carts stopped coming after the sky broke. Nobody in Karag Dun is sorry.
We're sorry about the rest. The quake took the east galleries and two hundred souls.
Every forge in the ward drinks from that channel. The lava comes from the king's well, far under.
Crown ingots on the left, delver tools on the right. Guess which pile's bigger.
You want to see a Deepforge ingot? Here. Feel it. Still warm after a year.
They come out of the Forge-Wurm, you know. Not the rock. The wurm eats ore and we dig out what it leaves.
I made the king's crown. Iron, no gems. He wore it to meet the Crown's envoy. They laughed.
He hasn't worn it since. He signed their paper instead.
We keep the forge-flame. It is the oldest fire in Karag Dun, older than the kings.
The dragonborn say it was a dragon's breath once. We say it was a gift. Both can be true.
Factor Pym is inside. He'll see you if you're paying. He'll see you faster if you're owing.
The Factor's gone. I'm still here. Nobody told me to stop.
Master Branna says I'm allowed to hold the tongs next year. This year I'm allowed to fetch water.
If you bring her ore she'll make anything. Heartsteel from the deep seams is best.
The Crown takes heartsteel and leaves us iron. Their dig south-east takes the rest before it's even ours.
The Crown Dig, they call it. The dragonborn call it worse.
Names cut into the rock, row on row. The newest rows are shallow. The mason ran out of time.
The last line: 'Deepforge, second shift. The wurm and the air. The debt.'
I cut the names. One a day now, when it used to be one a season.
The king comes at night, alone. He reads them all. Then he goes back in and signs whatever Pym brings.
The king sees petitioners. He doesn't always hear them.
Speak plain in there. He hates speeches. He's had enough of the Crown's.
You're the surface lot. Good. Father won't listen to delvers any more, maybe he'll listen to strangers.
Ask him about the debt. Watch his hands when you do.
Father sleeps now. First time in years. The mason's cutting fewer names.
My Toren's up there. Fourth row. They spelled it right, at least.
Anvil and Ale. Beds by the forge wall, warm all night. Forty crowns and you'll sleep like the dead.
...Sorry. Bad saying, this year.
Forty crowns. Boots off the blankets.
Deepforge was the richest seam in the Deep. Now it's a wurm's larder and the king's shame.
Somebody ought to go down and kill the thing. Somebody not us.
Nib, pedlar, at your service. Karag Dun to Railhead Nine and back, if the rails hold.
A tip for free: the Cinderlake ferrymen take coin or stories. Tell a good one.
Outfitters by royal charter. The charter's framed. The royal part's in pawn.
My husband's pick is by the door. The Crown sent a bill for it. Equipment not returned.
I paid it. I don't know why I paid it.
When I'm big I'm going to the Deepforge and I'm going to kill the wurm with Da's pick.
Branna Coalhand, master of this forge, and don't call me smith. Smiths make horseshoes.
Bring me ore. Iron for a start, heartsteel from the deep seams for real work, starmetal if you find a miracle.
Deepforge had the best heartsteel in the world. The wurm has it now. In its gut, mostly.
You're doing the king's errand? Good. If you kill that wurm, bring me what it's been eating.
Every delver in the city has a page. Some have two. The king has a whole book.
The Factor left with the good ledger. He forgot the bad one. I've been reading it.
The king wants the contract? It's here. It was always here. Nobody asked.
A Crown strongbox, bolted to the floor. Stencilled: KARAG DUN - PRINCIPAL AND INTEREST.
Surface folk. In my hall. The Crown sends worse, and more often.
You want something. Everyone who comes down here wants something. Ore. Iron. Air.
Majesty. Tell them about Deepforge.
...Deepforge was our best seam. A wurm came up through the floor and ate the heartsteel. Then the miners.
I owe the Crown for the pumps and the props and the lamps. I owe them for the wurm's leavings. I owe them for the dead.
I am King Under the Mountain and I have not paid a debt in eleven years. I have only signed for more.
No. It is not. Go on, then.
...Then clear it. Kill the wurm. Then come back and tell me what I should do with a mine that works again.
QUP3: King Horrach's Deepforge Mines are held by the Forge-Wurm. Clear the mines (south-west, past the rails), then return to the Stone Throne.
They tell me the wurm is dead. Some fool surfacer went into Deepforge and came out again.
...You. Stand where I can see you.
Deepforge. South-west, past Vaultmouth. The wurm is in the deepest gallery. Take lamps. Take more lamps.
The mine is free. The Crown will hear by week's end, and Pym will be at my door with a new page.
Majesty, the Factor holds the contract. Nobody in this hall has ever read it. Only signed it.
Then read it. You, surfacers. Go to the counting house in the Forge Ward and make Pym show you the paper.
QUP3: Deepforge is clear. Make Factor Pym show the Karag Dun debt contract (Crown Counting House, Forge Ward).
Pym. The counting house. The contract. I will not read it myself, I have tried. My eyes stop working.
We ship ingots to the Crown under a debt we understand now. It is smaller than they said. It is still a debt.
But I read it. That is the difference. I read every page.
No carts leave my gate for the Crown. They will come for it. Let them come down the stair and ask.
Thane Orsik, steward. I count what the king will not.
Eleven years of interest on pumps that failed. On props that cracked. On lamps that went out with men under them.
The Auger plans are the old kings' work. Your airship will bite rock like a delver's pick, when you have one to fit.
Factor Pym, Crown Deep Accounts. If you are not here to pay, you are here to waste my afternoon.
The delvers are good tenants. They never read the terms. I recommend the same to you.
The contract? It is Crown property. It is also, technically, the king's copy. He has never asked for it.
Threats. In a counting house. How very delver of you.
...Fine. It's no secret, only unread. Page nine. Clause the fourth. Please try not to shout.
The terms are the terms. Take it to your king. He signed it. Several times.
The Factor's desk is empty. His chair is on its side.
"Where principal cannot be met in ore, the Crown shall accept labour in lieu, to be valued at the Factor's discretion."
Below it, in the Factor's hand: every dead miner of the second shift, valued at four crowns each. Credited to the Crown.
He charged them for the men who died paying him.
QUP3: The contract values the dead at four crowns each and credits them to the Crown. Bring it to King Horrach.
Show me.
Horrach reads page nine. Then he reads it again. His hands are still.
Four crowns. My miners. Four crowns each, and I signed the page under it.
Majesty. With Deepforge open we can pay the true principal in two years. Without the lie in clause four.
Or we can stop paying at all. Burn it. Let the Crown come down the stair and collect from us in person.
Surfacers. You cleared the mine. You read the paper. You choose. I have chosen wrong for eleven years.

options.text: "Pay the true principal. Strike clause four."

cmds.text: Orsik. Draw up the true sum. We pay what we borrowed. Not a crown for the dead.
With pleasure, Majesty. With more pleasure than you know.
Horrach tears the page. Then the book. Hild laughs out loud in the hall.
Let Pym write that down.
One thing more. The old kings drilled downward with an engine of their own. Too big for a cart. Too big for a delver.
They called it the Auger. The plans are yours. If you ever have a ship that flies, it will dig as well.
(Obtained the Delver Auger plans. The Lanternwake can be fitted to drill into the Deep through the Great Pits.)
QUP3 complete: Karag Dun's debt is settled on the king's terms. The Delver Auger plans are ours.
A Crown valve wheel, chained and padlocked. The pipe beside it is cold outside and roaring inside.
Stamped on the collar: DEEP WORKS HEAT RECOVERY - DO NOT OBSTRUCT.
The pipe is cut and capped. Heat shimmers over the well again.
The valve is turned round. A delver tag hangs on it: KARAG DUN - MASTER FORGE.
I've tended the well sixty years. It was too hot to stand beside when I was a girl.
Now I can put my hand on the rim. That pipe came, and the well started going out.
It's warm again. Too warm to touch. I've never been so glad to burn my hand.
You found your way. Good. The Matron is in the hall, north side. The one with the banners.
She'll call it a debt. Don't let her. A debt is something you agreed to.
Are you a real dragon? Gran says we were dragons, a long way back, before we got small.
I'm going to be one again. I practise breathing fire every morning. It's mostly coughing.
Scale-cloth. We shed, we weave. It won't burn in the lava wind.
I've no one to sell to. The men who carried it to Karag Dun are digging for the Crown.
My brother's home. He hasn't said a word about the dig. He sits by the well and holds his hands over it.
That's our house, bricked up. The Crown's surveyor said an empty house is a fire risk.
My husband is forty-one of forty-one. They number them at the dig. I know because he wrote to me. Once.
I'm Hesk. Oriane's man. Number forty-one. I'll be pulling those bricks out with my teeth if I have to.
I sing the old songs at the well. There is one about a dragon who lost its heart-flame and would not die.
It sleeps in a bone vault, north and west. The Ossuary of Wings. Do not wake it for sport.
I guard a pipe. I cannot cut it: the Crown hangs a man for every cut pipe, and they don't care which man.
The pump is at their dig, south of here. Shut the pump and the pipe is only iron.
Crown survey. The well's output is down thirty per cent. I'm told to find the cause.
I've written 'natural decline'. The pipe is not in my remit.
Come from the Fungal Terraces with spore-salve. The ember-well dries the air - good for curing caps.
The terraces are west, past the Geode Wood. Follow the smell of bread and rot.
There is a hollow, far west, where a dragon's heart sleeps without its dragon. Drakesleep.
It will not open for strangers. It might for one who carries a fire of his own.
I'm from Cinderlake. Was. The lake rose after the sky broke and took the isles in a night.
The Matron took us in. Emberwell's crowded now. Nobody complains. That's how you know it's bad.
Warmstone beds. The stones sit in the well by day and under your blanket by night. Thirty crowns.
Thirty crowns. The stones are hot, mind your feet.
I'm a Karag Dun man, sent to buy scale-cloth. Nobody here will sell to a delver while the king pays the Crown.
Can't say I blame them. Can't say I'm going home without it either.
Shed-scale mail, ember-thread, a few Crown tonics we took in trade. Browse.
Scale-smith. I work shed scale and ember-glass. Bring me geode shards from the wood and I'll show you what they're for.
Heartsteel from the delvers takes an edge like a dragon's tooth. Iron is iron.
The Matron counts the Taken every night. Forty-one. She says the number out loud so the well hears it.
Strangers from the fallen quarry. Vessa said you would come. She said one of you burns inside.
Yes. You. The old fire looks out of your eyes when you're not watching it.
She sees me.
She sees something. Let's hear her.
The Crown came down five years ago and said the Deep was dangerous. They offered protection. We did not ask.
Then they sent the bill. When we could not pay in heat-stone, they took our young for their dig. Forty-one.
And they laid a pipe to our well. It drinks the fire that keeps us. It is going out.
Then warm yourselves while there is still warmth. The dig is south, past the lava fields.
Their foreman keeps a ledger - every name, every 'debt'. Find it. And stop the thing that pumps our well dry.
QUP1: The Crown Dig (south of Emberwell) holds forty-one dragonborn and pumps the ember-well cold. Find the foreman's ledger; stop the dig.
...But you've come from the south. They say the dig is silent. They say a machine lies broken at the face.
Then you have done half of it already. Did you find their ledger? Bring it, and I will tell you what it cost.
QUP1: The Crown Dig is stopped. Find the foreman's ledger in the dig's office and bring it to Matron Ysolde.
The dig is south, beyond the lava fields. The foreman's ledger, and the pump. Go carefully.
The dig is silent - I can feel the well breathing. But the ledger. Their office at the dig. Bring it.
The well is ours again, and ours alone. Hot enough to hurt. Forty-one came home. That number I will say every night too.
Our heat runs to the delvers' forges now, and their iron runs to us. Horrach sent a letter. It said sorry four times.
Show me the ledger.
She turns the pages slowly. Each line is a name and a sum: heat-stone owed, labour credited, 'protection' charged.
Forty-one names. And the price of the well, written as if it were theirs to sell.
The Taken are home. The dig is stopped. The pipe is still there. What do we do with it?
Cut it, and the well is ours alone. The Crown will send someone to ask why. We will be alone when they ask.
Or turn it round. Send our heat to the delvers' forges, for iron and for friends. Karag Dun owes the Crown too.
You carried the ledger. You choose.

options.text: "Cut the pipe. The well is Emberwell's."
"Turn it to Karag Dun. Stand together."

cmds.text: Vessa takes an axe to the chain. The valve spins free, the pipe coughs once, and the well flares white.
Hot enough to hurt. Good.
The valve is reversed and re-chained, a delver tag on it this time. The well steadies. Far off, a forge answers.
Horrach will grumble. Then he will send iron. Then, perhaps, an apology.
The Taken have a gift for you. They broke a brackhorn to the deep roads while they dug - a Deepstrider.
It will carry you through Emberdeep and nothing that lives down here will dare to follow.
(The Deepstrider brackhorn will carry the party through the Deep without random battles.)
QUP1 complete: the forty-one are home and the ember-well burns. The Deepstrider is ours.
Gathering, are you? Look for the crystals that hum. Hum means a node - a good one gives ore as well as glass.
Three nodes up the glade, if the wood hasn't grown over them. Don't touch the red ones; the hydra's been at them.
A warning post, scratched deep: 'HEART OF THE WOOD - MANY MOUTHS - TURN BACK.'
Under it, smaller, in a different hand: 'Or bring fire. It cracks.'
The crystal hums at a pitch you feel in your teeth. You strike it where the hum is loudest.
The node is quiet now. It will grow back, in a hundred years or so.
The crystal hums at a pitch you feel in your teeth. You strike it where the hum is loudest.
The node is quiet now. It will grow back, in a hundred years or so.
The crystal hums at a pitch you feel in your teeth. You strike it where the hum is loudest.
The node is quiet now. It will grow back, in a hundred years or so.
I came for the nodes and the wood moved. The path I came by is a tree now.
The north way is crystal-shut. West, there's a hollow full of prisms. The light's all wrong in there.
A slate by the light-well: 'West prism to the well. East prism to the well. South prism to the sky.'
'When all three agree, the heart-wall opens.'
You strike the crack in the slab. It sings, shivers, and falls in two. The way back to the wood's edge is open.
The broken slab. Daylight - or what passes for it down here - shows through.
A gatherer's coat around old bones. In the pocket, a note: 'It sleeps with its heads in the pool. Fire first. Then rock, when it breaks.'
(Faint, crystalline.) I heard it grow. Every shard it sheds becomes another mouth. Kill the heart, not the heads.
You turn the west prism. A blade of light swings across the hollow and drops into the light-well.
You turn the west prism away. The light-well dims.
The west prism holds its light steady on the well.
The east prism turns with a grinding chime. Its light crosses the first beam and both fall into the well.
The east prism turns aside. Its beam scatters on the ceiling.
The east prism holds.
You tilt the south prism up. Its light climbs to the roof of the hollow, out of the well's reach.
You tilt the south prism back down.
The south prism points at the sky that isn't there.
The three beams agree. The light-well blazes, and far off to the east something made of crystal breaks with a sound like a bell.
The alcove on the west wall splits open too.
The pool is not a pool. It is a back. Crystal shoulders rise out of it, and on each shoulder a head.
The heads ring as they turn. Every shard that drops from them twitches and starts to grow a mouth.
A heart inside the glass. Alive. It is not a dragon. It would like to be.
The hydra shatters from the heart outward. The wood goes quiet. The crystal trees stop growing, for now.
In the dry pool, where the heart lay, something glints.
Carved into the wing bone, in a script older than the Crown: 'Here the winged lie down. Here they are not used.'
'Not used.' They wrote that because someone already was.
I come from Emberwell to sweep the gate. The dragonborn say the dead here were our grandmothers' grandmothers.
Something still walks inside. It has no heart-flame and no reason, and it will not lie down.
Scratched in the floor, three marks and a verse: 'The deepest first, for the deepest sleep.'
'The highest next, for the flight. The middle last, for the lying down.'
A vertebra the size of a cart, split open along a seam. Inside, the bone is black, as if something was burned out of it.
(A delver ghost, very polite.) Mind the gaps. I didn't.
There's a ledge above, with a box on it. You get to it from the chapel stair, if the chimes let you through.
The deepest chime. The note goes down through your boots and keeps going.
The chime hangs still. The arch is open.
A high, thin note. It sours against the silence. The bone lattice in the arch shivers and tightens.
A high, thin note, like wind over wings. The first note is still humming under it.
The chime hangs still.
The middle chime rings alone and wrong. The gallery goes quiet, offended.
The middle note settles between the other two. The bone lattice in the north arch lies down, rib by rib.
The chime hangs still.
The skull's jaw is the size of a door. Inside, on the tongue-stone, the bone is scorched in the shape of a small flame.
Raven stops. His hand rises to the scorch mark on its own. His eyes go the colour of old fire.
I know this place. I was here when it had a roof of living wings.
We came to lie down, when we were tired of being large. The dragonborn sang. The delvers had not yet learned to dig.
Then the first Crown came with its engine and its promises, and it asked us for our hearts. Only for a while, it said.
Some said yes. I said yes. They cut me out of myself and put me in a stone, and the stone in a relay, and the relay in the dark.
And the rest of you?
Still here. Lying down. Waiting to be asked properly.
One did not lie down. It had its heart taken and would not die. It is on the roost above us. I will not say its name.
Why not?
Because it would hear. And it would come to me, and I have nothing to give it back.
The fire goes out of Raven's eyes. He takes his hand off the stone and looks at it for a long moment.
The scorch mark on the tongue-stone. Raven does not touch it again.
Something unfolds on the roost: a dragon, or the frame of one. Its chest is open and empty. Its eyes are empty too.
It turns its head as if listening for a heartbeat that should be there.
Do not look at its eyes. It is looking for what it lost. It will think it is you.
The Remnant folds, slowly, like something finally allowed to lie down. The roost is quiet.
...Thank you. It was tired. It did not know how to stop.
The skiffs are pumice hulls, sealed with delver tar. They float on lava like cork on soup. Mostly.
Tip the ferryman a story. He's heard every coin there is.
Crown landing tax, two crowns a head. Or you can go round. Round is a week of lava fields.
...I don't actually collect it. They'd have to send someone to count it, and nobody wants to come down here.
Lava eels. You hook them from the jetty with an iron line. They're sweet, if you don't mind the teeth.
We're waiting on the bell. The Deepforge's shut, so the family's going to the isles to fish instead.
My grandad dug for forty years. I'm going to learn to swim in fire. Progress.
The fault shook the lake up. Cinderlake's gone under. The channel west opened instead, clean to the Terraces.
Ferry's running. Where to? Mind, the Cinderlake crossing takes the long way round the rocks.
Bell's rung. Sit low and don't touch the sides. The sides are the lake.
The isles are gone, friend. The lake came up and took them in a night. I ferried the last of them out.
But the fault opened a channel west. Clean run to the Fungal Terraces now. Want it?
West it is. The channel's new, so it's full of things that don't know they're lava yet.
I'll be here. I'm always here. That's the job.
Smoked lava eel. We hang them over the lake on iron hooks. The lake does the cooking.
Karag Dun buys every eel we have. They're the only thing the Crown doesn't tax - they can't find us.
Pumice, tar, iron line. Everything a boat needs except courage, and I'm out of that.
Island mushrooms. They grow on the warm side of the rocks. Don't eat the blue ones, they eat back.
Three isles, forty families, one rule: nobody tells the Crown we're here. Four generations and it's held.
The lake's been restless lately. Rising a finger a month. The rocks are sweating.
I can jump from the boardwalk to the skiff and back. Ma says if I do it again she'll let the lake have me.
A skiff takes a year to build and a second to sink. The trick is not thinking about the second.
The delvers make the tar, the dragonborn weave the sails. We supply the madness.
Iron nets for the eels. Rope burns. Iron only glows. Remember that if you ever fish here.
I watch the east rocks for Crown lamps. Two years, nothing. Then last month, lights at the dig, bright as day.
The dig's on the far shore, south-east. If they come across the lake, we'll know.
I came back to look. There's nothing. The inn's roof is sticking out of the lake like a tooth.
We're all at Emberwell now. The Matron says we can stay as long as there's a well.
I read the lake by the colour of the crust. Orange is calm. Yellow is a warning. White means get in a boat.
It's been yellow for a month.
The Floating Hook. The floor tilts when the lake breathes. You get used to it. Twenty-five crowns.
Twenty-five. Sleep on your left side, the lake's on the right.
You came on Coll's skiff? He tells the same story every crossing. The one about the Crown taxman and the eel.
The taxman lost.
Boat stores, and whatever the delvers traded us this month.
Boatwright and tinker. I work pumice, tar and iron. Bring me eel-bone - it's harder than it has any right to be.
Heartsteel rivets would make a skiff that could cross the whole lake. If anyone could afford heartsteel.
My mother was born on a skiff halfway across. She always said she belonged to neither shore.
If the lake rises, I'll go out on a skiff and stay there. It's in the family.
Back to the Magma Ferry? Da taught me the rocks. Sit low.
I only come back for the boats. There's nothing else to come back for.
Suit yourself.
You're not on the roster. Nobody's on the roster. The roster's a list of the dead with a few of us at the bottom.
Go in if you want. Grisk won't notice. Grisk only notices the seam.
Number nine, they called me. I'm Tavish. Tavish of Emberwell. I'm going home.
I was a quarryman up top. They sent us down 'on loan'. Nobody said for how long. You said. Thank you.
Notches in a tent pole, in rows of seven. At the bottom, a name - Hesk - and then no more notches.

The empty token board.
I'm not deserting. I'm resting in a direction.
Nine of the lads went off to the Singing Chasm last week. Echoes hide footsteps. If you see Tamsin, tell her I'm coming. Eventually.

He hasn't been up from the face in nine days. He eats down there. He sleeps in the machine.

The upper belt is braked.

The lower belt is braked.
Number twelve. Kerrin of Emberwell. We work the sort from bell to bell. The foreman works the face.

Forty-one of us came. Thirty-eight now. Grisk writes the three in the ledger as 'wastage'.
A plunger box, wired to a charge set in the rockfall. The label says SHORTCUT - DO NOT FIRE - GRISK.

The spent plunger box.
Crates of blasting powder, stacked to the roof, stencilled with the Crown seal and a single word: OVERTIME.

Who's on the tube? Shift seven? Get down here. The seam's singing. We're not stopping till it's dry.
Overtime, lads! Overtime for everyone!
The foreman's desk. On it, open, a thick Crown ledger. The page headed EMBERWELL - PROTECTION ACCOUNT.
Forty-one names, each with a number beside it. Three are struck through: WASTAGE. Below, the ember-well itself, valued as collateral.

Visitors! On my face! You're not shift seven. Shift seven's dead. Doesn't matter. Pick up a shovel.

Grisk. It's over. Let them go.
Over? It's never over. It's overtime!
