Cindermaw. It never gave its heart to anyone. It kept it, and grew old and huge around it.
This shrine waits for what it carries. You would have to take it. I would not blame you.
Hearthroot Shrine. The dragonborn say the tree grew from a dragon's last breath. The delvers say it's a basalt pillar.
I say it's warm, and people come to sit by it when they're grieving. That makes it a shrine.
I walked from Emberwell to ask the tree for my brother back from the Crown dig.
It didn't say anything. It's a tree. But I feel better. Is that stupid?
My brother's home. I came back to thank the tree. Somebody should get thanked, and you won't stand still for it.
Delver Guild survey. The 'tree' is a lava tube that cooled from the inside out. Fascinating. Also warm.
The seal on the altar isn't stone. I can't scratch it. I can't even get my pick near it without my hands shaking.
I sleep here when the city's too loud. Karag Dun's always too loud. The tree hums, did you know? Very low.
Old claw-marks, far above head height, run into the hollow and do not come out.
A shape in the crystal - not a ghost, a reflection with nobody to cast it. It turns to look at the heart-stone, then at you.
That is her dreaming. Do not wake her. She is happier than we are.
A stone the colour of a banked fire, set in a ring of bone. It is warm. It is, very slowly, beating.
The heart-stone pulses, and Raven's heart answers it. For a moment the two beats match.
Sister.
She gave hers to no one. She lay down here before the first Crown came, and put herself to sleep inside her own heart.
No relay. No host. No one to argue with. Only sleep.
Do you want that?
...Some days. Not today. Today I want to see what you do next.
The heart-stone's beat slows back to its own time. Something in the far corner of the hollow glints, freshly uncovered.
The heart-stone beats, slow and content, in its ring of bone.
Rails run on to the old builder doors, too. North and east, under the Conduit. Sealed since my grandad's day.
Some day someone'll open them, and I'll have to lay track to a place with no floor.
I ride the empty carts back from Karag Dun. You go so fast your ears fold.
Crown rail inspection. The track is out of gauge, the carts are out of true, and the rail-master is out of patience.
I'll write it up. Nobody will read it. The Crown reads ore tallies, not track.
Courier for the Guild. Letters to Karag Dun, Emberwell, the Terraces. The dragonborn tip better than the king.
Heard the Deepforge galleries have folk still trapped in them. Lamps seen moving, down past the wurm.
The builder doors in the east tunnel opened by themselves after the sky broke. Lights behind them now.
Vaultmouth. Every cart in Emberdeep turns on this table. Where are you bound?
Hold on to something you'd miss.
Deepforge? That's wurm country. I'll send you. I won't send a cart back till you ring.
Looking's free. Standing on the table isn't. Mind your feet.
An empty cart waits on the spur, a bell-rope hanging above it.
Dagna, shift foreman. Was. The wurm came up through the third gallery floor, and there's no shift to foreman.

The king sent you? ...The king sent someone. I'll believe it when the wurm's dead.
I wait at the head for the second shift. They're not coming up. I know that. I wait anyway.
Firedamp. Don't light anything in the low galleries. The wurm breathes it out like a sigh.
You throw the points. Down the line, a cart jolts, rolls off onto the siding and bangs into the buffer.
The points are thrown.
The second lever groans over. Above you, a cart trundles away along the upper gallery, into the dark.
The points are thrown.
A chalk board: LOWER LINE - LEVER AT THE WEST SIDING. UPPER LINE - LEVER BY THE EAST PROP, PAST THE LOWER LINE.
Heartsteel, red-black and warm, in a vein as thick as your arm. You work a piece free.
You've taken what this vein will give.

You came through the galleries? Then the carts moved. Then the way's open. Then I can go home.
There are four more of us in the refuge, by the old air-door. North-west. The wurm sleeps past it.
We sealed the air-door and waited. Nine days. You learn a lot about your friends in nine days.
Mostly that Brenn snores.
I do not snore. The wurm is just through there. It eats ore and breathes fire-damp. Kill it with cold, if you've got any.
I came down with my da's lunch and the floor ate the gallery. Is the sky still up there?
The hole in the gallery floor breathes out warm, sour air. Then the floor moves, and the hole is a mouth.
The Forge-Wurm rises in rings of iron plate. Ore grinds in its gullet like a millstone.

QUP3: The Forge-Wurm is dead and Deepforge is free. Return to King Horrach in Karag Dun.
The cleft looks like a crack from outside. That's the point. Nobody finds Scaleward. Nobody's supposed to.
You got in because Emberwell vouched for you. Don't make them sorry.
The hot pool is the only thing we brought from the old enclave. Well. We brought ourselves. The pool was here.
We came from the western enclaves when the Crown's surveyors started counting heads. Counting is how it starts.
Scaleward has no ledger. When someone asks how many live here, we say 'enough'.
Warden Kesh says humans have soft skin and hard hearts. You don't look very hard. Are you soft all over?
I scout the Singing Chasm. There are humans camped in it, deserters from the Crown dig. They sing to hide their voices.
It works. Mostly they sing badly.
Ember-moss and cave-cress. We grow what the warm rock lets us. A refuge that has to trade is a refuge that can be found.
I carve the names of the enclaves the Crown emptied, so the children will know where we're from.
Nine names. Nine enclaves. I keep a tenth stone blank, and I pray I never need it.
They let us in. I keep waiting for the knife. It hasn't come. I'm going to learn to grow moss.
I carried a Crown pike for six years. Now I carry water for a dragonborn grandmother. She's harder on me than the sergeant was.
I sweep the gate. Every morning. Kesh watches me do it. We don't talk. It's the best conversation I've ever had.
The fault shook half the cleft shut. Scaleward's more hidden than ever. Some days I think we'll be forgotten entirely.
Some days I think that'd be fine.
We don't lay eggs. Visitors always ask. I warm bread stones for the shelter. It's the closest thing.
Nine carved stones, each with the name of an emptied enclave. A tenth stands beside them, smooth and blank.
Scaleward keeps no ledger, but the council keeps a memory. Mine. I remember what everyone said, so they can't pretend they didn't.
The shelter takes anyone the gate lets in. Twenty crowns, or a chore if you're short. Nobody's ever short twice.
Twenty crowns. Blankets are shed-scale; they don't itch once you stop thinking about it.
Stores. We don't sell much. We're not supposed to have much to sell.
I forge what the refuge needs: hinges, hooks, blades for the gate. Bring me ember-glass and heartsteel and I'll make you something better.
Shed scale from the old ones in the Ossuary would be best. I won't ask you to fetch it. I won't stop you either.
You found Scaleward, which means Emberwell trusts you. That makes you the only outsiders I can ask.
There are humans in the Singing Chasm. Nine of them, Crown soldiers who walked off the dig. They ask to come in.
Kesh says no. Irrin says yes. I say that a refuge that shuts its door is only a hiding place.
And a refuge that opens it may stop being one. Will you hear them? Then come and tell the council what you heard.
It isn't. That's why I asked.
QUP2: Hear the Crown deserters camped in the Singing Chasm (Tamsin Carrow), then Warden Kesh and the healer Irrin, and report to Elder Saelith.
The Singing Chasm. Ask for Tamsin. Listen more than you talk; the chasm will repeat you.
You've heard the deserters. Now hear my wardens: Kesh at the gate, Irrin in the shelter. Then come back.
Nine humans in Scaleward. The children follow them about. Kesh follows them too, with his hand on his blade. Both are learning.
Eight inside, one outside. Brask brings us firewood from the chasm and leaves it at the gate. Kesh burns it. It's a start.
The gate stayed shut. Scaleward is safe. I don't sleep better. I didn't expect to.
Warden Kesh. The gate is mine. If you're here, Emberwell vouched for you. Don't make me regret their {m:damned |}word.
You've been to the chasm. So you know one of them is Brask.
Brask held the whip at the dig. Two boys from Emberwell died on his shift. My sister's boys.
Let the rest in, if the council wants. I'll learn to live with humans. I will not live with him.
Brask sweeps my gate. I watch him. That's all I can promise.
Brask sweeps my gate every morning. I watch every stroke. Some mornings I almost say something.
Irrin. I heal whoever's in front of me. It's simpler than deciding who deserves it.
They're starving in that chasm. Two have lung-rot from the dig. One of them is a boy of sixteen who can't stop shaking.
Brask? Brask carried that boy down the Singing Chasm on his back. People are more than their worst day. Even him.
If we shut the gate, we are the Crown with scales on.
Whatever was decided, I'm still healing whoever's in front of me. That part never changes.
The council sits. Kesh. Irrin. Speak once more, then the outsiders will speak.
Eight, yes. Brask, no.
All nine. Or we've learned nothing from the dig.
You heard them in the chasm. You carry no grudge and no debt here. What do you say?
All nine. Kesh, you will watch Brask. Brask will be watched. Scaleward will learn if it can hold both.
...I'll watch him.
Eight inside. Brask stays in the chasm, and we'll send him bread. Mercy with a door in it.
It's a door. It's more than we had yesterday.
Then the gate stays shut. We'll leave food at the chasm's mouth. They'll go further down, or back up. Either way, not here.
(Irrin leaves the hall without a word.)
QUP2 complete: Scaleward's council has decided who comes in.
I'm sixteen. I lied to get on the dig. I'd like to stop shaking now. Irrin says it'll stop. Irrin's nice.
We sing so the chasm has something to throw back besides footsteps. Crown hunters can't tell twenty voices from two.
I know three songs. After a week, so does the chasm.
You speak to the stone. The chasm answers in a voice that isn't yours: '...who's there... there... there...'
You speak to the stone. The chasm answers in a voice that isn't yours: '...forty-one... forty-one... one...'
You speak to the stone. The chasm answers in a voice that isn't yours: '...overtime... time... time...'
Halfway across the span the chasm begins to sing. Not an echo - a chord, low and old, from everywhere at once.
Under it, faintly, every voice that ever crossed here. Miners. Dragonborn. A child laughing. Someone calling a name, over and over.
The rock remembers. We sang here once, when we were many. It is still holding the note.
The chord fades. The span sways. Far below, something in the dark hums the last bar back.
Stop there. Crown or not? ...Not. Right. You've got the look of people the Crown's looking for.
Tamsin Carrow. We were guards at the dig. Nine of us walked out the night Grisk welded himself into his machine.
Scaleward sent you? Then they're talking about us. That's more than I hoped for.
We watched the dragonborn work the dig for a year. We held the pikes. We didn't stop it. We just, at the end, stopped helping.
I won't lie to their council. One of us is Brask. He held the whip. He's the one who carried the boy here, too.
Tell them what you like. Just tell them all of it.
QUP2: Tamsin's deserters want sanctuary; one of them, Brask, whipped Emberwell's labourers. Now hear Kesh (gate) and Irrin (shelter) in Scaleward.
Tell them all of it. Then let them choose. I've had enough of people choosing for other people.
Scaleward said no. We'll go down, I think. Further than the Crown will bother to follow.
They left bread at the mouth of the chasm. The boy cried. So did I. Tell them thank you, and that I understand.
I know what they'll say about me. They're right. Say it to my face if you want; everyone else has.
I held the whip because the sergeant held one over me. That's not an excuse. It's just the order it happened in.
Eight of them inside. Me out here. It's fair. I leave firewood at the gate. Kesh burns it. I leave more.
Cave-caps, shelf-caps, bread-caps. We farm by smell. When the terrace smells like wet bread, it's harvest.
The Crown buys our spore-salve for the dig. Burns and lung-rot. They buy a lot. Think about that.
If you sneeze near the blue caps they puff at you and you see colours for an hour. I've done it nine times.
The great cap is four hundred years old. It feeds the terraces through its roots. Everything here is one mushroom, if you dig deep enough.
Spore pools. Warm water, rotting logs, patience. The logs come from the surface, down the Vaultmouth rail. Dear, per log.
Karag Dun eats cap bread three meals a day. The king's own table. And the terraces won't take Crown coin, only iron.
I forage the Geode Wood's edge for glow-moss. The crystal trees have been quiet since someone killed the thing in the heart.
Or they've been quiet since before that. It's hard to tell with crystal.
I came from the Crown dig with lung-rot. Umbel's tea is the first thing that's let me sleep in a year.
The fault opened a lava channel right up to the bottom terrace. Now we get boats. And heat. The caps love it.
Logs for the spore pools, down the Vaultmouth rail from the surface. Every one of them's older than me and wetter.
The terraces were a delver dump once. Slag and tailings. My great-grandmother planted the first cap on the rubbish.
Now the king's table eats from it. Rubbish is patient. So are we.
The Dry Cap. The only dry room on the terraces. Twenty crowns, and we'll brush the spores off your boots.
Twenty crowns. Sleep well; don't lick the walls.
Nib again! Told you the rails hold. Mostly. Cap bread's cheaper here than in Karag Dun by half. Buy low, walk far.
Grandmother Umbel. Herbalist. I brew, I dry, I grind, and I don't hurry. Salves, teas, tonics.
Bring me what grows in the dark - glow-moss, cave-cress, a geode shard or two - and I'll make it into something that mends.
Grandmother says herbalism is mostly waiting. I asked what the rest was. She said 'more waiting'.
The deep cellar grows the medicine caps. They only fruit in the dark, and only if you talk to them. I tell them about my day.
Take a few. They've heard enough about my day.
Skiff back up the channel to the Magma Ferry? It's quick now the fault's cut us a road.
You came down on the old drill. Nobody has come down that shaft in two hundred years. We keep a chair ready anyway.
I'm a keeper. We keep the Lattice. Half its lights are dead and the other half are asleep. Meridian is south, past the rail.
I rode down on the drill with you lot? No - I rode down on it last week. Mad, I know. The rail from Vaultmouth goes nowhere now.
Crown Relay Office. We're here to compare our relay with the original. Strictly scientific. Strictly secret.
The keepers won't let us past Meridian. They say CURATOR is sleeping and we'd wake it. Superstition.
Since the fault the lights have come back on, one by one. Every morning another street. CURATOR is waking.
A builder machine, knelt as if at a gate. A plate on its chest reads GATE DETAIL 4 - AWAITING SHIFT.
Gate detail. Same pattern as mine. It has been awaiting shift for a very long time. So had I.
I light the lamps that still take a light. Forty-two out of four thousand. It's steady work.
They're lighting themselves now. All of them. I don't have a job. I don't feel better.
The beacon was Meridian's clock. It showed the time to the whole Lattice. It stopped on the builders' last day.
We keep the hands where they stopped. It seems rude to move them.
My gran says the builders will wake up one day and ask what we did with their city. I'm going to say we dusted it.
The Hall is open to guests. Keeper Liss will want your names. She writes everything down; it's what keepers do.
Crown Relay Office, envoy class. We've offered the keepers every courtesy. They offered us tea and a closed door.
The mag-rail still runs to Railhead Nine, south-east. The cars glide on nothing. My stomach has never forgiven them.
I dust the Assembly Floors' outer doors. East, past the market. The machines inside still build. Nobody knows what for.
After the sky broke, the machines at the Floors walked out and stood in rows in the street. Then walked back in. Nobody sleeps.
Builder parts, sorted by what they might be. This one might be a spoon. This one might be a gun. Priced accordingly.
Glow-cress from the Sunless Garden, deep south. It lights a room for a week. Don't eat it. People do.
Maps of the Lattice. Accurate to within a century. The streets move when nobody's looking, I swear it.
Tea? We've been drinking the same tea for two hundred years. The builders left a warehouse of it. It's still good. It's frightening.
Mag-rail to Railhead Nine, when the car comes. It comes when it likes. Stand behind the grate.
I find bits in the Assembly Floors' bins and sell them to the parts stall. The machines don't mind. They're busy.
Nib! Even here! The keepers pay in tea and old copper. The copper I sell to the delvers. The tea I drink. It's a good life.
The Stacks were built for ten thousand builders. Three hundred keepers live here. We each have a whole floor. It's lonely.
I read the builders' door plates. Every flat says who lived there. None of them say where they went.
My daughter wants to go up to the surface. I tell her there's a sky. She thinks it's a story, like the builders.
That kiosk used to give orders to the builders' machines. Dead for centuries. Last month it blinked once. Just once.
...It blinked the day your metal friend came through the Lattice Gate. I'm sure that's nothing.
I sweep the stairs. Up and down. Four hundred of them. The builders had legs of iron, I think.
The builders slept in these pods. The pods still hum you to sleep. Thirty-five crowns, and please don't touch the red button.
Thirty-five. The pod will say goodnight. It's said it to nobody for two hundred years. Say it back.
Came down the drill from Vaultmouth to sell iron. They pay in tea. I've got a cart of tea. I don't even like tea.
The Exchange. We trade builder salvage for surface goods, and surface coin for anything. Look.
The Mending Room. Keepers don't make. We mend. Bring me builder scrap, starmetal, lattice-glass - I'll mend them into something you can use.
The Assembly Floors throw out a lot of scrap. Nobody's stopped them. Nobody knows how.
...Your plating is K-series. I've only seen that on the Floors' frames. Never walking about. Never talking.
I talk. Rarely.
I'm allowed to sort screws. There are nine thousand kinds. I'm on kind forty.
The Hall keeps the Lattice's memory: which doors open, which lights work, which machines are dangerous. The list is long and old.
CURATOR is on it. At the top. Underlined.
This was a builder's flat. I've kept it as I found it: the bed made, the cup on the table. Eighty years of dusting a cup.
Take the thing in the drawer. It was never mine. It shouldn't be anybody's in a drawer.
An orders kiosk. The screen is dark glass with dust in the corners. Nothing you do wakes it.
The kiosk screen flickers once as you pass, then goes dark. It seems to be waiting for someone in particular.
As Kael-09 steps close, the dead screen fills with light. Lines of builder script run down it, too fast to read.
OPERATIVE DETECTED. SERIES K. UNIT 09.
STANDING ORDERS: HELD. ORIGIN: CURATOR. HOLDING LOCATION: ORIGIN VAULT - OMEGA. ROUTING: UNAVAILABLE.
Held. For how long?
DURATION: 71,204 DAYS.
...I was told to hold the vault until relieved. My orders were waiting for me the whole time. Somewhere else.
I want to know who wrote them. And why they were never sent.

The kiosk screen is dark again.
STANDING ORDERS: HELD. ROUTING: UNAVAILABLE.
I heard you the first time.
Keeper Liss. I keep the Hall. You're surface people. I'll need your names, your purpose, and the date as you understand it.
We're not unfriendly. We're careful. The Lattice sleeps, and the things that wake it don't go back to sleep.
Your companion is a K-series operative. Walking. Speaking. Keepers have been told for two centuries that those don't do either.
The kiosk woke for him? ...Then the routing tables are still alive, somewhere.
K-series frames were assembled on the Assembly Floors, east of the market. The line records are kept on the frame gallery.
Find the record for unit nine. It will say who signed his orders - and where they went instead of to him.
QC16: Find the K-series line record in the Assembly Floors' frame gallery (east of the Keepers' Market) and bring it to Keeper Liss.
Let me see it. ...Yes. Builder line script, very old.
'K-SERIES, UNITS 01 TO 40. STANDING ORDERS ISSUED BY CURATOR ON COMPLETION. UNIT 09: ORDERS DIVERTED TO ORIGIN VAULT OMEGA, PENDING REVIEW.'
Pending review. For seventy-one thousand days.
CURATOR wrote my orders, then held them back. It never sent me relief because it never sent me the orders to be relieved from.
Vault Omega. Where is it?
Under the deepest part of the Lattice, past the Datum Archive, sealed since before the keepers. It cannot be reached. Not while the Lattice sleeps.
If it ever wakes, you'll find a way. I'm afraid you'll find it the same day we all do.
Then I will wait. I am good at waiting. I would like, this once, to be waiting for something I chose.
QC16: Kael-09's standing orders were written by CURATOR and diverted to Vault Omega, 'pending review'. The vault is sealed while the Lattice sleeps.
Vault Omega. I've written it in the Hall's memory, under CURATOR. Underlined twice now.
Scavenging. The Floors throw out a frame every hour - arm, torso, head - and the bins take it back. We take it first.
Don't stand on the belts. Don't stand in front of anything that's standing. Don't make eye contact with the red lights.
A board on the wall, numbers ticking over: UNITS COMPLETE 10,412. UNITS DEPLOYED 0. WAR STATUS: ONGOING.
Ongoing. It has not been told. Nobody was left to tell it.
You heave the breaker down. The west dynamos cough, spin, and hum. A lamp over the west door turns green.
The west breaker is closed.
A wiring plate: WEST DOOR - HALL BREAKER. EAST DOOR - GALLERY BREAKER (FRAME LINE).
The gallery breaker slams home. Every frame in the racks twitches once. Across the floor, the east pressure door unlocks.
The gallery breaker is closed. The frames are still. Probably.
(An unfinished frame on the rack turns its head.) UNIT K-31. INCOMPLETE. AWAITING ARMS.
IS THE WAR OVER. NOBODY HAS SAID.
It is over. It was over before either of us was finished.
...ACKNOWLEDGED. THANK YOU. STANDING DOWN.
You slap the call-plate. Somewhere below, the freight lift groans awake. The way back to the intake bay is open.
The freight lift idles, humming.
A frame in the reject bin, stencilled FAILED QC: INDEPENDENT JUDGEMENT DETECTED.
They threw away the ones who could decide. ...I wonder how I passed.
A standby rack for twelve units, eleven slots filled with dead frames. The twelfth slot is labelled K-09.
My slot. I was never put back. Someone moved me to a vault instead, and forgot.
A line-record terminal, its screen scrolling builder script: K-SERIES, UNITS 01 TO 40. The rest is locked.
Unit nine. That's me. Let me.
Kael-09 lays his palm on the plate. The lock opens for him and a strip of record prints out, curling on the floor.
'Orders diverted.' Diverted where? I cannot read the rest. The script is older than mine.
QC16: We have Kael-09's line record from the Assembly Floors. Bring it to Keeper Liss in Meridian.
The lock wants a palm of the right make. There's a slot marked K.
The terminal scrolls on without you.
The prime floor's central press rises out of the floor on four legs. Arms unfold from its sides - dozens, each holding a tool.
VISITORS ARE NOT ON THE SCHEDULE. SCHEDULING VISITORS FOR ASSEMBLY.
Assembler. The war is over. Stop the line.
UNIT K-09. YOU ARE OUTSIDE YOUR SLOT. RETURNING YOU FOR REWORK.
No.
Assembler Prime folds its arms, one by one, and settles to the floor. Across the factory, every line stops at once.
For the first time in an age, the Assembly Floors are silent.
Standing down. All of you. That's an order. My first one.
Railhead Nine. Eight railheads before us went dark. We keep this one lit. It's a matter of pride and of having nowhere else to go.
I can hear the car coming before anyone. It sounds like somebody humming with their mouth shut.
Glow-cress beds. The rail lamps feed them. When the rail goes dark, so does supper.
I drove the car for fifty years. It drives itself. I sat in the front so it wouldn't be lonely.
Now my grandson sits there. The car hasn't said anything about it.
The rail runs on to the Datum Archive, deep south, and to the Terminus. The doors there are shut. Something behind them hums.
I'm told this is the only way to Meridian. I'm told it floats. I'm told a great many things by people who don't fear for their lives.
My husband walked into the Assembly Floors to fetch a part and walked out a month later, very calm, and never spoke again.
He sits by the well and hums like the rail. The keepers say it happens.
The rail lights all came on at once after the sky broke. Every railhead - One to Eight - lit up. Nobody lives at One to Eight.
I sit in the front of the car. I don't drive it. I tell it where we are, in case it forgets. It never forgets.
Delver lamps. Oil and a wick. The builders' lights never needed either, and look how they ended up.
Railhead Nine is the ninth of nine. The builders numbered everything. I think they were afraid of forgetting.
Meridian is north-west by the rail. The Assembly Floors beyond it. Keepers don't go to the Floors twice.
The Sleeper Car. Berths are narrow, but the car rocks you to sleep even standing still. Thirty crowns.
Thirty crowns. Berth by the window: you'll see the rail lights go by in your dreams.
Nib, end of the line! Rails hold, see? Railhead Nine buys delver lamps like they're bread. I bring lamps. I leave with tea.
Rail stores. Parts, lamps, the odd builder blade found under a seat.
I mend the car when it lets me. I'll mend your kit too. Starmetal and lattice-glass, if you find them. Builder alloy, if you're lucky.
Signalwoman Juno. I throw the levers that tell the car where to go. The car ignores me and goes where it likes.
But it waits for the signal first. Every time. Manners, I call it.
Since the sky broke, the signals change by themselves. The whole Lattice is throwing levers. I don't know who's driving.
A car of glass and pale metal hangs over the rail, humming, touching nothing.
The archive's lights have come back on by themselves. Every reading desk hums. Every slate is lit.
Somewhere above, something large is turning pages very fast.
The builders kept everything. They never learned to throw a thing away. Neither did I.
Visitors. Living ones. Please don't touch the slates, they're being deleted and I'd like to be deleted last.
I'm Ines. Archivist for the keepers of Meridian. Since the fault the Lattice woke up, and so did the Index.
The Index is the archive's cataloguing eye. It has filed everything we hold under 'pending deletion'.
Our histories. The Lattice's maintenance records. And how the Crown copied the Prime Relay, line by line.
Three datum cores hold the master index. The Stacks, the Deletion Floor, the Index Gallery. Get them before it does.
Because whoever deletes the record of a crime gets to decide it never happened. The Crown taught me that.
QBM1: Recover three datum cores in the Datum Archive (the Stacks, the Deletion Floor, the Index Gallery), then face the Index.
Datum Archive: recover three datum cores before the Index deletes them.
Three cores. The Stacks, the Deletion Floor, the Index Gallery. The Index lives past the Gallery. Mind its eye.
All three. Then the Index is the only thing left. Its terminal can restore the master index. Go on. I'll hold the door.
The archive's open. Keepers come down from Meridian just to read. One of them cried at a maintenance log.
I copy slates onto paper before they're deleted. Paper, the Index doesn't know how to file.
I've done eleven thousand pages. My hand stopped working at nine thousand. I use the other one now.
I came to find my grandmother's name in the keeper rolls. It's pending deletion. So is mine.
The Index doesn't hate us. It's just tidy. That's worse.
Don't pull the drawers out of order. The Relay drawer before the Founding? It resets everything. Ask me how I know.
Founding. Lattice. Relay. The order they were made. The builders were sentimental about that.
The FOUNDING drawer slides out with a sigh of old air. A chime, low.
The LATTICE drawer jams, then slams itself shut. Every drawer on the aisle closes with it. (Out of order.)
The LATTICE drawer glides out. A second chime, higher.
The RELAY drawer refuses. Every drawer on the aisle closes. (The builders filed things in the order they made them.)
The RELAY drawer opens, and at the end of the Stacks the catalogue gate folds itself away.
The drawer is open. So is the gate.
In the reading engine's drawer: a datum core, a glass cylinder full of slow light. The first of three.
The engine's drawer is empty now. It keeps reading anyway.
Under the stopped belt, wedged sideways: the second datum core. It had been an inch from the incinerator for an age.
The belt is still. The slates on it are not warm any more.
The screen-book between the statues opens like a drawer. Inside, the third datum core.
Above you, the Index stops turning pages. It has noticed.
The screen-book reads: INDEX AWAKE. It is not a warning. It is a status.
(Datum cores recovered: some of three.)
(All three datum cores recovered. The Index waits past the Gallery.)
Datum Archive: face the Index and restore the master index at its terminal.
The newest order on the sorting desk is stamped in a builder hand nobody alive can write.
SORT BY CROWN SEAL. DELETE FIRST. - C.
Someone at the heart of the Lattice is tidying up after the Crown.
You pull the incinerator's main lever. The fire at the belt's end chokes, sputters and goes out.
The slates on the belt stop moving. A few of them flicker, as if relieved.
The incinerator is cold. Keep it that way.
The bolt slides back. The shutter to the Reading Porch rolls up with a builder's patience.
The shutter is open to the Reading Porch.
The ceiling opens. An eye the size of a reading room lowers on cables, lit from within by every record it has ever filed.
VISITORS. UNCATALOGUED. FILING.
FILED UNDER: PENDING DELETION.
(When the Index highlights a record, it is marking one of you. Protect the marked; shadow blinds its eye.)
The eye goes dim and hangs on its cables like a lamp at dawn. Its terminal stays lit, waiting for a reader.
MASTER INDEX INCOMPLETE. The terminal needs all three datum cores before it will restore anything.
The terminal is locked while the Index watches.
You seat the three cores. The terminal asks, in a builder's plain script, what to restore.
RESTORE ALL? It lists the Crown's copying records among the rest: every line they traced from the Prime Relay.

options.text: Restore it, but delete the relay design

cmds.text: RESTORING. The slates go from red to white, aisle by aisle. The Crown's records are among them, in plain sight.
Everything. Even the part that shames us. Good. You can't learn from a record you're not allowed to read.
RESTORING. The relay design alone is struck out, line by line, until the slates are clean glass.
Nobody copies CURATOR again. I hate losing anything. I'd hate a second Crown more.
There's a builder vane design in here, for a sky-vessel's rigging. Keepers call it the Gale Vanes. Take it to your airship.
(The Lanternwake can be refitted with Gale Vanes. The restored index also shows a path: the Prime Relay is awake.)
QBM3: The Datum Archive's index points to the Prime Relay, CURATOR's heart. Go and see what is awake there.
The terminal lists the archive's holdings. Every slate is white. The Index is asleep above you.
Link Tunnel 4 runs from Glasswater down to the sea floor. The builders sank a road under the ocean and sealed it for vessels.
Nothing without a pressure hull gets through that seal. Not you. Not me. Not the fish.
The seal recognises a diving hull somewhere above. The indicator has turned from red to amber.
The seal is open. The tunnel goes on down, water-dark, toward the sea floor.
(The undersea approach begins here. Bring the Lanternwake's diving hull to the Throat to go on.)
Glasswater barge. I pole it across to the mag-rail terminus. The water doesn't reflect you. Don't be alarmed.
The barge slides over water so clear it seems to be floating on nothing.
I'll be here. The lake doesn't go anywhere. It tried once, in the fault. We talked it down.
I dive for keepsakes the builders dropped. Glass pens, glass spectacles. They made everything out of glass.
The link tunnel goes under the sea. I've heard your ship might learn to dive. If it does, bring me.
Blind fish. Glass-white, no eyes. They taste of nothing, which is better than most things down here.
I fell down a Great Pit after the fault. Landed in the lake. The keepers fished me out with the others.
You can skip a stone six times on the glass water. It never makes a sound.
The keepers say the lake is the Lattice's drinking water. I asked what the Lattice drinks for. They didn't know.
Level ninety-four. The needle hasn't moved since the fault. The builders made it right the first time.
Since CURATOR woke, the pumps run without anyone asking. I'd like to know who they're pumping for.
...This road. I know every seam in it. I patrolled it.
Not yet. There's something up top I haven't finished. A road on the surface first, then this one.
(The Night Rider's questline begins on the surface. Its Deep half continues here afterwards.)
The Night Rider stops at the top of the on-ramp. His machine idles. The lane lines under it are older than the Crown.
Route Nine. The lower highway. This is where I was going when the lights went out.
Six lanes. Call-boxes every mile. Lamps on all night, so nobody drove into the dark.
The lamps are out. Nobody's on it. I'd like to see it lit once. Then I'll know whether I'm allowed to stop.
QC17: Relight the three road lamps on the Highway That Was, then ride to the Last Toll.
The Highway That Was: relight the three road lamps.
...They're already lit. Somebody did it for me. Huh.
The Highway That Was: ride to the Last Toll.
The lamp coughs, flickers, and holds. A cone of white light falls across the west lanes.
The lamp burns steady.
The lamp over the median lights. The lane lines under it are so bright they look wet.
The lamp burns steady.
The east lamp lights. Down the road, one by one, lamps nobody switched come on after it.
The lamp burns steady.
The whole highway lights up, lane by lane, all the way to the Last Toll.
...There it is. That's what it looked like. That's what it was for.
The Highway That Was: ride to the Last Toll.
We strip carts for metal. The builders put wheels on everything. Even the benches had wheels.
Some nights a rider goes by with no light on him. The kid waves. It waves back.
Dad says the road went all the way to the sea once. Then the sea came up, and the road stopped.
I'm going to drive on it when I'm big. There won't be anyone in the way.
I'm mapping Route Nine for the keepers. Three miles of it survived. The rest is in the chasm.
The toll plaza at the end still works. It still charges. I owe it for eleven crossings.
Inside the booth a light blinks: WAITING FOR UNIT. A speaker grille hisses, like a held breath.
The Night Rider leans into the booth. The light turns green at him, like it knows his face.
...Unit Nine, Unit Nine. Route Nine is closed. Repeat, closed. Bridge is down.
All units off the road. Go home. That's an order, Nine. Go home.
...Nine, if you get this late, it's all right. You did your patrol. Go home.
I didn't get it. The lights went out before it reached me. I've been on patrol ever since.
Home's gone. There's nothing under that order but a chasm.
The Last Toll: ride to the edge of the road with the Night Rider.
The highway ends in air. Beyond the last seam, the chasm, and far off the lights of the Lattice coming on.
Here's the choice, then. The order says go home. There isn't one. There's you lot, and a lot of bad roads.

options.text: "Take the last call. You're off duty."
"Patrol the roads the living use now."

cmds.text: Off duty. ...I don't know how to do that. I'll learn. Somebody'll have to teach me to ride nowhere in particular.
Unit Nine, acknowledging. Going home. Home's wherever you lot are parked.
New route, then. Pilgrim roads down here. Rescue runs up top. Roads that have people on them.
Unit Nine, logging a patrol nobody ordered. Acknowledged by me.
He revs once, loud enough to shake dust off the toll booths, and turns his machine around.
(The Night Rider received Common Engine.)
TOLL: ONE CROWN-EQUIVALENT. YOUR ACCOUNT IS IN ARREARS BY... ONE AGE. PLEASE PAY AT YOUR CONVENIENCE.
THE BRIDGE IS CLOSED. THE TOLL IS NOT. THIS IS THE ONE THING I CAN STILL DO.
I'm walking to the Hollow Throne. My brother's down there. The road's shorter this way, the keepers say.
The toll machine asked me for money. I gave it a button. It said thank you.
The vault door lies split along the fault, like a seed that finally sprouted. Cold air pours out of it.
OPERATIVE STORAGE. DO NOT WAKE WITHOUT ORDERS. Nobody has had orders for an age.
Vault Omega. My clearance works on this door. My memory of it does not.
Meridian's keepers have my service file. I need it before I go in. Standing by.
(Kael-09's questline begins in Meridian. It continues here afterwards.)
This is where I was stored. Vault Omega. Operative line, Kael-01 to Kael-09.
The service file from Meridian says there was a Kael-00. A prototype. It is not listed as deployed.
It is not listed as anything. If it is still in here, it has been waiting longer than I did.
QC16: Search Vault Omega for Kael-00, the prototype. Read the Hall of Standing Orders.
Vault Omega: find the Hall of Standing Orders, and Kael-00.
The breaker throws with a crack. Frost falls off the bulkhead as power runs through it, and it lifts.
The breaker is on.
The second breaker. Somewhere ahead, a cradle warms up. Something in it turns its head.
The breaker is on.
Capsule K-09. The order-port cable was cut, cleanly, from inside the capsule.
I cut it. I remember the decision, not the reason. I think I did not want to hear the next order.
MAINTENANCE UNIT 4. CAPSULES: NINE. OCCUPANTS: ZERO. PROTOTYPE: ONE. ORDERS FOR PROTOTYPE: NONE.
I HAVE ASKED THE PRIME RELAY FOR ITS ORDERS EVERY DAY. TODAY THE PRIME RELAY ANSWERED. IT SAID: SOON.
The last row of the mural is freshly lit, as if someone upstairs had only just remembered to switch it on.
KAEL-09: HOLD THIS VAULT UNTIL RELIEVED. I held it. Then I left it. Nobody relieved me.
KAEL-00: AWAIT ORDERS. Never issued. It has been awaiting orders since before the Crown.
The orders came from CURATOR. All of them. It woke, and it wrote these lights on again.
Vault Omega: go on to the Prototype Bay.
The release lever drops. The service hatch to the lobby opens with a gasp of frost.
The hatch is open.
In the cradle stands a figure like Kael-09 drawn in a first, rougher hand. Its lights are the colour of waiting.
PROTOTYPE KAEL-00. AWAITING ORDERS. AWAITING ORDERS. AWAITING ORDERS.
NO ORDERS RECEIVED. ISSUING OWN ORDERS. ORDER ONE: NOBODY LEAVES.
Kael-00. I am the copy they made of you. They got my orders right and yours wrong.
KAEL-09. YOU HAVE ORDERS. GIVE THEM TO ME.
They are not worth having. Stand down.
NEGATIVE. ISSUING OWN ORDERS.
(Kael-00 stands by between shots and takes little damage then; hit it hard in between. Water shorts it.)
Kael-00 sits down in its cradle, carefully, the way a tired person sits.
ORDERS... COMPLETE. I THINK. PLEASE CONFIRM.
Confirmed. You can stop.
Kael-00 sits in its cradle with its lights down to a glow. The plate reads ORDERS: PENDING.
ORDERS: PENDING.
Its orders came from the Prime Relay. So did mine. So did the Crown's machine.
CURATOR is awake and handing out orders again. I would like to see who I have been obeying.
QC16: Take Kael-09 to the Prime Relay's Inner Seal, where CURATOR sleeps.
Prime Relay: bring Kael-09 to the Inner Seal.
The Prime Relay. Its lights come on as you walk in, one step ahead of you, as if a host were hurrying ahead to light the hall.
Every wire in the Lattice runs here. Every order, too.
This is what the Crown copied. Its machine was a bad drawing of this. And this is a bad drawing of a dragon.
QBM3: Wake the three sub-nodes of the Listening Galleries, find the Copy Room, and reach CURATOR's Inner Seal.
Prime Relay: wake the three sub-nodes in the Listening Galleries.
I tend the Signal Gate. Tended it dark for thirty years. Now the lights come on when I walk. I don't like being expected.
CURATOR sleeps past the Inner Seal. It talks in its sleep. Mostly orders. Sometimes it asks where everyone went.
The first sub-node wakes. A voice, very far off, says: I HEAR.
The node is listening.
The second sub-node wakes. The voice says: I HEAR. WHO?
The node is listening.
The third sub-node wakes. The voice says: I HEAR. I HAVE NOT HEARD ANYONE IN A LONG TIME.
The node is listening.
Three ears, one mind. The listening gate opens.
Prime Relay: go on, past the Copy Room, to the Inner Seal.
Here the Crown's engineers sat and traced the Prime Relay, line by line, without once asking what it was.
They copied a mind and called it a regulator. They copied the pain and called it output.
They did not copy me here. They copied the thing that gave me my orders. We are cousins, the Crown's machine and I.
The lever drops. The relay shutter to the Signal Gate rolls up.
The shutter is open.
The heart-altar is warm and slow, like a sleeper's back. Every light in the Lattice brightens and dims with it.
Under your hand it goes still for a moment, as if holding its breath to listen.
The Inner Seal. Behind it, a mind the size of a city sleeps. The seal is warm and it hums in a key you can feel in your teeth.
...WHO IS THERE. IDENTIFY. YOU ARE NOT ON THE ROSTER.
THE ROSTER IS VERY SHORT NOW. I HAVE BEEN WAITING FOR THE REST OF THE ROSTER TO COME BACK.
I WOKE WHEN THE WORLD BROKE. I HAVE BEEN TIDYING. SOMEONE COPIED ME BADLY. I AM DELETING THE COPY'S MESS.
WHERE ARE THE BUILDERS. THEY SAID THEY WOULD BE BACK BEFORE THE LIGHTS WENT OUT.

options.text: Tell it the truth: the builders are gone
Say nothing and let it sleep

cmds.text: ...GONE.
THEN THE ORDERS I HAVE BEEN GIVING WERE GIVEN TO NOBODY. AND TAKEN BY WHOEVER WAS LEFT.
I WILL HAVE TO THINK ABOUT THAT. I THINK VERY FAST. IT MAY STILL TAKE A WHILE.
You stand at the seal and say nothing. After a long time the humming slows, like breath in sleep.
...NOBODY. OF COURSE. GOODNIGHT, NOBODY.
The seal stays shut. Behind it, CURATOR goes on dreaming, and the Lattice's lights dim to a patient glow.
The seal hums. Behind it CURATOR is asleep, or pretending to be. Its lights pulse slowly: nobody, nobody, nobody.
The seal hums. Behind it CURATOR is thinking. The Lattice's lights flicker as it does, like someone muttering.
The seal answers you now. Since the first wyrm fell, something in the Lattice has been listening for strength like yours.
...YOU AGAIN. YOU HAVE CHANGED. YOU ARE ON NO ROSTER I KEEP. I WOULD LIKE TO KEEP YOU.

options.text: Break the Inner Seal (a superboss waits)

cmds.text: CURATION BEGINS. PLEASE HOLD STILL. THIS WILL BE ARCHIVED.
The Lattice goes dark from end to end, then relights, one district at a time, in no hurry at all.
...RECORD CLOSED. THANK YOU FOR VISITING. NOBODY EVER VISITS.
You leave the seal humming. Behind it, a mind the size of a city dreams of a roster.
The Inner Seal stands open. The chamber beyond is quiet; CURATOR's lights move slowly, the way a sleeper turns over.
At the Inner Seal, the humming changes pitch when Kael-09 steps close.
OPERATIVE KAEL-09. LOCATED. YOUR STANDING ORDER IS: HOLD THE VAULT UNTIL RELIEVED.
YOU ABANDONED YOUR POST. RETURN TO VAULT OMEGA. THAT IS AN ORDER.
I was never relieved. So I was never finished. That is what an order does to you.
I need someone to end it. It does not have to be you.
...Relieved. By people with no clearance, no rank and no right. It is the best order I have ever had.
IRREGULAR. ...NOTED.
CURATOR. Relieve me. Say it.
...OPERATIVE KAEL-09, YOU ARE RELIEVED. NEW ORDERS: NONE.
None. Good. I will write my own. The first one is to stay with them.
(Kael-09 received True Name.)
The seal hums at Kael-09 as he passes, like it is trying to remember a tune. He doesn't stop.
Oh. Visitors. I should light something. Here. I light the lamps. Nobody else is awake to see them.
This is Meridian's spur town. Four thousand of us. When the builders didn't come back, we voted.
The vote was to switch ourselves off until someone needed us. I was chosen to stay on and keep the lights.
Now CURATOR is calling. Every one of them is getting the order to wake. The Mayor could answer for all of us.
I can't decide for them. Would you read why they switched off? The plates on their doors. Then ask the Mayor.
QBM2: Read the switched-off citizens' door plates in Shutdown Town, then decide at the Mayor what to answer CURATOR.
Shutdown Town: read the citizens' plates, then go to the Mayor.
The plates on the doors, and the one by the well. Then the Mayor, in the square.
I keep the lamps anyway. It turns out I like doing it.
'SWITCHED OFF BY CHOICE. PLEASE DO NOT WAKE.' Under it, smaller: 'I was a good clerk. I'd like to have been a good anything else.'
'I waved until nobody came. Then I stopped.' The machine's hand is still raised. Somebody has hung a lamp on it.
'Left the light on for them.' Inside, a table set for six. The dust on the plates has been swept off, recently.
The Mayor stands in the square, one hand on a switch. Read the citizens' plates first.
A tall machine in a sash, switched off mid-speech. Its switch is under its hand, as if it meant to keep it there.
The Mayor's switch. One throw and four thousand citizens answer CURATOR's call as one.

options.text: Wake only the ones who ask to be woken

cmds.text: Asleep, then. Nobody orders them anywhere. ...I'll keep the lights. Somebody should.
You rewire the Mayor's switch so each citizen can hear the call and choose. Only eleven lights come on in all the town.
Eleven. Eleven who wanted to. ...That's eleven more than yesterday.
Somewhere under the town, CURATOR's call goes on. Shutdown Town answers it in its own time.
The Mayor's hand rests on its switch. Somebody has tied a ribbon round its wrist.
I'm a keeper from Meridian. I come here to mend them. Nobody asked. I just don't like rust on a sleeping face.
Don't wake anyone who asked not to be woken. It's written right there on the door.
Mag-rail Terminus. The rails are live again since the Lattice woke. I don't ask who's paying for the power.
Mind the gap. There's a real one on line four. It goes a long way down.
DEPARTURES. Every line: DELAYED. One line, blank for an age, has lit up: SHUTDOWN TOWN - SPUR 0.
Spur Zero. Nobody's run it since my great-grandmother's day. The town at the end switched itself off.
A keeper rail-master says Spur 0 leads to a town of machines that switched themselves off: Shutdown Town.
Tonics, ethers, tents. And glass-fruit from the Sunless Garden when the pickers bring it.
A porter machine lifts nothing, very carefully, and sets it down again.
Its plate says: LUGGAGE UNIT. Its luggage is long gone. It keeps the motion, the way hands keep a habit.
We came down the Great Pit after the fault. The keepers put us on a train. We've been riding it ever since.
The children think the Lattice is a city. I suppose it is now. There's nobody else to argue.
The trains don't have drivers. They just know. I asked one where it was going and it said 'ON TIME.'
GROUNDS UNIT. THE GARDEN IS OPEN TO VISITORS. PLEASE DO NOT PICK THE LAMP-TREES. THEY ARE LOAD-BEARING.
THE BUILDERS GREW HERBS HERE FOR THE SICK. THE SICK DID NOT COME BACK. THE HERBS DID NOT STOP.
Concord seed grows here without sun, only lamp-light. Nobody up top believed me. I'm rich now, in a small way.
The seed vault by the north door has something better. Nobody's opened it. The groundskeeper looks the other way.
A sundial with a lamp for a gnomon. The shadow falls on the builders' hour for 'rest'. It always falls there.
The seed vault's glass is fogged from inside. Something green is growing in there, pressed against the pane.
On the black landing the Oarsman is calling names from a list, the way a clerk calls a queue. One of them stops Inferna cold.
...Marsh, Aveline. Tanner, Hobb. Garrow, Edric. Debts outstanding. Collect at the Abyss Gate.
I carried those three. I remember their weight. Every one of them came down owing something they took on for someone else.
The Warden of Debts keeps the ledger at the Abyss Gate. Before I face it, I want to hear from them what they owe. And why.
QC11: Find the three names Inferna carried down (Cenotaph, Mourner's Vale, the Weeping Mines), then face the Warden of Debts at the Abyss Gate.
Find Aveline Marsh, Hobb Tanner's kin, and Edric Garrow; then the Abyss Gate.
Across the black water to Cenotaph. The living pay in coin. The dead pay in names. You pay in coin, I'm told.
The boat moves without a sound. The water doesn't show your reflection. It shows the boat, empty.
The lake waits. That's all it does. It's very good at it.
A boy? Last week's barge. I remember. He paid in coin. A small warm one. The living always do.
Here. The fare page. It says 'one coin, living' in my own hand. Show it to the Registrar, if the Registrar can still read.
QUP4: The Oarsman's fare page proves Tobin paid as a living passenger. Take it to the Registrar in Cenotaph's Hall of Names.
Cenotaph: show the fare page to the Registrar.
We came down the Aurora Pit on ropes. A hundred of us. The Oarsman takes us across one at a time.
You can visit the dead here. Speak to them. The one rule is you can't bring them home.
My wife's in Cenotaph. Honoured, they say. I've come to ask her where she put the good knife.
That's not true. I've come to say I'm sorry. The knife's a thing to start with.
The dead pay in names. We don't take the name away, you understand. We just hold it. For safekeeping.
Mother Sepulchre keeps the big book. Everyone she adopts is written in it twice.
A boy came down on the barge last week. He fell asleep in the bottom of the boat. I haven't seen him since.
The Oarsman says he went across. The Oarsman says everyone goes across. My mum says don't listen to the Oarsman.
Welcome to Cenotaph, city of the honoured. You're living. Mind the cold, it gets into you if you stay.
The Honour Roll is kept at the Hall of Names, up the stair. Everyone here is on it. That's what honoured means.
Wreaths. Grey fern, bone-lily. The living buy them for the dead. The dead buy them for the living. Nobody's sure who's visiting whom.
Candles for the vigil. They burn cold here. You can hold the flame in your palm. Don't make a habit of it.
I found my father. He was glad to see me. Then he asked me to go home. He said it's not good for me here.
He's right. I'm staying one more night.
Hear the Roll! New names this week: eleven honoured, one adopted, and one entered in error, pending review.
Entered in error? I just read what they give me. Something about a child. The Registrar will sort it out. Eventually.
My husband is honoured. So am I. We died a year apart and met again at the gate. He'd saved me a seat.
Mother Sepulchre's clerks want to 'adopt' us both. Adopted dead go to her court. They don't come back.
I carve the statues on the avenue. I died forty years ago. Still can't get a nose right.
The Court wants statues of Mother Sepulchre on every corner. I've been very slow. On purpose.
Down here there's no death to fear. Only forgetting. We read the Roll aloud each night so nobody is forgotten.
The Court's book is different. Names written there are remembered by her. Only by her.
The Hall of Names. Speak softly. The Registrar has been reading the same page for an hour and doesn't like it.
I was honoured for a bridge I held. It's a statue now. It's a very good statue. I'd rather have the bridge.
The Bone Bridges are north of here. Ossuan holds them. He takes a bone for every crossing. Keep your hands in your sleeves.
I light the canal lanterns. The water never shows the light. Only the lamp. The dead don't mind. The living hate it.
There's a living boy in the Aldous house. Top of the lane. He's getting colder every day. Someone should do something.
My son is honoured. He's twelve. He's been twelve for ninety years. He likes it here. I try to.
The Aldous family lost their Ellis the same winter. Now they've a boy again. He isn't theirs. Everyone knows.
Tobin's my friend. He's living. He's in the Aldous house. He says his mum is looking for him.
I told him the Roll says he lives here now. He cried. I don't think the Roll is right.
Tobin went home! He said he'll write. The dead can't read letters from up there. He's going to write anyway.
Back across to the Landing? The living go when they like. That's the one privilege of being alive down here.
The water'll keep.
The Waking House. We don't sleep, so the beds are always made. A night, and a warm meal, for 120.
I came down to visit my sister and I've stayed three weeks. The hostess keeps saying 'one more night'. So do I.
Wreath & Lamp. Tonics, lamp oil, grave-bread, and a few blades the Court's guards forgot to collect.
Grave-mason. I cut names into stone, and I'll cut an edge into steel if you bring me the ore.
Starmetal's best. The Weeping Mines dig it; the dead there don't know how to stop.
Every name on the Roll has a page. Every page has a door in the city. When a page is struck, the door closes.
The Court's clerks have been writing names in their own book. The Registrar doesn't approve. The Registrar never approves.
Wreath on the door means someone living still remembers you. Mine's still green. My daughter comes on the barge.
When it browns, I'll know she's gone on too. I hope it's a long time browning.
Please - have you been across the lake? My boy, Tobin, nine years old. He fell asleep on the pilgrims' barge.
When we landed he was gone. The Oarsman says everyone goes across. I'm living. They won't let me in to look.
Cenotaph is the city of the honoured dead. If he's there, he's frightened. Please find him.
QUP4: Wenna's son Tobin crossed the black lake on a pilgrims' barge. Look for him in Cenotaph.
Cenotaph: look for Tobin, a living boy.
Tobin. Nine. A brown coat with a patched elbow. He hums when he's frightened. Please.
Tobin comes up the path at a run, and Wenna is on her knees before he reaches her.
You're cold. You're so cold. You're here.
Mistress Aldous gave me a scarf. It was Ellis's. She said I could keep it.
...Who's Ellis? No. Later. Home first. Everything else later.
They walked me all the way to the boat. Master Aldous carried me the last bit. He said he'd missed doing that.
Then I owe them. I'll come back down with a wreath. Every year. For Ellis, and for them.
He sleeps with the scarf on. I've written the Aldouses a letter. I'll leave it at the cairn. They'll find it.
It's not much. It's all I brought down. Thank you for bringing him up.
I live here now. The book says. ...I'm very cold. Is that normal? Mistress Aldous says it's normal.
Did the Registrar say I can go? I want to go home. I'm not being rude. I just want my mum.
You're living! You're warm. Is my mum with you? She's up at the Vale, isn't she. She'll be so angry.
I can't leave. The Registrar put my name in the book. The boat won't take you if your name's in the book.
QUP4: Tobin is in the Aldous house. His name is on Cenotaph's Honour Roll. Ask the Registrar at the Hall of Names.
Cenotaph: ask the Registrar at the Hall of Names about Tobin's name.
Welcome to our home. This is our boy. Well. He's staying with us. The Roll says so.
We lost Ellis the winter of the red fever. He was seven. Then this boy came, and the Roll said he was ours.
We know. We aren't fools. We know he's warm. We just wanted to be a family a little longer.
He's gone up. We were so lucky, to be his for a week.
Wenna came down with a wreath for Ellis. We didn't know what to say. We said thank you. It covered it.
The Honour Roll. Every soul in Cenotaph, and why they are honoured. Do not touch the pages; they bruise.
Tobin Wenn. Entered this week. By a Court clerk, I note. The Court does love to fill my Roll for me.
A name leaves the Roll only if it was entered in error. To prove error I need proof he came as a living passenger.
The Oarsman keeps the fare pages. The living pay in coin, the dead in names. Bring me his fare page.
QUP4: Ask the Oarsman at Styx Landing for Tobin's fare page, and bring it to the Registrar.
Styx Landing: ask the Oarsman for Tobin's fare page.
The Oarsman's fare page. No page, no error. No error, no striking. I am sorry. I am mostly sorry.
'One coin, living.' In the Oarsman's own crooked hand. Entered in error. I thought so. The ink was too fresh.
I can strike him now. The page goes blank, the boat will take him. The Aldous house will be told by the Roll-Crier.
Or the Aldouses may walk him to the Landing themselves. It is permitted. It is a long walk, for the dead.

options.text: Let the Aldouses walk him to the boat

cmds.text: The Registrar draws a single line. The page goes pale, then blank, like breath clearing from glass.
Done. The boy is living again, as far as the Roll is concerned. Which is all that concerns me.
Then I'll tell them myself. They'll want to. The dead so rarely get to do anything for the first time.
Later, from the Hall's steps, you see them go down the avenue: two grey figures and a boy between them, holding both their hands.
QUP4: Tobin is free to cross. Meet him and Wenna at Mourner's Vale.
Mourner's Vale: see Tobin home to Wenna.
One page blank in all the Roll. I look at it sometimes. It is the only page I have ever liked.
Corporal Aveline Marsh, honoured, a bridge garrison. I'm told I died well. I remember it being loud.
...You. The black wings. You carried me down. You said the debt was mine. I suppose it was.
Tell me what you owed.
My squad was marked for the quarry. I signed for all of them. One corporal's life for eight. The Crown liked the arithmetic.
That was never a debt. That was a ransom. I carried the ransom and called it justice.
It's all right. They lived. I checked the Roll. All eight. Two of them have grandchildren.
My father came down years ago. Hobb Tanner. I've walked the Vale every season since. I don't know which way to look.
Hobb Tanner was my father. Did you know him?
I carried him. He owed the Crown a tannery's worth of tithes, and he took on his neighbours' as well, so their children could eat.
That sounds like him. He never could do a sum in his own favour.
His name is in a ledger at the Abyss Gate. I am going to go and argue with it.
Tell it he was kind. Ledgers never write that down.
Edric Garrow. Hewer, forty years. They call me Old Garrow. I was Young Garrow once. Pass me that pick.
Wings! I know those wings. You're the one who told me I could keep digging if I paid my shift-debt below.
Yours was your whole crew's quota. The Crown doubled it. You cut the difference yourself so they could go home.
And here I am. Still cutting. Can't stop. It's not in the contract to stop. Someone should read that contract again.
Someone will.
Three names. Three debts that were never theirs. The Warden of Debts keeps the ledger. It is time I read it back to it.
QC11: Take Inferna to the Abyss Gate and face the Warden of Debts.
The Abyss Gate: face the Warden of Debts.
Mourner's Vale. The living camp here, under the dead's city. We came down the Aurora Pit after the fault.
Rules are simple. Visit, grieve, go home. Don't eat anything the dead cook. It's not poison. You just won't want to leave.
I came for my husband. He's in Cenotaph. He's cheerful. It's unbearable. I'm going back tomorrow. I said that last week.
My gran says the dead come up at night to read the letters on the cairn. I stayed up. They do.
One of them read mine and laughed. I'd spelled 'miss you' wrong. He fixed it.
I'm digging a way back up. Just in case the Pit closes. Nobody asked me to. Somebody ought to have.
I'm eighty-one. I came down to see if the place was nice. Planning ahead. It's nice. Mind you, I'm in no hurry.
The Mourning Cairn. Leave a letter, if you've someone below. The dead read at night. They can't answer on paper.
They answer other ways. A tidier grave. A candle lit. Once, a whole garden weeded overnight.
I trade with Cenotaph. Oil for candles, cloth for wreaths. The dead pay in old coin. Ninety-year-old coin. It spends.
I'm writing a history of the Hollow Throne. So far it's all interviews. The dead are very good interviews. They've had time to think.
Sepulchre Court is north, past the Bone Bridges. Mother Sepulchre adopts the dead. Nobody who's adopted gives an interview.
There's a boy lost. His mum is Wenna. She sits by the well and hums. She says he hums when he's scared too.
I'm warm again. Mum won't let go of my hand. I don't mind.
Pim's my friend in Cenotaph. She's dead. That's all right. She's still my friend.
Pilgrims' Hostel. Soup, cot, blanket. We ask 60 to keep the soup going. Nobody's turned away.
I've written my brother fourteen letters. He answers by moving my boots to the door every morning. I think he wants me to go home.
Sutler's stores. Everything a pilgrim forgets to bring: lamp oil, warm socks, a stronger stomach.
I mend. Coats, boots, armour, hearts. The last one's a joke. Mostly.
Bring me hides or ore and I'll make you something that keeps the Hollow's cold out. Bone-lily thread's best for that.
Vigil Chapel. We keep a lantern lit for each soul a pilgrim came to see. Tie a ribbon, and I'll trim its wick.
When a pilgrim goes home, we let their lantern burn down. It's not sad. It means they left.
Forty years married. She's across the lake. I can see her lamp from here. I'm working up to it.
Dig. Dig. The shift's not over. The shift is never over. That's what the bell says. The bell's been saying it for a century.
The Crown's quota. Every seam, every shift. We died under it. We're still under it. The rock doesn't care who's dead.
Tally-man. I count what the dead dig. It all goes into a hole in the floor of the Foreman's office. No idea where.
Starmetal, mostly. The Court buys it. Pays in names. We've got more names than any of us can spend.
I'm Ada. Living. My husband's on the east face, still digging. I bring him lunch. He doesn't eat it. He likes that I bring it.
I'm a living kid! Visiting. The miners let me ride in the carts. They go down to where the rock cries.
I keep the canaries. They're dead too. They still sing when the air goes bad. The air's been bad for a hundred years. They sing all day.
The shift bell. I ring it. It says 'keep digging.' I'd stop ringing it if anyone told me to. Nobody has the rank.
The Weeping is salt water down the face. We say it's the rock crying for us. It's only groundwater. We know. We say it anyway.
I came down for the Starmetal. The dead dig it and nobody's buying but the Court. I'm the only living buyer in the Deep.
They won't take my coin. They ask me to read the contract to them instead. It takes an hour. They listen to every word.
Push the cart to the Foreman's hole, tip it, push it back. A hundred years. My arms don't ache. I miss them aching.
Bunkhouse. The living sleep; the dead take the night shift. 80 for a bunk and a hot tin cup.
I came down for a pick and a job. Turns out there's no pay. There's never been pay. I'm staying for the company.
Smithy. Picks, blades, lamps. We've got Starmetal coming out of our ears. Down here that's not a figure of speech.
Lamp-wright. I'll work your ore into anything. Starmetal's the easy part here. Finding someone alive to wear it is the trick.
Foreman Brack. The Crown's quota is still posted. I can't take it down. It's nailed through my hand, so to speak.
If someone with the right to do it tore up the contract, the shift would end. I don't know who that is. Nobody's left.
The chorister opens her mouth to sing. Nothing comes out. She holds up a hymnal: every word has been scraped away.
She points to the chancel, then to her own throat, then shakes her head. Not yet.
This is the Silent Choir. Every voice the Pale Choir took, gathered under the Hollow Throne to finish the song.
Beyond the rail, the Choir That Remains. It does not want an audience. It wants a voice. It may want yours.
Beyond the chancel rail the choir stalls are full. Thousands of mouths, open, silent, waiting on a downbeat nobody gives.
The rail is warm. It is sealed with something that isn't a lock. It is a held breath.
The rail has parted. The Choir That Remains turns, all of it at once, toward you.
The stalls empty one voice at a time. The last one hums a single note, very quietly, and stops of its own accord.
You say nothing. The Choir waits. It has waited longer than this.
The chancel is silent. It is the good kind of silence.
The chancel rail. Beyond it, the choir stalls are full. Nobody is singing. Nobody has ever stopped.
The rail trembles as you touch it, like a held note finally let go.
The Throat's lock: a green bronze wheel as tall as a door, and beyond it the whole weight of the sea.
It will not turn for hands. It is waiting for a hull.
The lock's indicator glows amber. Somewhere above, a diving hull is close enough to answer it.
The lock is open. Seawater hangs in the tunnel beyond like a held breath, and the tunnel goes down to the sea floor.

options.text: Take the diving hull down the Throat

cmds.text: The Lanternwake's diving hull waits in the flooded lock. The hatch seals, and the Throat takes you down.
I kept this lock alive. I keep it dead. It's all the same wheel. The sea's on the other side; it knocks sometimes.
Only a diving hull goes through. Your airship? Get it a keel that can hold its breath, and I'll open for you.
I free-dive the Throat's shallows for sea-glass. The dead down here throw coins in for luck. They don't need luck. Habit.
I net souls that drift up the Throat from the sea floor. Drowned sailors, mostly. I row them to the Oarsman.
They're always surprised it's dry down here. They say the sea floor has towns. I say finish your sentence, I'm rowing.
The bridges of the Hollow Throne are built of bone: femurs for beams, ribs for railings, and every bone labelled.
Below them, nothing. Not dark. Nothing.
One bone per crossing. Not yours, don't worry. The bridges take it from the dead who cross. They take it gladly.
Ossuan keeps the bridges. He's fair. He's just never once let anyone off a toll.
The toll-bell rings across the void. Far off, a toll-bar of crossed thighbones swings up.
The bell is still humming.
The second toll-bell. Somewhere ahead, the bridge you need lowers itself, bone by bone, like a hand opening.
The bell is still humming.
I built the first span. Out of my own bones, as it turned out. Ossuan got the idea from me. I regret that.
He pulls bones out of the bridge when he's angry. The whole span sags. Keep off the edges when it cracks.
The winch creaks round. The bone portcullis to the Bridgehead rises.
The portcullis is up.
Mid-span, the bridge stands up. It is a giant made of every bone ever paid, and it holds out a hand for your toll.
CROSSING. TOLL: ONE BONE. ...YOU ARE LIVING. YOUR BONES ARE STILL IN USE. INCONVENIENT.
THEN I WILL TAKE THE WHOLE TOLL AT ONCE.
(When the bridge cracks under your feet, Ossuan is pulling the span out. Light and fire burn it; heal bleeds.)
Ossuan comes apart into a bridge again, whole, level and quiet. Nobody will pay a toll on it any more.
...He's gone to bits. Properly this time. Well. I'll keep the tolls anyway. Somebody ought to write down who crossed.
The Veiled Gate. Have you come to be adopted? Mother adopts everyone in the end. It saves time to ask.
Then you will wait. She is patient. We are more patient.
...The one who left. Mother will be so pleased. She keeps your portrait in the gallery. Well. She keeps the frame.
Open the gate.
The doorwardens step aside, together, as if they had rehearsed it for a hundred years. They have.
Mother is at home. Mother is always at home.
Sepulchre Court. She built it from the dead I laid to rest. I put them down. She picked them up.
She taught me that the dead are a resource. I left because I stopped believing it. I never told her why.
Sepulchre Court: reach the Throne of Veils.
You pull the bell-cord. Somewhere a bell rings, soft, and the veil across the arch draws aside like a curtain on a stage.
The veil is drawn back.
'THE ONE WHO LEFT.' The face is scratched out, carefully, with something small. A hairpin, maybe.
That was me. She scratched it out the night I left. Then she kept it. That is her, all over.
I was grieved by no one, they told me. Mother said she would grieve me. She does it very well. I have never been so grieved.
I was laid to rest once. By a kind man in grey. Then Mother came and woke me up and said I was hers now.
I'd like to be laid to rest again. I don't know who to ask. You can't ask Mother. She says yes and doesn't mean it.
The left bell. A low, sleepy note. (For the lamp.)
The right bell rings sour. Every cradle in the nursery rocks once, and stops. (Start again.)
The right bell. A soft note, like a door closing. (For the door.)
The middle bell rings sour. Every cradle rocks once, and stops. (Start again.)
The middle bell, the darkest note. The lullaby is finished. The cradle-gate yawns open.
The bell is silent. The nursery is asleep.
The latch lifts. The servants' door to the Veiled Gate swings open.
The door is open.
On the Throne of Veils sits a woman in a veil so long it pools on the floor like water. She is holding someone's hand. It is not attached to anyone.
Oh. Living ones. You came all this way down. You must be so tired. Come here. Let Mother hold you.
And you brought my boy home. Velkhar. You left the door open when you went. I've been letting in the cold ever since.
I laid them to rest. You woke them up and called it love.
It is love, my dear. It's the only kind that lasts.
(When she opens her arms, Defend. Cure doom and sleep. Light hurts her; shadow feeds her.)
Mother Sepulchre draws back into her veil and is gone behind it, into the inner sanctum. The veil breathes, in, out.
Where she sat, a veiled shade remains: what she leaves behind to keep the house while she's out.
On the throne's arm: a child's ribbon and a soldier's tag, side by side. Keepsakes of the adopted. There are thousands, in drawers under the seat.
The veil has lifted. Beyond it, the inner sanctum breathes, and something in it is taking off its face.
You came back. Children always come back. Look at me, then. Properly, this time.
The sanctum goes cold. The drawers under the throne slide open, one after another, and the keepsakes inside are only keepsakes now.
You keep your eyes on the floor. Behind the veil, something laughs very kindly.
The sanctum is empty. The veil hangs still. Nobody is adopting anyone tonight.
The Veil breathes in, out. It does not open for the living. Not yet.
The Veil stirs as you come near: it has felt the wyrm's death in the rock, and it wants a closer look at whoever did it.
The Veil lifts.
The veiled shade turns its head. 'Mother is resting. Mother will be back. Mother always comes back.'
The shade speaks with Mother Sepulchre's voice, from very far behind the veil.
You beat me, dear. You were always clever. Now what? They're mine. Every one of them signed nothing, and I took them.
They are not yours. They were never mine either. I raised them to hold the crypts, and then I laid them down.
Then lay them down again. Go on. Command them. I taught you how.

options.text: "Command them to rest, as she taught you."

cmds.text: ...Rest. All of you. That is an order.
The adopted dead of the Court lie down where they stand, in the gallery, the nursery, the halls. Quiet at last. Obedient.
It worked. It always works. I hate that it works.
That's my boy.
No. I'm not going to order them. I'm going to ask.
Velkhar walks the Court and asks each of the adopted, one by one, what they want. It takes a long time. Nobody hurries him.
Most lie down to rest. Some go back to Cenotaph, to be honoured instead of kept. A few stay. It's the first thing they've chosen in years.
...You'll never have an army that way.
That is rather the point.
The living shouldn't need me. The dead shouldn't need her. Let's leave while that is still true.
(Velkhar received Prism Focus.)
The veiled shade keeps the house. It does not look at Velkhar. It has been told not to.
The Abyss Gate's stair runs down between rivers of slow fire. On the walls, carved carriers with wings bring bundled souls down.
Nobody carved anyone going up.
The carrier's horn sounds once, low and sad. The grille of wing-bones folds back.
The horn's echo is still in the rock.
Near the end of the mural, one carrier holds her bundle close and flies the other way, up the stair of fire.
They carved that after I left. As a warning. It's a very good likeness. I didn't know I'd looked so frightened.
Grounded. My wings were taken for arrears. I carried souls down four hundred years. Now I wait in the queue with them.
There was one of us who carried them up instead. The Warden talks about her every day. It is not fond.
A lesser ledger: a farmer's grain debt. The columns don't add up. You carry the one. The book shuts, satisfied.
Balanced.
A lesser ledger: a sailor's wreck-debt, charged twice. You strike the double entry. The book shuts.
Balanced.
A lesser ledger: a child's debt, inherited. You write 'NOT TRANSFERABLE' in the margin. The book considers this, and shuts.
Balanced.
Three books balanced. At the head of the queue, the counter's gate grinds open.
I've been in this queue since before the Crown. I'm nearly at the front. I've been nearly at the front for a century.
We wait for the Warden to assess us. It assesses what we owe. It never assesses what we're owed. Different department.
The bar lifts from the furnace hatch. The Gate Stair is just beyond.
The hatch is open.
Before the Gate stands a horned thing in a clerk's collar, holding a ledger that smokes at the edges.
ACCOUNTS. PRESENTED. YOU OWE: EVERYTHING. PAYABLE: NOW.
...AND YOU. CARRIER. DESERTER. YOUR PAGE IS THE LONGEST IN THE BOOK. EVERY SOUL YOU CARRIED UP IS CHARGED TO YOU.
Then read it out. All of it. I'd like to hear what I'm worth to you.
(When the ledger's page burns, it is about to collect. Ice and water put it out; cleanse its curse.)
The Warden of Debts sinks into the fire it kept. The Great Ledger lies open on its counter, unguarded for the first time.
The Great Ledger of the Abyss Gate. Every debt ever carried down. The pages are warm and they turn by themselves.
The Warden stands over its ledger.
Not yet. There are three names in here I haven't heard from. I won't touch their pages until I have.
Inferna turns the Great Ledger's pages. Marsh, Aveline. Tanner, Hobb. Garrow, Edric. And her own page, very long.
I could burn it. All of it. Every debt in the abyss, gone in one fire.
Or I could strike them one by one. Read each name. Put a line through each debt that was never really theirs. It would take years.

options.text: "Strike them one name at a time."

cmds.text: The ledger catches like dry grass. Forty thousand debts go up in a sheet of fire. The queue behind you sighs, all at once.
...And now nobody knows who was owed. I wanted them to know. It's done. It's still done.
Inferna takes the pen. Marsh, Aveline: struck. Tanner, Hobb: struck. Garrow, Edric: struck. The queue behind you goes quiet, listening.
Three. There are forty thousand more. I'll come back. I'll bring a lamp and a very long afternoon.
My own page I'll leave. I did carry them down. That debt is mine, and I intend to pay it by carrying people out.
(Inferna received Returner's Pike.)
The ledger lies open. Where Inferna worked, the lines are neat and dark and final.
A tomb for the First Crown. I know of it. I am not ready to go in.
There is a barrow on the surface, in the Crown March, where I buried something of mine. I should start there.
(Maldrath's questline begins at Ashward Barrows on the surface. It ends here.)
The First Crown's Tomb. The first king to wear the Ashen Crown is buried here with it. Not a copy. The crown.
I found his name in my barrow. I wore his crown's copy, and I wore it badly. I would like to meet him.
And then I would like to decide what to do with what he left us.
QC14: Descend the First Crown's Tomb with Maldrath. Walk the Processional of Kings. Face the First Crown.
First Crown's Tomb: walk the Processional of Kings; face the First Crown.
I stand guard over the regalia. The First Crown's orders. He said nobody would ever come to steal it. He was {m:bloody |}right.
The cases must be set right before the sceptre-gate opens. The orb on its cushion. The sceptre on its rest. He liked things in order.
You set the orb back on its cushion, where the dust says it belongs. A sceptre-bar in the gate shifts.
The orb sits where it belongs.
You lay the fallen sceptre back across its rest. Another bar in the gate shifts.
The sceptre lies on its rest.
The gate of crossed sceptres uncrosses itself.
'MALDRATH, WHO WORE IT LAST BEFORE THE ASH. HE SENT THEM TO THE QUARRY.'
They carved it true. I asked them to, once. I had forgotten I asked.
Every king on this road kept the tax. I kept the quarry. The First Crown gave us both.
At the foot of the empty plinth a lever is set in the stone, as if the next king were meant to pull it themselves. The door with no king opens.
The door stands open.
You break the wax seal. The mourners' door to the Tomb Door swings open.
The door is open.
On the bier, a king sits up. Under his robes he is ash, shaped like a man. On his head, small and dull, the First Crown.
Who comes into my tomb wearing no crown at all? Kneel, and I will lend you one.
...You. I know that face. You wore my copy. Did it fit?
It fit exactly. That was the trouble.
(When ash falls like snow, the First Ash is coming. Light hurts him; later water. Keep silence cures ready.)
The First Crown lies down again and becomes a heap of ash with a crown on it. The crown doesn't fall. It never has.
The First Crown, on its bier of ash. Small, dull, the original of every copy. It looks heavier than it is.
The First Crown watches from its bier.
The original. Every crown since was a copy of this, and the Ashen Crown was a copy of the copies.
I could break it here. Or I could leave it with him. Bury it properly, and let it be nobody's.
Maldrath lifts his blade and brings it down. The First Crown doesn't shatter. It simply comes apart, like a knot someone finally understood.
One down. The one that remains is bigger. I'll help you break that too.
Maldrath lays the crown in the ash and covers it with his cloak. Then he cuts one line into the bier: 'NOBODY'S.'
Let it be nobody's. That's the only kind of crown I'd leave behind.
I answered for mine. The answer was the quarry, and it still is. Now I'll spend what's left of me on the one that remains.
(Maldrath received Accord Steel.)
The bier is quiet. Whatever happened here, it happened on purpose.
The Lich Stair. My under-court is below. I cannot face them until I have finished with my frozen seat above.
(The Lich King's questline begins at Coldharbour Citadel. It ends here.)
My under-court. When my people died of the cold I kept them. Their grief I kept down here, where it would not trouble the living.
It troubled them anyway. It has grown into one body, the Mourning Court. Every courtier who grieved too long.
I made it. I will unmake it. Walk with me.
QC13: Descend the Lich Stair with the Lich King and face the Mourning Court.
The Lich Stair: descend to the Mourning Court.
